description: Enriched seed vocabulary for the Defne parent-child pilot. Includes the parent backlog terms with reviewed definitions and multiple approved examples for contextual practice.

entries.definition: Left empty or alone by people, often because it was no longer wanted or safe, so it is not looked after.
entries.example: The abandoned house at the end of our road had broken windows and ivy over the porch; neighbours said no one had lived there for years and bats nested in the eaves.
examples: The abandoned house at the end of our road had broken windows and ivy over the porch; neighbours said no one had lived there for years and bats nested in the eaves.
I found an abandoned puppy shivering under the bin on a rainy day, and we wrapped it in an old jumper before asking the rescue centre for help.
During the walk, we passed an abandoned railway platform where wildflowers grew between the rails and rabbits made tunnels in the soil.
entries.spellingNote: Ends with -ed because it describes something left in the past; base verb is abandon.

entries.definition: A person's home or the place where someone lives or stays.
entries.example: Grandpa said his little cottage by the sea would always be his proper abode, where he kept maps and tiny shells from every holiday he remembered.
examples: Grandpa said his little cottage by the sea would always be his proper abode, where he kept maps and tiny shells from every holiday he remembered.
When the school trip arranged different rooms, my temporary abode in the hall was a sleeping bag on the floor, but I still loved the late-night games.
The judge asked the witness to state their usual abode before the hearing, so the court knew where letters and documents should be sent.
entries.spellingNote: Short word: a-b-o-d-e; it means a home, not the verb 'abide'.

entries.definition: more than enough; plentiful
entries.example: After weeks of spring rain, the allotment had abundant strawberries, beans, and mint. Grandma filled one basket, then laughed because the plants still looked almost untouched.
examples: After weeks of spring rain, the allotment had abundant strawberries, beans, and mint. Grandma filled one basket, then laughed because the plants still looked almost untouched.
In the rock pool, tiny creatures were abundant once the children looked closely. What seemed like plain water was crowded with shrimp, snails, and flickering fish.
The night sky above the desert looked abundant with stars because there were no city lights to hide them. Defne could see so many points of light that counting felt impossible.
entries.spellingNote: Starts with a-bun, like 'a bun'.

entries.definition: Moved or happened faster than before; increased speed or rate.
entries.example: As the storm clouds arrived, the rain accelerated so quickly that puddles turned into small streams across the playground within minutes.
examples: As the storm clouds arrived, the rain accelerated so quickly that puddles turned into small streams across the playground within minutes.
When the coach shouted 'Go!', Mina accelerated down the final straight and overtook three runners to win the school race in a burst of speed.
The learning programme accelerated once we used the new games and explanations, and the whole class remembered facts much faster than before.
entries.spellingNote: Has a double 'c' early on: a-c-c-e-l-e-r-a-t-e-d.

entries.definition: Exactly correct or true, with no mistakes.
entries.example: Our science teacher told us that to record an accurate temperature reading we must keep the thermometer away from direct sunlight and not touch the bulb.
examples: Our science teacher told us that to record an accurate temperature reading we must keep the thermometer away from direct sunlight and not touch the bulb.
I tried to draw the map with accurate labels so my friend could find the hidden oak tree, the stream, and the little bridge without getting lost.
The clock in the hall is accurate to the minute, which helped the whole team arrive at the match on time and avoid a frantic dash.
entries.spellingNote: Has two c's in a row: a-c-c-u-r-a-t-e.

entries.definition: To get, gain or learn something, often through effort, buying, or time.
entries.example: By reading every day and asking questions, Lucy hoped to acquire new words that would make her writing much more exciting and clear to her teacher.
examples: By reading every day and asking questions, Lucy hoped to acquire new words that would make her writing much more exciting and clear to her teacher.
The museum's scheme lets children acquire a free book after they visit three galleries and answer a simple quiz about the exhibits they saw.
To acquire the special badge, we had to learn how to tie five different knots and show the leader we could do them without help.
entries.spellingNote: Contains 'qu' in the middle: a-c-q-u-i-r-e.

entries.definition: To change the way you do things so they suit a new situation or condition.
entries.example: When we moved to a hillier town, my bike shoes took longer to dry, so I had to adapt my morning routine and leave earlier to avoid being late.
examples: When we moved to a hillier town, my bike shoes took longer to dry, so I had to adapt my morning routine and leave earlier to avoid being late.
A chameleon can adapt its skin colour to hide from predators or show friends, which helps it stay safe among leaves and branches.
During the flood drill, the class had to adapt the plan quickly because the usual exit was blocked, and we used the playground gate instead.
entries.spellingNote: One 'p' in adapt; don't confuse it with 'adopt'.

entries.definition: Able to change or be changed easily to suit different conditions or uses.
entries.example: An adaptable jacket with zip-off sleeves is perfect for camping because it becomes a coat in cold weather and a light top when the sun comes out.
examples: An adaptable jacket with zip-off sleeves is perfect for camping because it becomes a coat in cold weather and a light top when the sun comes out.
The new tablet proved adaptable for drawing, reading and schoolwork, so Sita kept it for homework, art club and quiet reading on the sofa.
A fox is adaptable in the countryside; it eats different foods and uses barns, hedges or small caves for shelter when the seasons change.
entries.spellingNote: Formed from adapt + -able; keep both a's: a-d-a-p-t-a-b-l-e.

entries.definition: Very good at something because of practice; skilled and quick to do it well.
entries.example: Riya was adept at climbing the ancient oak in the park; she moved silently and reached the highest branch where she could see the whole town.
examples: Riya was adept at climbing the ancient oak in the park; she moved silently and reached the highest branch where she could see the whole town.
Our chess club captain is adept at spotting threats and planning moves three steps ahead, which makes him very hard for other players to beat.
The gardener was adept with pruning shears, knowing exactly where to cut each branch so the roses would bloom fuller the next spring.
entries.spellingNote: Ends with -ept (a-d-e-p-t); do not spell it 'adeptt' or mix with 'apt'.

entries.definition: Good enough for a need or purpose, though not excellent or extra.
entries.example: We packed an adequate picnic that filled our tummies during the long hike, with sandwiches, apples, and a small treat for energy breaks.
examples: We packed an adequate picnic that filled our tummies during the long hike, with sandwiches, apples, and a small treat for energy breaks.
The old torch was adequate for finding the path in the dark wood, though a stronger beam would have made the walk easier and less worrying.
Her homework was adequate to pass the test, but the teacher suggested extra practice to raise her work from okay to excellent.
entries.spellingNote: Starts with ad-, then 'equate' sound: a-d-e-q-u-a-t-e.

entries.definition: Either a person who strongly supports an idea or leader, or something that sticks firmly to a surface.
entries.example: The small crowd of adherent fans gathered outside the theatre, holding homemade banners and singing songs to welcome the actors after the final show.
examples: The small crowd of adherent fans gathered outside the theatre, holding homemade banners and singing songs to welcome the actors after the final show.
The bandage remained adherent to the cut during the puddle jump, keeping it clean until we could get proper plasters from the nurse.
In the debate one adherent of the new rule spoke clearly and calmly about why the playground needed changes to keep everyone safer.
entries.spellingNote: Related to 'adhere' (to stick); spell as a-d-h-e-r-e-n-t.

entries.definition: Next to or touching something else; very near.
entries.example: The classroom adjacent to ours had a roaring science experiment, so we could hear fizzing and the excited voices next door through the thin wall.
examples: The classroom adjacent to ours had a roaring science experiment, so we could hear fizzing and the excited voices next door through the thin wall.
A picnic blanket was spread on the grass adjacent to the pond, and we watched ducks swim by while eating sandwiches.
The two shops are adjacent on the high street, so it only takes a minute to walk from the baker's to the toyshop when you need both.
entries.spellingNote: Starts with 'adj-' like 'adjust' and ends '-cent'; spell a-d-j-a-c-e-n-t.

entries.definition: To look at someone or something with pleasure and respect because they are good, brave, beautiful or skilful.
entries.example: I admire the way my friend stood up for the new pupil and helped them join our game, because that made everyone feel included and brave.
examples: I admire the way my friend stood up for the new pupil and helped them join our game, because that made everyone feel included and brave.
At the gallery I had to stop and admire the bright painting that showed a storm at sea; its colours looked like crashing waves and lightning.
We all admire the old lighthouse keeper for working through fog and storms to keep ships safe, a job that needs patience and care.
entries.spellingNote: Spell with 'm' then 'ire': a-d-m-i-r-e; not 'admier'.

entries.definition: Permission to enter a place, join an event or school, or the fee that someone pays to go in.
entries.example: I felt nervous at the museum because the sign said we needed a timed admission slot, so we queued outside until our admission time began and hurried in.
examples: I felt nervous at the museum because the sign said we needed a timed admission slot, so we queued outside until our admission time began and hurried in.
At the school fair, Mum kept my raffle ticket safe because the teacher said admission to the magician's tent would be by ticket only.
Sam forgot his payment and worried he might miss admission to the swimming gala when the gate was closing and the teacher called his name.
entries.spellingNote: Admission has a double 's' and ends with '-sion' like the word 'mission'.

entries.definition: A difficult or unlucky situation that causes trouble, such as illness, loss or other hard times.
entries.example: The hikers faced real adversity when the storm knocked out their map and one boot tore, so they had to share supplies while they found shelter.
examples: The hikers faced real adversity when the storm knocked out their map and one boot tore, so they had to share supplies while they found shelter.
After the flood, the town showed how people can meet adversity together by fixing homes and helping neighbours with food and tools.
Jade kept practising her piano through family adversity and surprised everyone by playing a calm piece at the fundraising concert.
entries.spellingNote: Remember 'adver-' then '-sity' like 'university' but with 'ad' at the start.

entries.definition: Friendly and pleasant; easy to talk to so people feel comfortable around you.
entries.example: Our new teacher was affable and smiled at every question, so even shy pupils felt brave enough to raise their hands on the first day.
examples: Our new teacher was affable and smiled at every question, so even shy pupils felt brave enough to raise their hands on the first day.
At the bake sale an affable neighbour chatted about recipes while passing round free biscuits, making everyone laugh and relax.
Leo's dog is affable and greets every visitor with a wagging tail, which makes anyone who feels nervous feel happier straight away.
entries.spellingNote: Affable starts with 'aff-' (double f) and ends with '-able', like 'comfortable' without the 'comfort'.

entries.definition: Having plenty of money and nice things; wealthy.
entries.example: The town by the river looked affluent with big houses and tidy gardens, which made the old schoolyard feel smaller in comparison.
examples: The town by the river looked affluent with big houses and tidy gardens, which made the old schoolyard feel smaller in comparison.
She wrote an essay about how affluent families could donate books to the library to help children who had fewer resources.
An affluent neighbourhood had a playground with colourful equipment, while the other park nearby had only a worn bench and weeds.
entries.spellingNote: Affluent has 'affl-' not 'afl-'; remember the double 'f' and the '-luent' ending like 'fluent'.

entries.definition: Quick, light and able to move easily and quickly in different directions.
entries.example: The gymnast was very agile, flipping over the beam and landing neatly while the audience held its breath at each splendid move.
examples: The gymnast was very agile, flipping over the beam and landing neatly while the audience held its breath at each splendid move.
A fox slipped through the fence because it was so agile, twisting between the posts while the farmer watched in surprise.
During the obstacle race Zara stayed agile, darting under ropes and leaping over logs to keep ahead of the other teams.
entries.spellingNote: Agile is short: 'a-g-i-l-e' — the 'g' is soft, like in 'giant'.

entries.definition: upset, nervous, or restless
entries.example: The horse became agitated when thunder cracked above the stable. It stamped, tossed its head, and refused the carrot it usually loved.
examples: The horse became agitated when thunder cracked above the stable. It stamped, tossed its head, and refused the carrot it usually loved.
The crowd grew agitated as the delayed train disappeared from the board again. People checked their phones, sighed loudly, and pressed closer to the platform edge.
The beaker turned cloudy and agitated when the tablet fizzed inside it. Bubbles raced upward so quickly that the liquid seemed to shiver.
entries.spellingNote: agitate + d.

entries.definition: Very strong pain or worry that is hard to bear, whether it is physical or emotional.
entries.example: Tom felt agony when he twisted his ankle on the trail, and he sat down breathing fast while his friends ran back for help.
examples: Tom felt agony when he twisted his ankle on the trail, and he sat down breathing fast while his friends ran back for help.
Watching the poor lost puppy tremble in the rain caused real agony in Lina's chest until she wrapped it in her coat and phoned for help.
During the final exam, Sofia chewed her pencil in agony because she couldn't remember the last answer and time was running out.
entries.spellingNote: Agony is spelled A-G-O-N-Y; the 'g' makes a hard sound and it ends with '-ony'.

entries.definition: Having a strong desire to achieve success, to be better at something or to reach a big goal.
entries.example: Rina set an ambitious plan to learn three new songs on the violin by summer, practising each evening even when she was tired.
examples: Rina set an ambitious plan to learn three new songs on the violin by summer, practising each evening even when she was tired.
The school's ambitious project to build a community garden asked everyone to help plant, water and design the signs for each bed.
He wrote an ambitious story about exploring Mars; his characters faced storms and found strange rocks, which impressed the teacher.
entries.spellingNote: Ambitious has 'ambi-' like 'ambidextrous' and ends with '-tious' — remember the 'ti' before 'ous'.

entries.definition: Friendly and pleasant in behaviour; easy to like and get on with.
entries.example: Our class mascot is an amiable stuffed owl that sits on the windowsill and seems to cheer everyone up on grey days.
examples: Our class mascot is an amiable stuffed owl that sits on the windowsill and seems to cheer everyone up on grey days.
Mr Khan was amiable at the science fair, kneeling to explain experiments kindly so all the children could understand.
Even when the team lost, the captain stayed amiable and shook hands with the other players, which made the crowd applaud.
entries.spellingNote: Amiable begins with 'ami-' like 'amigo'; the 'i' comes before the 'a' in the middle of the word.

entries.definition: In the middle of or surrounded by other things or events.
entries.example: Amidst the thundery roar the lighthouse blinked steadily, guiding the fishing boats back to the harbour through the dark sea.
examples: Amidst the thundery roar the lighthouse blinked steadily, guiding the fishing boats back to the harbour through the dark sea.
Amidst the piles of old maps and torn letters, Isla found a tiny sketch that seemed to point to a hidden garden behind the school.
The picnic was peaceful amidst the tall oaks until a sudden gust scattered sandwiches and plates, turning calm into a scramble.
entries.spellingNote: Amidst is 'amid' with an extra 'st' at the end; you can also say 'amid' or 'amongst'.

entries.definition: Made louder, stronger or clearer, often by using a device like a speaker or by increasing a signal.
entries.example: When the microphone failed, the teacher's whisper was amplified by the PA system and suddenly everyone in the hall could hear clearly.
examples: When the microphone failed, the teacher's whisper was amplified by the PA system and suddenly everyone in the hall could hear clearly.
The scientist amplified the tiny heartbeat sound on the screen so the whole class could watch how fast it pulsed during the experiment.
The chorus practiced outdoors and the wind amplified their singing in strange ways, making the tune echo around the playground.
entries.spellingNote: Amplified is 'amplify' with '-ed' for past tense: a-m-p-l-i-f-i-e-d.

entries.definition: Very old; from a time long ago, much earlier than the present.
entries.example: We found an ancient coin near the stream that looked like it might be hundreds of years old, and we took it to the museum to learn more.
examples: We found an ancient coin near the stream that looked like it might be hundreds of years old, and we took it to the museum to learn more.
The class visited an ancient castle with cold stone rooms and narrow stairs, where the guide told tales of knights and long-ago feasts.
Under the sand the archaeologists uncovered ancient pottery, shards painted with faded pictures of fish and ships from another age.
entries.spellingNote: Ancient starts with 'an-' and has a soft 'c' pronounced like 'sh': 'ayn-shent'.

entries.definition: To make something move or seem alive, or to be full of life and energy.
entries.example: The puppeteer could animate the tiny dragon so well that the children forgot it was made of wood and laughed at its cheeky expressions.
examples: The puppeteer could animate the tiny dragon so well that the children forgot it was made of wood and laughed at its cheeky expressions.
In class we used clay and wire to animate a frog model, making legs bend and eyes blink for our stop-motion film.
A lively debate can animate a quiet classroom, with voices rising and hands waving as ideas are shared enthusiastically.
entries.spellingNote: Animate is A-N-I-M-A-T-E; the root 'anim-' means life, like in 'animal' or 'animation'.

entries.definition: To expect that something will happen and sometimes get ready for it beforehand.
entries.example: I didn't anticipate the sudden thunderstorm on our nature walk, so we hurried to the shelter and my sketchbook got soaked before I could save the drawings.
examples: I didn't anticipate the sudden thunderstorm on our nature walk, so we hurried to the shelter and my sketchbook got soaked before I could save the drawings.
The teacher asked the class to anticipate the experiment's result and write predictions so we could compare them to what happened under the lamp and notes later.
Mum had to anticipate my football kit getting muddy after the match, so she put it in a plastic bag and wrote a note to remind me to wash it straight away.
entries.spellingNote: Remember the middle letters 'ci' in anticipate (an-ti-ci-pate), not 'cate' or 'crate'.

entries.definition: The way someone or something looks to other people at a particular time.
entries.example: Her sudden appearance at the assembly surprised everyone because she had a bright hat and a big smile, making even the grumpy caretaker look up.
examples: Her sudden appearance at the assembly surprised everyone because she had a bright hat and a big smile, making even the grumpy caretaker look up.
When the tortoise changed its appearance after shedding old skin, the class gasped at how shiny and clean its shell looked under the lamp.
The magician's appearance on stage was dramatic: a puff of smoke, a silver cape, and a hush from the crowd ready for tricks and laughter.
entries.spellingNote: Appearance has a double 'p' and an 'a' after the 'r' — a-pp-ea-r-a-n-c-e.

entries.definition: A little worried or nervous that something bad or unknown might happen.
entries.example: She felt apprehensive before the school play because her lines were long and the lights made the stage look huge and strange compared to the quiet classroom.
examples: She felt apprehensive before the school play because her lines were long and the lights made the stage look huge and strange compared to the quiet classroom.
Tom was apprehensive about opening the old shed door alone, imagining creaks and cobwebs, until his friend shone a torch and they laughed together.
Before the science test, I stood apprehensive at my desk, fingers tapping and pencil ready, hoping the questions were like the practice ones at home.
entries.spellingNote: Apprehensive begins with 'appre' (as in 'appreciate' but different) and ends with 'hensive'.

entries.definition: Related to people from very old, rich, or powerful families who often have special titles or privileges.
entries.example: At the museum, we read about an aristocratic family who owned the manor and dressed in fine coats and gloves while their gardeners tended the long lawns.
examples: At the museum, we read about an aristocratic family who owned the manor and dressed in fine coats and gloves while their gardeners tended the long lawns.
The old photograph showed an aristocratic couple sitting in a grand hall, their posture proper and their silver cutlery polished for a large feast.
In the play, the aristocratic character spoke very politely and wore a tall hat, which made the other villagers whisper about his fancy life.
entries.spellingNote: Aristocratic has 'aristo' then 'cratic' — remember the 't' before 'ic' at the end.

entries.definition: thinking you are better than other people
entries.example: The arrogant striker celebrated before the ball reached the goal, then watched the goalkeeper catch it easily. His teammates groaned because confidence had turned into foolish pride.
examples: The arrogant striker celebrated before the ball reached the goal, then watched the goalkeeper catch it easily. His teammates groaned because confidence had turned into foolish pride.
An arrogant explorer ignored the local guide's warning about the river. Ten minutes later, his boots were full of water and his map was floating away.
The robot in the story sounded arrogant when it announced that humans were too slow to solve the puzzle. Then it failed because it had not read the final clue.
entries.spellingNote: Double r in arrogant.

entries.definition: Feeling bad or embarrassed because you think you have done something wrong or silly.
entries.example: He felt ashamed after he accidentally broke his sister's toy and tried to hide it, then saw her sad face and decided to say sorry instead of keeping quiet.
examples: He felt ashamed after he accidentally broke his sister's toy and tried to hide it, then saw her sad face and decided to say sorry instead of keeping quiet.
Lucy was ashamed when she forgot her lines and the class clapped politely; later she practised until she felt ready to try again with a smile.
After cheating in the game, Mark felt ashamed and returned the prize, learning that being honest mattered more than winning for himself and his friends.
entries.spellingNote: Ashamed has 'a' then 'shamed' — remember the 'sh' sound at the start.

entries.definition: Confidently saying what you think or need in a calm and honest way, without being rude.
entries.example: Ada was assertive when she told her friends she needed quiet time to finish her homework, and they agreed to meet later in the playground.
examples: Ada was assertive when she told her friends she needed quiet time to finish her homework, and they agreed to meet later in the playground.
During group work, Jamal was assertive about which science idea to try, explaining his plan clearly so everyone could understand and vote.
At the club, being assertive helped Zoe ask the coach for more practice, and soon she improved because she spoke up politely and often.
entries.spellingNote: Assertive has two 's' letters in the middle: a-s-s-e-r-t-i-v-e.

entries.definition: Very surprised in a way that shows you did not expect something at all.
entries.example: We were astonished when the tiny seedling in the science box grew a tall stalk overnight, its leaves shining under the classroom lights like magic.
examples: We were astonished when the tiny seedling in the science box grew a tall stalk overnight, its leaves shining under the classroom lights like magic.
The whole street was astonished to see the fox calmly walking down the lane at dawn while people opened curtains and pointed in disbelief.
When the old clock started chiming again after years of silence, the family looked astonished and clapped because they had thought it was broken forever.
entries.spellingNote: Astonished has 'aston' then 'ished' — watch the 'sh' before the 'ed' ending.

entries.definition: Clothes or outfit someone is wearing for a particular occasion.
entries.example: For the historical day, everyone chose special attire: Emily wore a long dress and the boys borrowed hats to look like people from the old photographs.
examples: For the historical day, everyone chose special attire: Emily wore a long dress and the boys borrowed hats to look like people from the old photographs.
The explorer's attire included a warm coat, sturdy boots and a big hat, which helped him stay dry while crossing the windy moorland on the map.
Grandad checked his attire carefully before the wedding, polishing his shoes and fastening his tie until it sat perfectly under the jacket lapel.
entries.spellingNote: Attire is short and starts with double 't' — a-t-t-i-r-e.

entries.definition: Very plain, simple, and without any decoration; can also mean strict or severe in behaviour or rules.
entries.example: The classroom felt austere after the renovation: bare walls, neat desks in rows, and the teacher's firm look making the room feel serious and quiet.
examples: The classroom felt austere after the renovation: bare walls, neat desks in rows, and the teacher's firm look making the room feel serious and quiet.
The monk's cell was austere with only a small bed and a wooden table, showing he chose a simple life without bright things or many toys.
During the winter, the garden looked austere with leafless trees and stiff hedges, but the children still found patterns in the frost for their sketchbooks.
entries.spellingNote: Austere begins with 'aus' (like 'August' without the 'g') and ends with 'tere' — a-u-s-t-e-r-e.

entries.definition: real and not copied or false
entries.example: The archaeologist placed the authentic Viking comb in a glass case, with soil still caught between its tiny teeth. A modern copy sat beside it so visitors could compare the real object with the replica.
examples: The archaeologist placed the authentic Viking comb in a glass case, with soil still caught between its tiny teeth. A modern copy sat beside it so visitors could compare the real object with the replica.

At the food festival, the chef made authentic Turkish gozleme on a hot metal plate, using the recipe her grandmother taught her. It tasted different from the frozen version because every fold was made by hand.
The film crew wanted an authentic steam train, not a computer image, for the station scene. When the engine arrived, smoke rolled across the platform and every actor turned to stare.
entries.spellingNote: au + then + tic.

entries.definition: The power or right to give orders, make decisions, or be in charge; also a person or organisation with that power.
entries.example: The headteacher had authority to change the timetable, so when the buses were late she called a quick meeting to rearrange the day and keep everyone safe.
examples: The headteacher had authority to change the timetable, so when the buses were late she called a quick meeting to rearrange the day and keep everyone safe.
When the river flooded, the local authority sent workers to build barriers and tell people when it was safe to return to their homes and shops.
Ben spoke to his coach because she was the authority on training; he trusted her decisions about which drills would make him faster and stronger.
entries.spellingNote: Authority has 'thor' in the middle: a-u-t-h-o-r-i-t-y; don't forget the 'h' after the 't'.

entries.definition: To give official permission for something to happen or for someone to do something.
entries.example: The teacher will authorise the trip permission slip only after parents sign it, so we must remember to bring the forms back by Friday lunch.
examples: The teacher will authorise the trip permission slip only after parents sign it, so we must remember to bring the forms back by Friday lunch.
The librarian had to authorise my late return because the book was part of a special study set and needed an extra day for homework research.
Before the experiment, the science leader had to authorise the use of the chemicals, checking safety rules and gloves for everyone working at the table.
entries.spellingNote: In British English use 'authorise' with an 's' rather than a 'z'.

entries.definition: Not comfortable or easy; causing people to feel embarrassed or clumsy in a situation.
entries.example: It felt awkward when my chair squeaked loudly during the quiet test, and everyone glanced at me while I wished the floor would swallow me up for a second.
examples: It felt awkward when my chair squeaked loudly during the quiet test, and everyone glanced at me while I wished the floor would swallow me up for a second.
Carrying the tray full of soup was awkward on the windy playground; I stepped carefully and nearly tripped but managed to save most bowls by holding them steady.
The conversation turned awkward when both kids said sorry at once and then started giggling, unsure who should stop apologising first to calm things down.
entries.spellingNote: Awkward is unusual because the 'w' appears after the 'a' and before the 'k' — a-w-k-w-a-r-d.

entries.definition: Land or soil that is barren cannot easily grow plants and looks empty or unable to support crops or many animals.
entries.example: The old field looked barren after the hard winter; the children searched for any green shoot but only found dry soil and scattered stones beneath the grey sky.
examples: The old field looked barren after the hard winter; the children searched for any green shoot but only found dry soil and scattered stones beneath the grey sky.
On the school trip, the hill near the moor was barren and windy, so the teacher explained how some plants need richer soil to grow well.
The astronaut's drawing showed a barren alien plain with no trees or rivers, which helped the class imagine why water is so important for life.
entries.spellingNote: Remember the double r: b-a-r-r-e-n.

entries.definition: Decorated or covered with things that make something look festive, fancy or attractive.
entries.example: The village square was bedecked with colourful ribbons and lanterns, so everyone said it looked ready for a feast and celebration.
examples: The village square was bedecked with colourful ribbons and lanterns, so everyone said it looked ready for a feast and celebration.
At the play, the stage was bedecked with fake trees and painted stars, which made the story feel like a real forest under a night sky.
For the parade, Grandad's bicycle was bedecked with flowers and tiny flags, and he rode slowly while children cheered from the pavements.
entries.spellingNote: bedecked has 'be-' prefix and double c not needed; b-e-d-e-c-k-e-d.

entries.definition: Kind and wanting to help other people or animals; showing goodwill and generosity.
entries.example: The new librarian had a benevolent smile and always stayed after school to help anyone who struggled with reading or finding a book.
examples: The new librarian had a benevolent smile and always stayed after school to help anyone who struggled with reading or finding a book.
A benevolent farmer left extra carrots at the village gate so local children could feed the hungry rabbits near the hedgerow.
During the cake sale, Mrs Patel was benevolent with her time and baked extra cupcakes to make sure everyone could have a treat.
entries.spellingNote: Note the -olent ending: b-e-n-e-v-o-l-e-n-t.

entries.definition: very confused
entries.example: When the train announcement changed platforms three times, the tourists looked bewildered and spun around with their suitcases. Each new message seemed to cancel the last one.
examples: When the train announcement changed platforms three times, the tourists looked bewildered and spun around with their suitcases. Each new message seemed to cancel the last one.
The puppy looked bewildered when the automatic door opened by itself. It barked once, backed away, and stared as if the building had learned a magic trick.
Amira felt bewildered by the first page of the music score. There were notes, rests, dots, and symbols everywhere, and she could not yet see the pattern.
entries.spellingNote: be + wilder + ed.

entries.definition: In a way that is very obvious and shows no attempt to hide something, often in a rude or wrong way.
entries.example: He blatantly ignored the 'No Entry' sign and walked straight into the lab, so the teacher had to remind him about safety rules in front of everyone.
examples: He blatantly ignored the 'No Entry' sign and walked straight into the lab, so the teacher had to remind him about safety rules in front of everyone.
She blatantly copied the answers from the board, and the whole class watched as the teacher spoke quietly to her about doing her own work.
The poster blatantly used bright colours and giant letters to promise prizes, making it clear to everyone that the fair would be a big event.
entries.spellingNote: blatantly ends with -ly because it is an adverb: b-l-a-t-a-n-t-l-y.

entries.definition: A top that girls or women wear, usually lighter and more dressy than a T-shirt and often with buttons or a collar.
entries.example: Iris picked a blue blouse for the school concert because it moved softly when she danced and had little buttons along the front.
examples: Iris picked a blue blouse for the school concert because it moved softly when she danced and had little buttons along the front.
In art class, Lulu sketched her friend wearing a striped blouse and tried to draw the way the fabric folded at the sleeves.
The uniform rules say a plain white blouse should be worn with the tie, so Tom's sister ironed hers carefully before the assembly.
entries.spellingNote: Blouse is spelled b-l-o-u-s-e; the 'ou' makes the sound similar to 'ow'.

entries.definition: To talk with too much pride about something you have done or own, often to make others impressed.
entries.example: After scoring the goal, Leo could not help but boast to his friends about how he dribbled past three players, although he felt a bit cheeky doing it.
examples: After scoring the goal, Leo could not help but boast to his friends about how he dribbled past three players, although he felt a bit cheeky doing it.
The older pupil would boast about his medals at lunchtime, which made some children admire him and others roll their eyes.
When Ava found a rare coin, she did not want to boast, so she quietly showed it only to her closest friend to keep it safe.
entries.spellingNote: Simple spelling: b-o-a-s-t. The 'oa' makes a long o sound.

entries.definition: Noisy, energetic and full of lively behaviour that can be a little out of control.
entries.example: The classroom became boisterous after lunch as children played a loud game, so the teacher opened the window and asked them to take deep breaths and calm down.
examples: The classroom became boisterous after lunch as children played a loud game, so the teacher opened the window and asked them to take deep breaths and calm down.
At the seaside, the boisterous wind knocked over the bucket and sent sand flying, which made the picnic a messy but fun adventure.
The puppy's boisterous barking woke the neighbours, and Mum laughed while carrying the wagging dog back inside to settle him down.
entries.spellingNote: Notice the -ster- in the middle: b-o-i-s-t-e-r-o-u-s.

entries.definition: Brave and willing to take risks; also used for colours or actions that are bright, clear and noticeable.
entries.example: When the class needed a volunteer to lead the experiment, Nora felt bold and put her hand up even though she felt nervous inside and wanted to help everyone try.
examples: When the class needed a volunteer to lead the experiment, Nora felt bold and put her hand up even though she felt nervous inside and wanted to help everyone try.
She chose a bold red paint for the door frame, and the bright colour made the whole corridor look cheerful and new.
Tom made a bold choice to speak about his mistake in front of the class, which made other pupils respect him for being honest.
entries.spellingNote: Short word, four letters: b-o-l-d.

entries.definition: Provided in large amounts; plentiful and generous, especially for food or helpful things.
entries.example: After the harvest festival, the kitchen had a bountiful table of bread, apples and pies so every family could take food home and share with neighbours.
examples: After the harvest festival, the kitchen had a bountiful table of bread, apples and pies so every family could take food home and share with neighbours.
They found a bountiful patch of blackberries by the stream and spent the afternoon collecting bowls full for jam and crumbles.
The library's book sale was bountiful with picture books and stories, so the class brought extra coins to buy presents for younger siblings.
entries.spellingNote: Remember the -tiful ending, not -ful: b-o-u-n-t-i-f-u-l.

entries.definition: To speak proudly about what you have done, often to make others think you are better; similar to boast but usually more annoying.
entries.example: After getting full marks, Jamie began to brag loudly about the quiz and soon his friend asked him to stop so the class could focus on the next activity.
examples: After getting full marks, Jamie began to brag loudly about the quiz and soon his friend asked him to stop so the class could focus on the next activity.
Even though she wanted to brag about her painting, Mia gave a copy to the art teacher to enter quietly in the competition.
He tends to brag about how fast he runs, which makes races less fun because others feel he is not being modest.
entries.spellingNote: Short and simple: b-r-a-g.

entries.definition: Very clever or excellent; can also mean very bright in light or colour.
entries.example: Sam had a brilliant idea to reuse old jars as plant pots, and the whole class loved how colourful the window looked with tiny green seedlings inside.
examples: Sam had a brilliant idea to reuse old jars as plant pots, and the whole class loved how colourful the window looked with tiny green seedlings inside.
The scientist gave a brilliant explanation that made the tricky experiment make perfect sense to everyone, and hands went up with new questions.
The sunrise was brilliant with streaks of orange and pink, and the children stood quietly on the hill to watch the sky change colours.
entries.spellingNote: Double l in the middle: b-r-i-l-l-i-a-n-t.

entries.definition: Quick, energetic and fresh; describing speed or an invigorating feeling, like a brisk walk or a brisk wind.
entries.example: We took a brisk walk to the pond and the cool air made our cheeks rosy, while the dog ran ahead and barked at the jumping fish.
examples: We took a brisk walk to the pond and the cool air made our cheeks rosy, while the dog ran ahead and barked at the jumping fish.
The teacher spoke in a brisk voice to tidy the class quickly, and everyone returned chairs and books faster than usual.
On the field trip, a brisk breeze picked up the kites and sent them soaring high above the laughing children below.
entries.spellingNote: One s: b-r-i-s-k.

entries.definition: hard but easily broken
entries.example: The brittle biscuit snapped before Talia could dip it into her tea. It looked solid on the plate, but one small bend broke it cleanly in two.
examples: The brittle biscuit snapped before Talia could dip it into her tea. It looked solid on the plate, but one small bend broke it cleanly in two.
After weeks without rain, the brittle grass crackled under every footstep. The park keeper banned barbecues because one spark could race across the field.
The ancient parchment was brittle, so the librarian turned each page with a soft brush. A normal finger could have torn a corner away forever.
entries.spellingNote: Double t in brittle.

entries.definition: The act of putting a dead person or animal into the ground or a tomb, often with a ceremony to remember them.
entries.example: At the seaside, the family held a simple burial for their pet rabbit, placing flowers on the sand and saying a few quiet words before covering the little grave.
examples: At the seaside, the family held a simple burial for their pet rabbit, placing flowers on the sand and saying a few quiet words before covering the little grave.
The history class learned how archaeologists opened a bronze-age burial and found tools and beads that told stories of everyday life long ago.
When the old farmer died, neighbours helped with the burial in the churchyard and everyone shared memories under the grey sky.
entries.spellingNote: Burial comes from 'bury' but is spelled b-u-r-i-a-l; do not write 'buriel'.

entries.definition: A terrible event that causes a lot of damage, loss or suffering, such as a major accident, storm or disaster.
entries.example: When the river flooded the market, people called it a calamity because stalls, food and important papers were lost overnight and families had to move.
examples: When the river flooded the market, people called it a calamity because stalls, food and important papers were lost overnight and families had to move.
The sudden storm was a calamity for the picnic, soaking the cakes and sending everyone running across the grass to find shelter.
The late frost proved a calamity for the orchard; the blossom froze and the farmers feared there would be almost no fruit that year.
entries.spellingNote: Calamity is spelled c-a-l-a-m-i-t-y; remember the 'ty' ending.

entries.definition: A chart or book that shows the days, weeks and months of the year, used to plan events and count days.
entries.example: Hana circled her birthday on the classroom calendar and counted the days until the school fair, excited to see who would bring cake.
examples: Hana circled her birthday on the classroom calendar and counted the days until the school fair, excited to see who would bring cake.
The farmer marked moon phases and planting dates on a farm calendar so seeds went into the soil at the right time.
When the coach checked the fixtures on the calendar, he realised two important matches were on the same weekend and hurried to rearrange one.
entries.spellingNote: Calendar is c-a-l-e-n-d-a-r; many people mistakenly spell it 'calender'.

entries.definition: A cover or roof-like layer that hangs over something, such as the top layer of trees in a forest or a shelter over a seat.
entries.example: We walked beneath the rainforest canopy where leaves made a green roof and tiny frogs sang from the damp branches above.
examples: We walked beneath the rainforest canopy where leaves made a green roof and tiny frogs sang from the damp branches above.
Dad fixed a canvas canopy over the picnic table so we could eat even when sudden rain began to fall.
The museum put a glass canopy above the statue to protect it from weather while letting the sunlight show every carved detail.
entries.spellingNote: Canopy is spelled c-a-n-o-p-y; note there is one 'n' and it ends with '-opy'.

entries.definition: The skill, power or quality that makes someone or something able to do a particular job or task.
entries.example: The robot showed its capability by carefully stacking ten blocks without dropping any, surprising everyone at the school science fair.
examples: The robot showed its capability by carefully stacking ten blocks without dropping any, surprising everyone at the school science fair.
Swimming every week improved Mia's capability to swim across the pool without getting tired.
The new camera's capability to take clear night photos made it the favourite gadget on our camping trip.
entries.spellingNote: Capability is c-a-p-a-b-i-l-i-t-y; note there is only one 'l' before the '-ity'.

entries.definition: careful because there may be danger or a problem
entries.example: On the icy pavement outside school, Leyla took cautious steps and kept one hand near the wall. Everyone else rushed ahead, but she had already seen two people slide in the same shiny patch.
examples: On the icy pavement outside school, Leyla took cautious steps and kept one hand near the wall. Everyone else rushed ahead, but she had already seen two people slide in the same shiny patch.
The wildlife photographer was cautious near the nesting puffins, speaking softly and moving only when the birds settled. One careless step could frighten the whole colony into the air.
Before sharing the dramatic storm video, Omar was cautious and checked where it came from. The clip looked real, but the date showed it was from a hurricane years ago.
entries.spellingNote: Remember cau + tious.

entries.definition: To stop something happening or to bring an activity or sound to an end.
entries.example: The teacher asked the noisy class to cease their chatter so she could explain the experiment carefully and everyone could listen.
examples: The teacher asked the noisy class to cease their chatter so she could explain the experiment carefully and everyone could listen.
When the heavy rain began to cease, the children jumped from under the shelter and counted puddles on the playground.
The old clock's ticking did not cease even during power cuts because the mechanism ran on a wound spring.
entries.spellingNote: Cease is spelled c-e-a-s-e; don't confuse it with 'seize'.

entries.definition: To care for and hold someone or something dear, keeping it safe and thinking about it with love.
entries.example: Grandma would cherish the little blue cup because it reminded her of sunny mornings at the seaside when she was a child.
examples: Grandma would cherish the little blue cup because it reminded her of sunny mornings at the seaside when she was a child.
Tom decided to cherish the friendship bracelet his best friend made, wearing it to every football match.
We cherish old family photographs and pass them around so each child can learn about their great-grandparents.
entries.spellingNote: Cherish starts with 'ch' and ends '-ish' — remember not to add an extra 'e'.

entries.definition: A serious and fast-spreading illness that causes very bad diarrhoea and vomiting, often passed on through dirty water.
entries.example: In history we learned how cholera swept through towns when clean water was scarce, making many people ill before better sanitation was introduced.
examples: In history we learned how cholera swept through towns when clean water was scarce, making many people ill before better sanitation was introduced.
After the flood, health teams taught villagers how to boil water and use clean latrines to stop cholera spreading.
The clinic set up rehydration stations because quick treatment can save lives when someone gets cholera and becomes dehydrated.
entries.spellingNote: Cholera is c-h-o-l-e-r-a; note the single 'l' and the 'ch' at the start.

entries.definition: A group of families or people who are related or who share a strong sense of belonging and common traditions.
entries.example: The two families formed a clan and gathered by the bonfire each year to tell stories about their ancestors late into the night.
examples: The two families formed a clan and gathered by the bonfire each year to tell stories about their ancestors late into the night.
In the game my clan defended the village and everyone promised to help protect each other's crops and homes.
At the festival the Highland clan wore tartans and sang traditional songs so visitors could see which family group they belonged to.
entries.spellingNote: Clan is short and simple — c-l-a-n; do not add an 'e' or extra letters.

entries.definition: Quick at learning or thinking; good at finding smart or new ways to solve problems.
entries.example: Lina was clever when she fixed the broken robot with just a paperclip and a rubber band, and the class gave a surprised cheer.
examples: Lina was clever when she fixed the broken robot with just a paperclip and a rubber band, and the class gave a surprised cheer.
The clever fox outwitted the farmers' traps by slipping through a hole no one had noticed, winning its freedom.
When the clever idea to use recycled jars for lanterns became the bake-sale plan, everyone made colourful lights for the stall.
entries.spellingNote: Clever is c-l-e-v-e-r; keep the two 'e's in that order and don't add extra letters.

entries.definition: Awkward when moving or handling things; likely to trip, drop or break things by accident.
entries.example: Because he was clumsy, Ben tipped his paint pot and the classroom carpet got a rainbow of blobs, which made everyone gasp and laugh.
examples: Because he was clumsy, Ben tipped his paint pot and the classroom carpet got a rainbow of blobs, which made everyone gasp and laugh.
The clumsy kitten kept tripping over its own paws and knocked the plant pot off the windowsill with a crash.
During the play a clumsy stagehand missed a mark and two cardboard trees fell, causing the audience to giggle at the chaos.
entries.spellingNote: Clumsy is c-l-u-m-s-y; remember the 's' before the 'y'.

entries.definition: Clear and easy to understand because the parts fit together logically and make sense.
entries.example: Her story was coherent, with events in the right order and a clear reason why the treasure map led to the old oak tree.
examples: Her story was coherent, with events in the right order and a clear reason why the treasure map led to the old oak tree.
The scientist wrote a coherent report so the whole class could repeat the experiment exactly the same way.
Even after a long lesson, the teacher's coherent explanation helped every pupil solve the tricky puzzle on the board.
entries.spellingNote: Coherent is c-o-h-e-r-e-n-t — remember the 'h' after the 'o'.

entries.definition: To fall down suddenly or to fail completely, often because something is broken, too weak, or overloaded.
entries.example: During the storm the old shed began to collapse when the roof gave way, and everyone ran outside to check nobody was trapped inside.
examples: During the storm the old shed began to collapse when the roof gave way, and everyone ran outside to check nobody was trapped inside.
The scientist warned the tiny bridge could collapse under too much weight, so we tested with a single backpack before walking across.
After the marathon a runner felt tired and dizzy and nearly collapse, so teammates helped them sit down and gave them water.
entries.spellingNote: Remember it has a double l in the middle: col-lapse.

entries.definition: To begin or start something, usually used for events, lessons, or formal actions.
entries.example: The teacher told the class to sit quietly while the exam would commence in five minutes, so everyone put their pens down and waited.
examples: The teacher told the class to sit quietly while the exam would commence in five minutes, so everyone put their pens down and waited.
When the lights dimmed, the concert would commence and the orchestra began their first quiet tune to the eager crowd.
After the safety talk the science experiment could commence, and the children followed the instructions step by step.
entries.spellingNote: Starts with com- and has -mence like 'sentence' but with 'commence' spelled c-o-m-m-e-n-c-e.

entries.definition: A product or raw material that is bought and sold, often in large amounts, such as grain, oil or metals.
entries.example: The farm sold grain as a commodity to markets across the country, and the money helped buy new tools for the workers.
examples: The farm sold grain as a commodity to markets across the country, and the money helped buy new tools for the workers.
Coffee became an important commodity for the town, so many families grew beans and traded them at the weekly fair.
When the river froze, transport of a key commodity like timber slowed, which caused shortages of wood for building nearby houses.
entries.spellingNote: Remember the double m after 'co' and the -ity ending: com-mo-di-ty.

entries.definition: kind concern for someone who is suffering
entries.example: After the race, Noor showed compassion by sitting beside the runner who had fallen instead of rushing to collect her medal. She shared water and waited until the first-aid team arrived.
examples: After the race, Noor showed compassion by sitting beside the runner who had fallen instead of rushing to collect her medal. She shared water and waited until the first-aid team arrived.
The vet spoke with compassion when the old dog was frightened by the scanner. She lowered her voice, warmed the blanket, and let him sniff the machine before the test began.
When a new pupil forgot his lunch, the class showed compassion without making a show of it. Three children quietly offered pieces from their own boxes so he would not feel embarrassed.
entries.spellingNote: Double s in the middle.

entries.definition: showing kindness and concern for others
entries.example: The compassionate bus driver stopped when he saw an elderly man drop his shopping in the rain. Instead of honking, he waited and helped gather the rolling apples from the road.
examples: The compassionate bus driver stopped when he saw an elderly man drop his shopping in the rain. Instead of honking, he waited and helped gather the rolling apples from the road.
A compassionate teacher noticed that Zara was silent after the fire drill. She did not scold her for being slow; she asked what had scared her and walked back with her calmly.
The rescue centre needed compassionate volunteers because injured animals can panic. The best helpers moved slowly, spoke gently, and cared more about trust than speed.
entries.spellingNote: Compassion + ate.

entries.definition: To force someone to do something because of a rule, need, or strong reason.
entries.example: When the campsite rules said to put food away, the rangers had to compel campers to follow them to protect the wildlife.
examples: When the campsite rules said to put food away, the rangers had to compel campers to follow them to protect the wildlife.
A sudden storm and blocked roads may compel our class to stay at school until parents can collect everyone safely.
The kind teacher used clear reasons, not loud shouting, to compel the group to tidy the lab before leaving for break.
entries.spellingNote: Starts with com- and ends with -pel; don't confuse the single p with a double p.

entries.definition: Feeling that you must do something because of pressure, duty, or a strong need; forced to act.
entries.example: She felt compelled to return the lost wallet to the office because she knew it would worry the owner and it was the right thing to do.
examples: She felt compelled to return the lost wallet to the office because she knew it would worry the owner and it was the right thing to do.
After reading the urgent message about a trapped kitten, the neighbours were compelled to search the garden until they found it asleep in a shed.
He was so worried about the experiment that he felt compelled to redo the measurements, even though the teacher said they were likely correct.
entries.spellingNote: Past tense of 'compel' adds -led: compel → compelled with two l's in the middle.

entries.definition: To admit that something is true or to accept defeat, often after first disagreeing or arguing.
entries.example: After seeing the clear maps, Ben decided to concede that the other team had found the correct route and congratulated them politely.
examples: After seeing the clear maps, Ben decided to concede that the other team had found the correct route and congratulated them politely.
The clever scientist had to concede the experiment failed when repeated tests gave the same result every time.
When Mum showed the photo evidence, Tom had to concede he had taken the cookie and then promised to help bake more.
entries.spellingNote: Has the prefix con- and ends with -cede, like 'recede' or 'proceed'.

entries.definition: To hide something so that it cannot be seen or easily found.
entries.example: Ella tried to conceal her sketchbook behind a pile of blankets, not wanting anyone to see her secret drawings before the show.
examples: Ella tried to conceal her sketchbook behind a pile of blankets, not wanting anyone to see her secret drawings before the show.
The frog can conceal itself among wet leaves, making it very hard to spot during the afternoon nature walk.
He chose to conceal the surprise party invitations in a drawer so the birthday child would not discover them.
entries.spellingNote: Starts with con- and has 'ceal' at the end; don't mix the e and a: c-o-n-c-e-a-l.

entries.definition: To invent or make up something, often a story, plan or mixture, sometimes in a clever or secret way.
entries.example: Sam and Nia would concoct a fantastic tale about pirates and lost treasure to amuse the class during reading time.
examples: Sam and Nia would concoct a fantastic tale about pirates and lost treasure to amuse the class during reading time.
In the kitchen the scientist decided to concoct a new jam recipe, not a strange potion, and it tasted surprisingly good.
The detectives thought the thief might concoct a clever story, so they checked the facts and found a few details that did not match.
entries.spellingNote: Contains the odd -coct ending after con-: c-o-n-c-o-c-t; notice the c before the t.

entries.definition: Sweets, chocolates, and other sweet treats sold in shops, or the shop that sells them.
entries.example: At the fair the little stall labelled 'confectionery' smelled of warm caramel and invited everyone to try a colourful lollipop.
examples: At the fair the little stall labelled 'confectionery' smelled of warm caramel and invited everyone to try a colourful lollipop.
Grandad bought a tin of assorted confectionery to share on the picnic, and the children argued gently over their favourite sweets.
The seaside shop had so much confectionery that choosing between fudge, toffee and chocolate became a pleasant, tricky task.
entries.spellingNote: Long word with -fectionery; remember the -ery ending: c-o-n-f-e-c-t-i-o-n-e-r-y.

entries.definition: A serious disagreement or fight between people, groups, or ideas; when things do not match or clash.
entries.example: A conflict in the playground broke out over the last skipping rope, so teachers stepped in to help the children share and take turns.
examples: A conflict in the playground broke out over the last skipping rope, so teachers stepped in to help the children share and take turns.
The book shows a conflict between the village and the builders, with villagers worried about losing the old oak tree.
When two stories about the same event had different details, the classmates learned how to resolve the conflict by checking facts together.
entries.spellingNote: Has the Latin root 'con-' and 'flict' like 'afflict'; note the single f after con-: c-o-n-f-l-i-c-t.

entries.definition: Very crowded or blocked, so movement or flow is slow or difficult, like roads or noses.
entries.example: The road outside school was so congested with cars that the bus was late and the teacher told parents about better drop-off times.
examples: The road outside school was so congested with cars that the bus was late and the teacher told parents about better drop-off times.
After running, Mia's nose felt congested and she needed a tissue and some steam to breathe more easily during the cold evening.
The market became congested on market day, with shoppers brushing past stalls and finding it hard to move between the displays.
entries.spellingNote: Has -gested like 'digested'; remember the ge in the middle: c-o-n-g-e-s-t-e-d.

entries.definition: Something that happens as a result of an action or choice, often a result you must face later.
entries.example: Liam learnt that leaving muddy boots in the hallway had the consequence of tracked dirt, so he started to clean them by the door.
examples: Liam learnt that leaving muddy boots in the hallway had the consequence of tracked dirt, so he started to clean them by the door.
The scientists explained that a dropped oil spill had a serious consequence for sea birds, which made the whole team work harder to fix it.
If you forget to water the plants, the consequence is that the leaves droop and the flowers stop opening, so Pam set reminders to water them.
entries.spellingNote: Has -quence at the end; remember it's spelled c-o-n-s-e-q-u-e-n-c-e, not 'consequent'.

entries.definition: Always careful and putting in a lot of effort to do tasks properly and not make careless mistakes.
entries.example: Leyla is conscientious about her homework and checks each answer twice so she does not lose marks before handing it to her teacher.
examples: Leyla is conscientious about her homework and checks each answer twice so she does not lose marks before handing it to her teacher.
The conscientious class captain arranged pencils, collected registers and made sure everyone understood the art task before we started.
Tom's conscientious brushing of the dog before the show helped its fur shine, and the judge noticed his careful preparations.
entries.spellingNote: Split it up: con-sci-en-tious; remember the 'scien' part like the start of 'science' and the '-tious' ending.

entries.definition: To build or put parts together to make something, such as a model, building or a plan.
entries.example: For the science fair we had to construct a bridge from spaghetti that could hold a toy car across a gap on the classroom table.
examples: For the science fair we had to construct a bridge from spaghetti that could hold a toy car across a gap on the classroom table.
Our team will construct a small weather station in the school garden to measure wind and rain during the summer project.
Grandad showed me how to construct a simple birdhouse step by step, and we painted it together when the glue had dried.
entries.spellingNote: Ends with '-struct' like 'structure'; remember the prefix 'con-' meaning 'together'.

entries.definition: To think about something carefully and for a while, often when deciding or imagining.
entries.example: On the hill, Lila sat to contemplate the map and decide which path through the woods would be safest for their expedition.
examples: On the hill, Lila sat to contemplate the map and decide which path through the woods would be safest for their expedition.
Before answering the tricky test question, Jamal took a minute to contemplate each possibility so he wouldn't rush into a mistake.
We had time to contemplate the photograph of the old ship and wonder how sailors navigated by the stars long ago.
entries.spellingNote: Break it into parts: con-tem-plate; note the 'plate' ending, not 'plat' or 'plant'.

entries.definition: Belonging to the same time or happening now; modern rather than very old.
entries.example: The museum had a contemporary painting with bright colours that looked very different from the old black-and-white photographs in the next room.
examples: The museum had a contemporary painting with bright colours that looked very different from the old black-and-white photographs in the next room.
My aunt collects contemporary music, so her playlist is full of songs that were made in the last few years.
When studying history, we compared Roman stories with contemporary news to see how life and ideas have changed.
entries.spellingNote: Con-tem-po-rary: watch the 'po' syllable and the final '-ary' ending so you don't drop the middle letters.

entries.definition: 1) Feeling happy and satisfied. 2) The things or information contained in something, like a book, box or website.
entries.example: After finishing her reading, Sara felt content and smiled as she put the book back on the shelf beside her teddy.
examples: After finishing her reading, Sara felt content and smiled as she put the book back on the shelf beside her teddy.
The website blocked some content because it was not suitable for children, so we reported it to our teacher.
The lunch box was full, and Max checked the content to see if his favourite sandwich was hiding under the apple.
entries.spellingNote: The same spelling is used for both 'happy' (adjective) and 'stuff inside' (noun); check the sentence to find which one.

entries.definition: To say or show the opposite of something someone else has said; to disagree with a statement.
entries.example: When the witness tried to contradict the first statement, the teacher asked both children to explain exactly what they saw.
examples: When the witness tried to contradict the first statement, the teacher asked both children to explain exactly what they saw.
If your science notes contradict the experiment, check your measurements to find where the mistake happened.
Tom didn't want to contradict his friend in front of everyone, but he knew the map showed a different route.
entries.spellingNote: Starts with 'contra-' meaning 'against' and ends with '-dict' meaning 'say' — think 'against saying'.

entries.definition: Following the usual way of doing things or traditional rules; not new or strange.
entries.example: For the play, the director chose a conventional stage with curtains and simple props because it suited the old story better.
examples: For the play, the director chose a conventional stage with curtains and simple props because it suited the old story better.
We learned that some scientists follow conventional methods for safety while others test new ideas carefully to improve them.
Grandma's conventional pie recipe used butter and sugar, but we tried a new version with honey and spices and everyone loved it.
entries.spellingNote: Con-ven-tion-al: remember the 'tion' in the middle like 'action' and the final '-al'.

entries.definition: Warm, friendly and polite in a kind way.
entries.example: Even though they had never met, the new pupil received a cordial welcome with a smile and an offer to sit with us at lunch.
examples: Even though they had never met, the new pupil received a cordial welcome with a smile and an offer to sit with us at lunch.
The headteacher wrote a cordial note to the class parents thanking them for helping tidy the garden after school.
At the town fair the stallholders were cordial, offering samples and explaining their games with kind voices.
entries.spellingNote: Ends with '-ial'; pronounce it 'CORD-ial' with the stress on the first part.

entries.definition: Showing bravery and being willing to face danger, difficulty or fear.
entries.example: The small, courageous mouse kept returning to the field to carry seeds even when the wind was strong and the night was dark.
examples: The small, courageous mouse kept returning to the field to carry seeds even when the wind was strong and the night was dark.
During the fire drill, Sienna was courageous and helped guide a younger child who was crying to the nearest exit.
The team's courageous climb up the wet hill taught them how to support each other when things felt risky.
entries.spellingNote: Made from 'courage' + '-ous'; watch for the middle 'rage' letters and the final '-ous'.

entries.definition: Not straight or bent out of shape; it can also mean dishonest or not honest.
entries.example: The crooked fence leaned after the storm, and we had to carefully step around each bent post to reach the orchard.
examples: The crooked fence leaned after the storm, and we had to carefully step around each bent post to reach the orchard.
The crooked trader in the market tricked customers with unfair weights, so the villagers warned each other to be careful.
I drew a crooked line on my map by mistake, and my friend laughed because the path now looked like a wobbly snake.
entries.spellingNote: Remember the double 'o' in the middle: c-r-o-o-k-e-d.

entries.definition: Extremely important or necessary for success or for a result to happen.
entries.example: It was crucial we remembered to bring the telescope on the clear night because we could see the comet only for a short hour.
examples: It was crucial we remembered to bring the telescope on the clear night because we could see the comet only for a short hour.
Choosing the right ingredients was crucial for the cake to rise properly and taste sweet at the school bake sale.
During the race the coach gave a crucial tip about pacing, which helped Mia save energy for the final sprint.
entries.spellingNote: Split it: cru-cial; note the '-cial' ending rather than '-tial'.

entries.definition: Relating to cooking, the kitchen, or the art of preparing food.
entries.example: At the club we did a culinary challenge, making tiny pizzas while learning how to chop tomatoes safely with an adult's help.
examples: At the club we did a culinary challenge, making tiny pizzas while learning how to chop tomatoes safely with an adult's help.
Grandma's culinary skills meant she could turn plain vegetables into a meal that everyone asked for again and again.
In science class we learned how heat changes food, and the teacher linked the experiments to culinary techniques used in restaurants.
entries.spellingNote: Starts with 'culin-' like 'cuisine' and ends with the adjective '-ary'.

entries.definition: Showing clever planning or skill, often used to get what you want by tricking others a little.
entries.example: The detective noticed the cunning plan the fox used to steal food from the farmer's shed, with tiny pawprints that seemed to trick everyone who tried to follow them.
examples: The detective noticed the cunning plan the fox used to steal food from the farmer's shed, with tiny pawprints that seemed to trick everyone who tried to follow them.
At school, Mia made a cunning timetable to finish all her homework early and still have time to play football and practise the piano each day.
A cunning trick at the fair left the crowd guessing where the coin had gone, and no one could find the small secret pocket hidden in the table.
entries.spellingNote: Note the double n in cunning: c-u-n-n-i-n-g; the root ends with a double consonant before -ing.

entries.definition: A strong wish to learn or know about things, asking questions and wanting to explore.
entries.example: Her curiosity about the ants made her sit for an hour noting each trail, drawing a careful map of where they went and why they met at certain leaves.
examples: Her curiosity about the ants made her sit for an hour noting each trail, drawing a careful map of where they went and why they met at certain leaves.
Curiosity made Jamal open the dusty trunk in the attic, and he found letters and photographs that told his great-grandmother's secret story across the years.
The scientist's curiosity about clouds led her to collect rain samples after storms and compare them, hoping to learn how weather changed over the town.
entries.spellingNote: Curiosity ends with -osity (c-u-r-i-o-s-i-t-y) and comes from the adjective curious.

entries.definition: A strong wall or barrier built across a river to hold back water and make a lake or control floods.
entries.example: The village built a large dam across the fast river to create a lake for fishing, and children watched as frogs, ducks and dragonflies arrived along the new shore.
examples: The village built a large dam across the fast river to create a lake for fishing, and children watched as frogs, ducks and dragonflies arrived along the new shore.
When the engineers inspected the old dam before winter they found small cracks that would need careful fixing to stop heavy rains from flooding nearby fields.
A family of beavers worked all night to add sticks and mud to their dam, creating a deep pond where ducklings could swim safely and foxes could not reach them.
entries.spellingNote: Dam is short and has one m: d-a-m; do not add another m at the end.

entries.definition: Covered in spots or patches of different shades or light, often used about sunlight on the ground or a patterned coat.
entries.example: The dappled sunlight on the forest floor looked like a patchwork quilt as the children tiptoed past the birch trees, making shifting shapes on leaves and boots as they walked.
examples: The dappled sunlight on the forest floor looked like a patchwork quilt as the children tiptoed past the birch trees, making shifting shapes on leaves and boots as they walked.
Her horse had a dappled coat with pale spots that caught the afternoon light when it rolled happily in the grass after a sudden summer shower.
They set up a picnic under the dappled canopy, where light and shadow danced across sandwiches, storybooks and the sleepy faces of their little dog.
entries.spellingNote: Dappled is spelled d-a-p-p-l-e-d with a double p followed by -led.

entries.definition: Extremely bright, impressive or exciting in a way that almost takes your breath away or makes you look twice.
entries.example: The magician's final trick ended with a dazzling flash of light and glitter that left the audience clapping, squinting and whispering about how it could be done.
examples: The magician's final trick ended with a dazzling flash of light and glitter that left the audience clapping, squinting and whispering about how it could be done.
After the lake was polished smooth by wind and sun, the glare was so dazzling that the children had to put on sunglasses even on a partly cloudy afternoon.
She wore a dazzling silver dress to the school concert and walked onto the stage so confidently that every spotlight seemed to find her and the crowd cheered loudly.
entries.spellingNote: Dazzling has a double z: d-a-z-z-l-i-n-g; keep both z letters when adding -ing.

entries.definition: Something, usually money, that you owe to another person, shop or bank and should pay back later.
entries.example: After the shop's loan to buy new ovens, the bakery kept a careful list showing how much they still owed, planning each month to pay off the debt before the next winter rush.
examples: After the shop's loan to buy new ovens, the bakery kept a careful list showing how much they still owed, planning each month to pay off the debt before the next winter rush.
Tom took an evening job to earn pocket money and help reduce the debt the school trip organisers had after extra buses were needed, writing down every pound he saved.
When the family borrowed flour from a neighbour and later returned it, they still wrote the amount down as a debt to be cleared the following week so things stayed fair.
entries.spellingNote: Debt is spelled d-e-b-t with a silent b; the b is not pronounced.

entries.definition: to make someone believe something that is not true
entries.example: The fake treasure map was designed to deceive tourists into walking toward the souvenir shop. The dotted line looked ancient, but the ink smelled brand new.
examples: The fake treasure map was designed to deceive tourists into walking toward the souvenir shop. The dotted line looked ancient, but the ink smelled brand new.
Some insects deceive birds by looking like leaves or sticks. A hungry robin may stare straight at dinner and see only a twig.
The edited photo tried to deceive people into thinking the moon was twice its real size. A quick check of the original image revealed the trick.
entries.spellingNote: i before e here: deceive.

entries.definition: Tricked or led to believe something that is not true, often by someone hiding the real facts or lying.
entries.example: Lila felt deeply deceived when the old map promised a treasure marked with an X but only led her to a pile of empty shells on the beach where someone had hidden a prank.
examples: Lila felt deeply deceived when the old map promised a treasure marked with an X but only led her to a pile of empty shells on the beach where someone had hidden a prank.
The pupils were deceived by the pretend spell and gasped in surprise when the teacher revealed the bright paper decorations and explained how the trick worked.
He realised he had been deceived after the email promising free games turned out to be a trick to take his password, and he told his parents straight away.
entries.spellingNote: Deceive and deceived are written with ei after c: d-e-c-e-i-v-e, d-e-c-e-i-v-e-d; remember the ei after c.

entries.definition: A choice you make after thinking about the different options, or the act of choosing.
entries.example: Her decision to join the art club meant she could paint with others every Wednesday after school, and she felt excited about learning new colours and tricks from friends.
examples: Her decision to join the art club meant she could paint with others every Wednesday after school, and she felt excited about learning new colours and tricks from friends.
The captain's decision to change the route saved the team from walking into the thunderstorm during the expedition, and they found shelter just in time under a big oak.
Dad made a quick decision to bake extra buns when he saw more friends arriving than expected, and the extra warm bread soon disappeared with laughing hands and hungry smiles.
entries.spellingNote: Decision is spelled d-e-c-i-s-i-o-n; notice only one s, not two.

entries.definition: An official order or rule given by someone in authority, like a town leader or a court, that people must follow.
entries.example: The mayor issued a new decree that the town library would stay open later during the summer holidays, and volunteers quickly set up extra sessions and lists for readers.
examples: The mayor issued a new decree that the town library would stay open later during the summer holidays, and volunteers quickly set up extra sessions and lists for readers.
