After the storm, a royal decree ordered extra rations to be sent to the coastal villages, and workers loaded crates through rain and wind to help families recover.
In a playful mood the teacher made a light decree that anyone who wore silly hats on Friday could lead the line at lunch, which sent the whole class into cheerful planning.
entries.spellingNote: Decree ends with a double e: d-e-c-r-e-e; pronounce the long ee sound at the end.

entries.definition: Showing resistance to rules or authority, openly refusing to obey or accepting a challenge.
entries.example: She crossed her arms in a defiant stare when told to tidy the art area, as if daring anyone to make her stop drawing the picture she had promised to finish.
examples: She crossed her arms in a defiant stare when told to tidy the art area, as if daring anyone to make her stop drawing the picture she had promised to finish.
The defiant wind ripped the kite straight out of their hands and snapped the string, but the children laughed and chased it across the wet playing field anyway.
He gave a defiant shout at the bully and stood his ground until a teacher came to listen and helped both sides talk calmly about what had happened.
entries.spellingNote: Defiant is spelled d-e-f-i-a-n-t; note the -ant ending rather than -ent.

entries.definition: Clear and certain, not likely to change or be open to doubt.
entries.example: There was a definite sound of footsteps in the attic above, so the family checked carefully together with torches before switching on any other lights or making noise.
examples: There was a definite sound of footsteps in the attic above, so the family checked carefully together with torches before switching on any other lights or making noise.
She gave a definite answer that she would join the choir next term, so the teacher could write her name on the list and arrange a new music book.
The map had a definite red cross marking the start of the trail, so none of the explorers got lost on the first morning and the group kept to the right path.
entries.spellingNote: Definite is often misspelled as 'definate'; remember it's d-e-f-i-n-i-t-e with an i before the n.

entries.definition: Easily broken or needing very careful handling; also gentle, subtle or needing care and attention.
entries.example: The glass ornament was so delicate that Mia wrapped it in soft tissue and carried it with two careful hands all the way to the high shelf to keep it safe from knocks.
examples: The glass ornament was so delicate that Mia wrapped it in soft tissue and carried it with two careful hands all the way to the high shelf to keep it safe from knocks.
The doctor used a delicate touch to remove the tiny splinter from Ben's finger without making him cry, praising how calmly he sat while she worked.
They handled the tiny newborn chick in a delicate way, whispering so it would stay calm and keeping it warm under a soft towel until it could stand.
entries.spellingNote: Delicate is spelled d-e-l-i-c-a-t-e; the second syllable is 'li' and the final e is silent.

entries.definition: Very pleased and happy about something that happened.
entries.example: Mum was delighted when my class art was chosen for the school display, and she took a photo of me grinning with my paint-splattered apron.
examples: Mum was delighted when my class art was chosen for the school display, and she took a photo of me grinning with my paint-splattered apron.
I was delighted to see the lost puppy waiting outside the library, wagging its tail as if it knew help had finally arrived for it and me.
The whole team were delighted after the science fair because our volcano model worked, the judges smiled and everyone clapped loudly for our effort.
entries.spellingNote: Ends with -ed to show a feeling; remember the single l in delighted, not 'dellighed'.

entries.definition: Very bad or shocking in a way that deserves strong disapproval.
entries.example: The playground was left in deplorable condition after the storm, with broken fences and rubbish everywhere, which made the teachers very worried.
examples: The playground was left in deplorable condition after the storm, with broken fences and rubbish everywhere, which made the teachers very worried.
People described the river pollution as deplorable because fish were sick and the water was full of plastic and chemicals near the old factory.
The inspector wrote that the cramped, damp houses were deplorable, and he said changes had to be made to keep families safe and warm.
entries.spellingNote: Starts with de- and has -able at the end; watch the single p and -orable spelling.

entries.definition: Removed from an important position of power, often a leader or ruler.
entries.example: The old village mayor was deposed after the election, and a new leader promised better roads and safer crossings near the school.
examples: The old village mayor was deposed after the election, and a new leader promised better roads and safer crossings near the school.
In the history lesson we read how the king was deposed by his own nobles and forced to leave the castle in the middle of the night.
The club captain was deposed when a vote showed most members wanted someone else to organise the matches and training sessions.
entries.spellingNote: Deposed is de- + posed; do not confuse the s and p order, and pronounce the -ed at the end.

entries.definition: Empty and lonely, with little or no life or activity.
entries.example: The old farm looked desolate in winter, with leafless trees and a quiet farmhouse where windows were dark and no smoke rose from the chimney.
examples: The old farm looked desolate in winter, with leafless trees and a quiet farmhouse where windows were dark and no smoke rose from the chimney.
After the festival the field looked desolate, trampled and muddy, as if all the colour and music had been taken away overnight.
We climbed to the top of the cliff and saw a desolate beach below, empty shells scattered like forgotten toys under a grey sky.
entries.spellingNote: Has a single s and ends with -olate; do not write 'desolute' which is a different word.

entries.definition: A feeling of having no hope and being very upset or worried.
entries.example: After losing the map on the river trip, Tom felt a wave of despair, imagining they might be lost until someone found the right path again.
examples: After losing the map on the river trip, Tom felt a wave of despair, imagining they might be lost until someone found the right path again.
She almost gave up painting in despair when her colours ran out, but then a friend lent her paints and she kept going until it looked brilliant.
The team felt despair when the final goal went in, but their coach reminded them that next season offered a new chance to train harder.
entries.spellingNote: Contains 'spair' at the end; don't confuse with 'despairing' which adds -ing to show action.

entries.definition: very unhappy and without hope
entries.example: After the robot failed for the fourth time, the team grew despondent and stared at the scattered wires. Then their teacher reminded them that every failed test had taught them something exact.
examples: After the robot failed for the fourth time, the team grew despondent and stared at the scattered wires. Then their teacher reminded them that every failed test had taught them something exact.
The football captain looked despondent when the rain cancelled the final. She had trained for months, and for a moment even the silver trophy on the table seemed pointless.
When the rescue search paused overnight, the family became despondent. The harbour lights looked cheerful to everyone else, but to them each minute felt heavy.
entries.spellingNote: des + pond + ent.

entries.definition: Extremely unpleasant or hateful; something you strongly dislike and find morally wrong.
entries.example: The bully's mean scheme was detestable, and everyone felt angry that someone would try to trick a friend for a laugh.
examples: The bully's mean scheme was detestable, and everyone felt angry that someone would try to trick a friend for a laugh.
The museum guard described the vandal's graffiti as detestable because it ruined paintings and calendars with ugly marks.
She found the idea of cheating in the game detestable, so she told the referee and refused to be part of it even if it meant losing.
entries.spellingNote: Starts with de- and ends with -able; remember the single t after de- and the 'able' ending.

entries.definition: The strong will to keep trying until you reach a goal, even when it is hard.
entries.example: Her determination showed when she practised the piano every night for weeks until she could play the difficult piece perfectly in the concert.
examples: Her determination showed when she practised the piano every night for weeks until she could play the difficult piece perfectly in the concert.
The team's determination to finish the project meant they stayed after school, sharing ideas and fixing mistakes until the model was ready.
With quiet determination he climbed the hill step by step, stopping only to breathe, and finally reached the top as the sun rose.
entries.spellingNote: Has -tion at the end; remember the middle has 'terminate' root spelled with 'term' not 'therm'.

entries.definition: Having made a firm decision and not likely to change, showing strong will to do something.
entries.example: He was determined to win the race, training every evening and refusing to skip sprints even when it was cold and raining.
examples: He was determined to win the race, training every evening and refusing to skip sprints even when it was cold and raining.
She was determined not to let the mistake stop her, so she corrected it carefully and handed in the work again with a smile.
The scientists were determined to find the answer, testing the experiment again and again until the results were clear and steady.
entries.spellingNote: Two r's are not needed; it's determined with one r and -ed at the end for past/adj form.

entries.definition: To put someone off doing something by making them afraid of the results or convinced it is not worth trying.
entries.example: The tall fence was built to deter foxes from getting into the henhouse, with a strong gate and spikes to make it hard to climb.
examples: The tall fence was built to deter foxes from getting into the henhouse, with a strong gate and spikes to make it hard to climb.
Clear signs and a friendly lifeguard helped deter swimmers from going past the roped area when the water was dangerous.
Teachers hoped that talking about rules would deter late arrivals, so pupils understood why being on time mattered for everyone.
entries.spellingNote: Only four letters: d-e-t-e-r; do not confuse with 'deteriorate' which is a longer word.

entries.definition: Extremely shocked and very upset, often after something very bad has happened.
entries.example: The family was devastated when the old oak tree fell in the storm, because it had been where they played and took photos for years.
examples: The family was devastated when the old oak tree fell in the storm, because it had been where they played and took photos for years.
She was devastated by the news of the lost medals, having worked so hard and then seeing the box empty on the school shelf.
The town felt devastated after the fire, with shops closed and people sharing stories of what they had lost and what they hoped to rebuild.
entries.spellingNote: Has a -ated ending; the root is devastate, so the past form keeps the -ed with one t after 'deva'.

entries.definition: To move away from a plan, path, or usual way of doing something.
entries.example: The hikers had to deviate from the map because the path was flooded, so they followed animal tracks until they found a safe route down.
examples: The hikers had to deviate from the map because the path was flooded, so they followed animal tracks until they found a safe route down.
When the inventor chose to deviate from the usual design, her machine worked in a surprising new way and solved the problem.
Please do not deviate from the recipe unless you know what you are doing, because small changes can make a cake collapse or burn.
entries.spellingNote: Has 'viate' in the middle; don't swap letters—it's deviate, not 'deveate' or 'deviatte'.

entries.definition: To eat something quickly and hungrily, or to read or watch something with great eagerness.
entries.example: After the long hike we devour sandwiches so fast that crumbs covered our knees, and everyone laughed at how hungry we were.
examples: After the long hike we devour sandwiches so fast that crumbs covered our knees, and everyone laughed at how hungry we were.
She would devour any adventure book she found, finishing one and immediately starting the next as if the stories were treasure.
The kitten began to devour its dinner, tumbling paws-first into the bowl and finishing before the adult cats could reach it.
entries.spellingNote: Remember 'devour' with -our at the end in British English; it is not 'devor'.

entries.definition: working carefully and with effort
entries.example: The diligent engineer checked every bolt on the bridge model before the class tested it with weights. Her friends wanted to hurry, but she knew one loose join could ruin the whole experiment.
examples: The diligent engineer checked every bolt on the bridge model before the class tested it with weights. Her friends wanted to hurry, but she knew one loose join could ruin the whole experiment.
Every morning, the diligent violinist practised the same four tricky bars until her fingers stopped stumbling. By concert night, the difficult passage sounded effortless.
The diligent young reporter wrote down names, times, and exact quotes after the town meeting. Later, her article was the only one that got every detail right.
entries.spellingNote: di + li + gent.

entries.definition: to become or make something smaller or less important
entries.example: The sound of the parade began to diminish as the drums turned the corner and moved away. A minute later, only the faintest beat reached the classroom window.
examples: The sound of the parade began to diminish as the drums turned the corner and moved away. A minute later, only the faintest beat reached the classroom window.
The medicine helped diminish the swelling around Ava's ankle. It did not vanish at once, but each hour the puffiness looked a little smaller.
Planting trees can diminish the force of wind across an open playground. The wind still blows, but the leaves break up its power before it reaches the children.
entries.spellingNote: di + min + ish.

entries.definition: A measurement in one direction, such as length, width or height; it can also mean a particular aspect or part of something.
entries.example: The spaceship model had three dimensions: length, width and height, so Anna measured each dimension carefully with a ruler before building the tiny craft.
examples: The spaceship model had three dimensions: length, width and height, so Anna measured each dimension carefully with a ruler before building the tiny craft.
When the museum showed maps of another dimension of history, pupils saw how people's homes and clothes changed over hundreds of years and gasped at the differences.
In the art lesson, Leyla changed one dimension of her painting by adding more height to the towers, which made the castle look taller, darker and strangely more magical.
entries.spellingNote: dimension is spelled d-i-m-e-n-s-i-o-n; the ending -sion is pronounced like "-shun".

entries.definition: Being careful, polite and clever with words when dealing with people so you do not upset them and can help everyone agree.
entries.example: At the school meeting, Sam was diplomatic when the clubs argued, using gentle words to calm everyone and helping both sides find a fair plan to share the hall.
examples: At the school meeting, Sam was diplomatic when the clubs argued, using gentle words to calm everyone and helping both sides find a fair plan to share the hall.
When the two countries' teams met, the coach was diplomatic, smiling and choosing words that praised effort instead of blaming problems after the match.
During the art sale, Mrs Patel was diplomatic about the broken picture, offering a kind explanation and a helpful idea so the buyer did not feel upset.
entries.spellingNote: diplomatic is spelled d-i-p-l-o-m-a-t-i-c; remember the middle is "plom" not "plan".

entries.definition: Causing very great harm, damage or failure; something that goes very wrong and leads to serious trouble.
entries.example: A sudden hailstorm proved disastrous for the farmers' crops, smashing leaves and fruit so quickly that fields turned brown and worried families counted their losses.
examples: A sudden hailstorm proved disastrous for the farmers' crops, smashing leaves and fruit so quickly that fields turned brown and worried families counted their losses.
The computer crash before the fair was disastrous: the project files disappeared, the team could not present and the whole class felt stunned and upset.
When the small fire spread in the lab, the situation became disastrous, forcing the students out, spoiling experiments and costing the school many hours of work.
entries.spellingNote: disastrous is spelled d-i-s-a-s-t-r-o-u-s; it comes from the word "disaster" plus -ous.

entries.definition: Careful and quiet about what you say or do so you do not attract attention or reveal private information.
entries.example: Sofia was discreet when she slipped a tiny surprise note into her mum's lunchbox, peeking around the kitchen to make sure no one else saw her secret plan.
examples: Sofia was discreet when she slipped a tiny surprise note into her mum's lunchbox, peeking around the kitchen to make sure no one else saw her secret plan.
The headteacher was discreet about a family problem, speaking quietly with the pupil so their classmates would not learn something private and feel embarrassed.
The detective kept the witness's tip discreet until there was proof, hiding the papers and sharing them only with the team to avoid causing panic.
entries.spellingNote: discreet has a double e before the t (d-i-s-c-r-e-e-t); do not confuse it with the similarly spelled word "discrete".

entries.definition: Made up of many different kinds of things or people; showing variety rather than being all the same.
entries.example: The library's shelves were diverse, with picture books, fact books, stories from other countries and science guides, so every child found something exciting to read.
examples: The library's shelves were diverse, with picture books, fact books, stories from other countries and science guides, so every child found something exciting to read.
The forest walk amazed the class because the path was diverse: oak, pine, ferns and tiny flowers all grew close together and insects buzzed everywhere.
On multicultural day the kitchen served diverse dishes and the playground rang with songs in many languages, so pupils tasted new flavours and learned new dances.
entries.spellingNote: diverse is spelled d-i-v-e-r-s-e; it is related to the word "diversity" but ends in -se.

entries.definition: To have control over something, to be the strongest or most important, or to be most common in a place or situation.
entries.example: In the playground match, the older team began to dominate the game, taking the ball quickly, scoring goal after goal and forcing the others to change tactics.
examples: In the playground match, the older team began to dominate the game, taking the ball quickly, scoring goal after goal and forcing the others to change tactics.
The tall pines dominate the hill now, their trunks and shadows covering most of the slope so hikers see mainly green and brown when they climb.
Along the riverbank the invasive weed started to dominate the water, growing so thick that native plants and tiny fish had far less space to live.
entries.spellingNote: dominate is spelled d-o-m-i-n-a-t-e; the ending -ate is pronounced clearly as '-ate'.

entries.definition: To feel very worried or frightened about something that might happen, often imagining the worst outcome.
entries.example: Lara began to dread the dentist visit after hearing a friend's story about loud drills, so she pictured each noise and felt her stomach twist with worry.
examples: Lara began to dread the dentist visit after hearing a friend's story about loud drills, so she pictured each noise and felt her stomach twist with worry.
We all dread surprise maths tests because the idea of unknown questions makes pencils shake and hearts race for a little while before the bell.
At night Tom felt dread before the thunderstorm; he hugged his teddy, closed his curtains and waited for the loud bangs to pass so he could sleep again.
entries.spellingNote: dread is spelled d-r-e-a-d; do not add extra letters or confuse it with 'bread'.

entries.definition: Very bad, unpleasant or making people feel upset or afraid; something that causes strong dislike or worry.
entries.example: The long bus delay before the final match felt dreadful; players sat cold and nervous, worried they would miss the kickoff and lose their chance to play.
examples: The long bus delay before the final match felt dreadful; players sat cold and nervous, worried they would miss the kickoff and lose their chance to play.
A dreadful smell came from the bin after the picnic was left in the sun, forcing everyone to open windows and hurry the rubbish outside.
The loud thunder during the dark film was dreadful to some pupils, who covered their ears and wished the screening would end quickly and quietly.
entries.spellingNote: dreadful is formed from "dread" + "ful" and is spelled d-r-e-a-d-f-u-l; note it uses "-ful" not "-full".

entries.definition: A long period with very little or no rain, causing plants to die, rivers to shrink and water to become scarce.
entries.example: After six months with hardly any rain the village suffered a drought; farmers watched their cracked fields, stored water carefully and prayed for clouds to appear.
examples: After six months with hardly any rain the village suffered a drought; farmers watched their cracked fields, stored water carefully and prayed for clouds to appear.
A drought made the river shrink so much that fish were crowded into small pools and children saw mud where boats had once floated freely.
The school's weather project showed how drought makes food harder to grow and how families, shops and animals all feel the effect when rain does not arrive.
entries.spellingNote: drought is spelled d-r-o-u-g-h-t; the "ough" is pronounced like "owt", which is a tricky sound to remember.

entries.definition: A place where a person, family or animal lives, such as a house, flat, den or hut.
entries.example: The robin built a tiny dwelling in the eaves, a warm, hidden nest that sheltered her chicks through wind and rain until they learned to fly.
examples: The robin built a tiny dwelling in the eaves, a warm, hidden nest that sheltered her chicks through wind and rain until they learned to fly.
After the storm the family slept in a temporary dwelling at the village hall, sharing blankets and soup while their house was repaired over weeks.
Archaeologists found an old stone dwelling on the hill, full of pottery and tools that told stories about the people who once lived there long ago.
entries.spellingNote: dwelling is spelled d-w-e-l-l-i-n-g; remember the starting sound is "dw" and there are two l's before -ing.

entries.definition: to become smaller or less over time
entries.example: The pile of emergency biscuits began to dwindle as the snow kept the village indoors for a third day. By Friday, only the broken ones at the bottom of the tin remained.
examples: The pile of emergency biscuits began to dwindle as the snow kept the village indoors for a third day. By Friday, only the broken ones at the bottom of the tin remained.
The applause started loud but began to dwindle when the magician took too long finding the missing card. Soon only his proud aunt was still clapping.
As the river dried, the number of fish in the shallow pools started to dwindle. Herons gathered at the edges because the water was shrinking fast.
entries.spellingNote: Starts dw-, like dwarf.

entries.definition: Serious and sincere in meaning or action; showing you really mean what you say and are not joking.
entries.example: Lina made an earnest promise to look after the class hamster, writing a daily plan and meaning every word so her teacher and friends trusted her completely.
examples: Lina made an earnest promise to look after the class hamster, writing a daily plan and meaning every word so her teacher and friends trusted her completely.
The player gave an earnest apology after the accidental push, and the other team accepted it so the match could continue in good spirit.
When Tom practised the piano in earnest before the concert, he focused so fully that the rest of the family tiptoed past his door to avoid interrupting.
entries.spellingNote: earnest is spelled e-a-r-n-e-s-t; do not confuse it with the name Ernest, which is capitalised but sounds the same.

entries.definition: To flow back or away from the land (about the tide) or to become smaller or weaker over time.
entries.example: As the tide began to ebb, the beach widened quickly and children ran out to explore pools left behind full of crabs and shiny shells along the sand.
examples: As the tide began to ebb, the beach widened quickly and children ran out to explore pools left behind full of crabs and shiny shells along the sand.
Her excitement started to ebb after the train delays and cancelled plans, so she tucked the party decorations away and tried to cheer up the guests instead.
The team's confidence began to ebb after three losses in a row, so the coach held a long talk to remind them of their strengths and plan new practise drills.
entries.spellingNote: ebb is spelled e-b-b with a double b at the end; do not drop the second b.

entries.definition: Extremely happy and excited, feeling joyful in a wide, lively way.
entries.example: When Mia found the lost dog waiting on the doorstep, she felt ecstatic and shouted for her family to come and see the surprise.
examples: When Mia found the lost dog waiting on the doorstep, she felt ecstatic and shouted for her family to come and see the surprise.
After the whole class's volcano erupted perfectly, the teacher was ecstatic and clapped while we all grinned and high-fived each other.
Grandpa was ecstatic when his chess club sent him a letter inviting him to the county final; he danced a little in the kitchen that evening.
entries.spellingNote: ecstatic is spelled e-c-s-t-a-t-i-c with 'ec' at the start and ending '-tic'.

entries.definition: A large, important building, often impressive or long-lasting.
entries.example: The old stone edifice on the hill had tall windows and a hidden room; the children dared each other to knock and explore at dusk.
examples: The old stone edifice on the hill had tall windows and a hidden room; the children dared each other to knock and explore at dusk.
Our town's new library is an impressive edifice with glass walls that catch sunlight and shelves that smell of fresh books on wooden aisles.
Archaeologists studied the ruined edifice, sketching carved stones and guessing which god the builders once worshipped beside the broken steps.
entries.spellingNote: edifice is spelled e-d-i-f-i-c-e and ends with '-ice', not '-ise' or '-ace'.

entries.definition: Working well without wasting time, energy or materials; getting good results quickly.
entries.example: Sam's method of sorting the pens by colour was so efficient that lining them up took just two minutes and the whole class applauded his tidy system.
examples: Sam's method of sorting the pens by colour was so efficient that lining them up took just two minutes and the whole class applauded his tidy system.
The new heating system is efficient; it warms every classroom quickly while using less electricity than the old boilers did last winter.
An efficient team passed the raft test: they fixed leaks, shared tools and crossed the river before the sun dipped behind the trees at camp.
entries.spellingNote: Write efficient with two f's at the start (eff-) and the ending '-cient'.

entries.definition: Very happy and excited, often because something good has just happened.
entries.example: When the team heard their names announced as the winners, they felt elated and jumped up, hugging each other under the bright gym lights.
examples: When the team heard their names announced as the winners, they felt elated and jumped up, hugging each other under the bright gym lights.
Priya was elated on her birthday morning when she opened a hand-written card from her best friend tucked under her pillow on the bed.
After passing the hard piano exam, Tom walked home elated, practising the smile that would not stop on his face as he hummed the tune.
entries.spellingNote: elated has one 'l' and ends in '-ated'; remember it's e-l-a-t-e-d.

entries.definition: graceful, stylish, and attractive
entries.example: The engineer found an elegant solution to the bridge problem: one curved support instead of five heavy beams. It looked simple because the hard thinking was hidden inside the design.
examples: The engineer found an elegant solution to the bridge problem: one curved support instead of five heavy beams. It looked simple because the hard thinking was hidden inside the design.
The dancer made an elegant turn, landing so quietly that the bells on her costume barely sounded. Every movement looked controlled, light, and graceful.
The mathematician wrote an elegant proof that filled only half a page. Nobody called it plain; they called it beautiful because every line mattered.
entries.spellingNote: el + e + gant.

entries.definition: able to express ideas clearly and beautifully
entries.example: The eloquent student did not just say the park mattered; she described the toddlers learning to cycle, the old men playing chess, and the trees cooling the street. By the end, the council listened.
examples: The eloquent student did not just say the park mattered; she described the toddlers learning to cycle, the old men playing chess, and the trees cooling the street. By the end, the council listened.
Martin Luther King Jr. gave eloquent speeches that turned a demand for justice into words people could remember and repeat. The power came from meaning, rhythm, and courage together.
The museum guide was eloquent when explaining the tiny fossil. In two minutes, she made a grey stone feel like a message from an ancient sea.
entries.spellingNote: elo + quent.

entries.definition: Gases or tiny particles sent out into the air, often from cars, factories or chimneys.
entries.example: When the town recorded high emissions from lorries, children made posters to warn drivers and suggest walking or cycling more to help clean the air.
examples: When the town recorded high emissions from lorries, children made posters to warn drivers and suggest walking or cycling more to help clean the air.
Scientists measured the car's emissions during the test drive and found a small leak that pushed the pollution numbers higher than expected.
After the factory fixed its chimneys, local emissions fell and the blue hills looked clearer on the next morning walk along the lane.
entries.spellingNote: emissions is spelled e-m-i-s-s-i-o-n-s and has a double 's' before the 'ion' ending.

entries.definition: A ruler who governs a large group of countries or an empire, usually more powerful than a king.
entries.example: The museum's gold crown belonged to an emperor who once ruled many islands; the plaque told stories of grand ceremonies and ocean voyages.
examples: The museum's gold crown belonged to an emperor who once ruled many islands; the plaque told stories of grand ceremonies and ocean voyages.
In the history lesson we read how a young emperor wrote letters to faraway governors to keep peace along the long roads of the empire.
The emperor's old coin was dug up by the riverbank during the dig, and the class guessed which century it might come from before lunch.
entries.spellingNote: Emperor is spelled e-m-p-e-r-o-r; note the two 'e's in the word and the final '-or'.

entries.definition: To show that something is important or to give it more attention than other things.
entries.example: To emphasise the safety rule, Miss Clark drew a red circle around the steps and asked everyone to practise slowing down on the stairs.
examples: To emphasise the safety rule, Miss Clark drew a red circle around the steps and asked everyone to practise slowing down on the stairs.
He used a bright poster to emphasise the science fair date so no one would forget to bring their project on Friday morning.
The coach would often emphasise listening to teammates, not just winning, and our games grew kinder and better because of that lesson.
entries.spellingNote: Use the British spelling emphasise with an 's' rather than a 'z' (emphasise vs emphasize).

entries.definition: To give someone a job or to make use of something for a particular purpose.
entries.example: The school will employ a new librarian who loves stories and plans cosy reading afternoons with hot chocolate for Year 5.
examples: The school will employ a new librarian who loves stories and plans cosy reading afternoons with hot chocolate for Year 5.
We decided to employ a ruler and protractor for the craft project so the lines would be neat and the stars would look even.
My aunt will employ her baking skills to make enough cakes for the charity sale and she practised the recipes all week.
entries.spellingNote: Employ ends with '-ploy' like the word 'ploy'; do not add an extra 'e' at the end.

entries.definition: To meet someone or something, often unexpectedly, or to experience a situation.
entries.example: On the woods walk the class was amazed to encounter a shy fox that watched from behind the brambles before slipping away into the ferns.
examples: On the woods walk the class was amazed to encounter a shy fox that watched from behind the brambles before slipping away into the ferns.
The sailor hoped not to encounter rocks in the fog, so she listened carefully for the warning bell near the harbour wall.
During the seaside trip we were surprised to encounter jellyfish near the rocks, and the ranger explained how to stay safe and leave them alone.
entries.spellingNote: Encounter is spelled e-n-c-o-u-n-t-e-r; remember the 'en-' start and the 'counter' ending.

entries.definition: To continue through difficulty or pain without giving up, or to last for a long time.
entries.example: The tiny lighthouse had to endure fierce storms every winter, but it stood firm and guided sailors through the dark nights.
examples: The tiny lighthouse had to endure fierce storms every winter, but it stood firm and guided sailors through the dark nights.
She tried to endure the long practice without complaint, knowing that patience and practice would make her piano playing better.
Old songs endure in the village because grandparents teach them to children at summer fairs and the tunes are sung year after year.
entries.spellingNote: Endure is spelled e-n-d-u-r-e; do not confuse it with ensure or insure.

entries.definition: Very, very large in size, number or amount.
entries.example: The blue whale skeleton in the museum looked enormous to us, stretching across the gallery like a sleeping dragon over the benches.
examples: The blue whale skeleton in the museum looked enormous to us, stretching across the gallery like a sleeping dragon over the benches.
When the pumpkin contest ended, people stood around the enormous squash that filled half the farmer's trailer and laughed at its size.
An enormous pile of autumn leaves blocked the path, and we had to work as a team to push our bicycles through the crunchy heap.
entries.spellingNote: Enormous is spelled e-n-o-r-m-o-u-s; watch the order of the letters and do not insert an extra 'u'.

entries.definition: Very excited and keen about something, showing strong interest and energy.
entries.example: Lara was enthusiastic about the nature club, arriving early with binoculars and a notebook full of questions for the leader.
examples: Lara was enthusiastic about the nature club, arriving early with binoculars and a notebook full of questions for the leader.
The whole class was enthusiastic during the science experiment, cheering when the colours changed and being careful with the glassware.
Dad wasn't enthusiastic about early mornings, but he cheered when the family picnic turned into a treasure hunt by the lake.
entries.spellingNote: Enthusiastic contains 'thusi' in the middle and ends in '-astic'; remember the 'th' sound after 'en'.

entries.definition: A disease that spreads quickly and affects a large number of people in the same area at the same time.
entries.example: When the epidemic made many pupils cough, the school closed for two weeks and Mrs Khan taught lessons online while worried parents waited outside the gate.
examples: When the epidemic made many pupils cough, the school closed for two weeks and Mrs Khan taught lessons online while worried parents waited outside the gate.
The town's market grew quiet during the epidemic as families stayed indoors, and volunteers organised food deliveries for elderly neighbours.
Doctors tracked the epidemic by testing people at the clinic and drawing maps to show where new cases were appearing in the streets.
entries.spellingNote: Remember the -emic ending, like in 'pandemic'; the word starts with epi- (on or upon).

entries.definition: Continuing forever or for a very, very long time with no end.
entries.example: The children thought the ancient hillside felt eternal because the path had been walked for hundreds of years and the same sun rose every morning above it.
examples: The children thought the ancient hillside felt eternal because the path had been walked for hundreds of years and the same sun rose every morning above it.
Grandad told stories about the stars and how their light seemed eternal to him, as if those tiny points in the sky had never changed.
The summer day seemed eternal when the family picnicked under a huge oak and no one wanted to leave, as if time had slowed just for them.
entries.spellingNote: Note the -ernal ending, not -ional; it is spelled e-t-e-r-n-a-l.

entries.definition: A short part taken from a longer text, book, speech, or film.
entries.example: For the book report Mia read an excerpt from the middle chapter to the class so everyone could hear the funniest scene with the school trip.
examples: For the book report Mia read an excerpt from the middle chapter to the class so everyone could hear the funniest scene with the school trip.
The teacher played an excerpt of the old radio drama during history because the short clip showed how people talked in the 1940s.
Tom saved an excerpt of the poem on his phone and practised saying those lines until he could recite them out loud without stopping.
entries.spellingNote: Remember the exc- start and -erpt ending; there is no s after the x.

entries.definition: Very tired in body or mind, with little or no energy left.
entries.example: After the sports day that lasted all afternoon, Anna was exhausted and fell asleep on the sofa with her muddy trainers still on beside her bag.
examples: After the sports day that lasted all afternoon, Anna was exhausted and fell asleep on the sofa with her muddy trainers still on beside her bag.
The scientist worked through the night and was exhausted by morning, but she smiled when her experiment finally gave the result she had hoped for.
By the time the dog returned from the long hike, it lay sprawled on the porch, exhausted and dreaming of the river they had crossed together.
entries.spellingNote: Note the double s in the middle: e-x-h-a-u-s-t-e-d.

entries.definition: Extremely beautiful, delicate, or made with great skill and care.
entries.example: Lila found an exquisite shell on the beach, its spiral shining like tiny paintwork and so detailed she kept it on her windowsill as a treasure.
examples: Lila found an exquisite shell on the beach, its spiral shining like tiny paintwork and so detailed she kept it on her windowsill as a treasure.
The cake at the village fair had exquisite icing roses that looked almost too perfect to eat, and everyone asked the baker how she had made them.
A jeweller showed the class an exquisite pendant from long ago and explained how careful tools had been used to make every tiny pattern.
entries.spellingNote: Watch the -quisite ending (q-u-i-s-i-t-e); it is not spelled with a c after the q.

entries.definition: Full of energy, excitement, and cheerful enthusiasm.
entries.example: The playground was full of exuberant children after the summer concert, shouting and dancing with handmade flags until the sun began to set.
examples: The playground was full of exuberant children after the summer concert, shouting and dancing with handmade flags until the sun began to set.
In spring the garden felt exuberant as bright tulips and daffodils burst into colour and bees darted happily from flower to flower.
The puppy greeted everyone at the door with exuberant jumps and wagging tail so that the postman laughed and forgot about the parcels for a moment.
entries.spellingNote: Remember the -uber- in the middle and the -ant ending: e-x-u-b-e-r-a-n-t.

entries.definition: A building where goods are made or assembled using machines and people.
entries.example: On the school trip we visited a factory that made bicycles, and we watched wheels and frames move down the line as workers checked each part.
examples: On the school trip we visited a factory that made bicycles, and we watched wheels and frames move down the line as workers checked each part.
The factory's tall chimneys stood against the grey sky and the guide explained how different teams worked together to pack the toys before they were sent to shops.
Mum told a story of how she used to work in a small chocolate factory where every bar was wrapped by hand during busy holidays.
entries.spellingNote: A factory ends with -ory, not -ary; remember f-a-c-t-o-r-y.

entries.definition: To hesitate or lose strength or confidence for a short time; to stop briefly or speak unsteadily.
entries.example: Just before reading her poem, Meg's voice began to falter, then she took a deep breath and continued more slowly until the applause arrived.
examples: Just before reading her poem, Meg's voice began to falter, then she took a deep breath and continued more slowly until the applause arrived.
The young runner did not falter even when the hill steepened; he slowed a little but then found energy to finish the race with a grin.
The lamp's light started to falter during the storm, flickering so that the family played cards by the safer glow of a torch instead.
entries.spellingNote: Falter is spelled f-a-l-t-e-r; the l comes after the a, not before.

entries.definition: great tiredness
entries.example: After cycling across the island, fatigue made Arda miss the turning even though the sign was bright red. His legs were not the only tired part; his thinking had slowed too.
examples: After cycling across the island, fatigue made Arda miss the turning even though the sign was bright red. His legs were not the only tired part; his thinking had slowed too.
The astronaut described space fatigue after weeks of alarms, experiments, and floating sleep. Even exciting missions can exhaust the body and brain.
During the long chess final, fatigue changed the game. The players still knew the rules perfectly, but tired eyes began to miss obvious moves.
entries.spellingNote: Ends with -gue.

entries.definition: All the animals living in a particular place or during a particular time.
entries.example: The school nature walk booklet showed the local fauna, with pictures of foxes, hedgehogs and many birds that could be seen in nearby fields.
examples: The school nature walk booklet showed the local fauna, with pictures of foxes, hedgehogs and many birds that could be seen in nearby fields.
Scientists studying the island's fauna found unusual beetles and colourful frogs that lived nowhere else in the world, which made the research exciting.
In the museum a display explained how the fauna of the ancient forest differed from today, with fossils proving that giant insects once lived there.
entries.spellingNote: Fauna starts with f-a-u-; remember the vowel pair au like in 'autumn'.

entries.definition: Very weak or without much strength, power, or force.
entries.example: After the long illness his voice sounded feeble on the phone, barely loud enough to tell his family he was feeling a little better today.
examples: After the long illness his voice sounded feeble on the phone, barely loud enough to tell his family he was feeling a little better today.
The candle gave a feeble light in the attic, so Tom crawled back downstairs to fetch a torch before he could read the old map properly.
Grandad made a feeble attempt to reach the jar on the top shelf and laughed when his granddaughter handed it down to him with a grin.
entries.spellingNote: Feeble has the unusual -eble ending; remember the e before the b: f-e-e-b-l-e.

entries.definition: Very strong, violent, or full of intense feeling; powerful and sometimes aggressive.
entries.example: A fierce wind blew off the roofs of the market stalls, and everyone rushed to hold down their umbrellas as papers scattered down the street.
examples: A fierce wind blew off the roofs of the market stalls, and everyone rushed to hold down their umbrellas as papers scattered down the street.
The debate grew fierce when the teams argued loudly about science class rules, but afterwards they shook hands and laughed about it.
At the zoo we watched a fierce tiger protect her cubs, padding close with eyes bright whenever anyone came near the glass.
entries.spellingNote: Fierce is spelled f-i-e-r-c-e; the ie comes before the r, not after.

entries.definition: bright, confident, and attracting attention
entries.example: The actor arrived in a flamboyant purple coat with silver stars stitched across the sleeves. Even the photographers forgot the red carpet and stared at the coat first.
examples: The actor arrived in a flamboyant purple coat with silver stars stitched across the sleeves. Even the photographers forgot the red carpet and stared at the coat first.
A peacock's flamboyant tail is not subtle; it flashes blue, green, and gold like a moving fan. The bird seems to announce itself before it takes a step.
The bakery made a flamboyant birthday cake shaped like a volcano, with red sugar lava pouring down the sides. It was impossible to pretend the cake was ordinary.
entries.spellingNote: flam + boy + ant.

entries.definition: A group of ships, aircraft, or vehicles operated together; also can mean moving quickly.
entries.example: At dawn the harbour filled with a fleet of small fishing boats returning with boxes of shiny mackerel, and gulls dived noisily above them.
examples: At dawn the harbour filled with a fleet of small fishing boats returning with boxes of shiny mackerel, and gulls dived noisily above them.
The delivery company had a fleet of vans that left the depot each morning, racing across narrow lanes so parcels arrived before lunch.
During the race the runner was fleet of foot, darting between competitors and finishing the final lap with a quick, proud smile.
entries.spellingNote: Fleet has a double e: f-l-e-e-t; remember the long ee sound.

entries.definition: All the plants that grow in a particular place or at a particular time, from tiny mosses to tall trees.
entries.example: The botanist pointed to the chalk cliff and said the rare chalk grassland is full of unique flora that you won’t find in the nearby pine forest.
examples: The botanist pointed to the chalk cliff and said the rare chalk grassland is full of unique flora that you won’t find in the nearby pine forest.
On the island trip the children recorded the coastal flora, like sea thrift and samphire, and drew careful pictures beside each name.
In the school nature trail we learned local flora by pressing leaves in a book and labelling each one with where we found it.
entries.spellingNote: Flora is short and ends in -a; it refers to plant life, not just a single flower.

entries.definition: To grow or develop strongly and healthily, or to do something with a bold, lively movement.
entries.example: After weeks of care the tomato plant began to flourish in the sunny window, sprouting thick stems and bright fruit that surprised everyone in the class.
examples: After weeks of care the tomato plant began to flourish in the sunny window, sprouting thick stems and bright fruit that surprised everyone in the class.
At the school play the actor gave a small flourish with his hat as the audience laughed, making the final scene feel proud and bright.
In her sketchbook leaves began to flourish across the page as she mixed greens and blues and the drawing looked like a wild garden.
entries.spellingNote: Remember the 'ou' in flourish and the ending '-ish'.

entries.definition: The part of a picture or scene that is nearest to the viewer; the area that looks closest.
entries.example: In the photograph the little red bike sits in the foreground while the castle stands far away, making the bike look very large in the scene.
examples: In the photograph the little red bike sits in the foreground while the castle stands far away, making the bike look very large in the scene.
When we draw a park, we put big trees in the foreground to show they are closer and smaller people near the horizon to seem far away.
The teacher said the frog in the foreground looked worried because you could see its face clearly while the pond behind was fuzzy.
entries.spellingNote: Foreground is one word, not two (not 'fore ground').

entries.definition: To lose something or give it up because of a rule, a mistake, or as a penalty.
entries.example: Because the team arrived late for the match they had to forfeit their warm-up and start with fewer players, which made them nervous and quiet.
examples: Because the team arrived late for the match they had to forfeit their warm-up and start with fewer players, which made them nervous and quiet.
When Iris broke the class rules she had to forfeit her art afternoon, learning that some choices can cost you special time.
If you forget to water the school greenhouse plants you might forfeit the chance to harvest beans for the science fair.
entries.spellingNote: Spell it forfeit — not 'forfiet'.

entries.definition: To make something stronger or safer, for example by adding protection or extra nutrients.
entries.example: The village began to fortify its old stone walls with extra timber before the storm season, stacking beams and sandbags to keep everyone safe.
examples: The village began to fortify its old stone walls with extra timber before the storm season, stacking beams and sandbags to keep everyone safe.
Many makers choose to fortify breakfast cereals with vitamins so growing children get extra nutrients for strong bones.
The scout troop learned how to fortify a tent by piling rocks around the edges to stop water running in after heavy rain.
entries.spellingNote: Fortify ends with '-ify' (not '-ize').

entries.definition: A large amount of money or a person’s luck and chance of good or bad events.
entries.example: Nana told a story about how a small apple tree grew into an orchard and made the family a quiet fortune when the market for cider rose.
examples: Nana told a story about how a small apple tree grew into an orchard and made the family a quiet fortune when the market for cider rose.
In the story the pirate lost his fortune to a storm, reminding us that fortune can change quickly and is not always about coins.
At the fair Tom tried his luck at the ring toss and joked that striking the big prize would bring him a fortune in stuffed toys.
entries.spellingNote: Fortune has two syllables: for-tune; it can mean money or luck.

entries.definition: to crack or break, or a crack or break
entries.example: The X-ray showed a thin fracture in Leo's wrist after he fell from the climbing frame. It was not a dramatic break, but the doctor still wrapped it in a cast.
examples: The X-ray showed a thin fracture in Leo's wrist after he fell from the climbing frame. It was not a dramatic break, but the doctor still wrapped it in a cast.
A tiny fracture ran across the windscreen after a stone flew up from the lorry. By morning, the cold had stretched the crack from one side to the other.
Geologists found a fracture in the cliff where rainwater had frozen and expanded. The line looked harmless until a whole slab finally split away.
entries.spellingNote: frac + ture.

entries.definition: easily broken or damaged
entries.example: The museum worker lifted the fragile Roman cup with both hands and carried it over a padded table. It had survived nearly two thousand years, but one clumsy bump could still crack it.
examples: The museum worker lifted the fragile Roman cup with both hands and carried it over a padded table. It had survived nearly two thousand years, but one clumsy bump could still crack it.
After the storm, a fragile bird egg lay in the grass below the hedge. Mia did not pick it up; she called an adult because the shell looked thinner than paper.
The coral reef looked like a colourful underwater city, but it was fragile. A careless fin kick could break a piece that had taken years to grow.
entries.spellingNote: The middle sounds like 'jile' but is spelled gile.

entries.definition: The ability to choose, move, or say things without being controlled by others; independence.
entries.example: When the school bell rang the children felt a burst of freedom as they raced into the playground to choose games and run wild for half an hour.
examples: When the school bell rang the children felt a burst of freedom as they raced into the playground to choose games and run wild for half an hour.
The rescued bird was given freedom back into the wild, and the class watched it fly to the nearest oak with cheering.
In group work Mia suggested a rule to let everyone pick a role, giving each pupil more freedom to try something new.
entries.spellingNote: Freedom is written as one word, not 'free-dom' or 'freedon'.

entries.definition: Feeling annoyed or upset because something is not working or because you cannot do what you want.
entries.example: Sam felt frustrated when his paper plane kept nosediving, even after trying different folds and asking friends for advice.
examples: Sam felt frustrated when his paper plane kept nosediving, even after trying different folds and asking friends for advice.
The puzzle made the whole group frustrated until Lila found the clever corner piece that linked everything together.
After waiting ages for the paint to dry, the artist felt frustrated when a cat's paw left a print across the drying picture.
entries.spellingNote: Frustrated ends with -ed for the feeling; the verb is frustrate.

entries.definition: Unlikely to succeed or pointless to try; something that will not work no matter what you do.
entries.example: Climbing the slippery fence without shoes felt futile, because every time they reached the top their feet slid and they fell back down.
examples: Climbing the slippery fence without shoes felt futile, because every time they reached the top their feet slid and they fell back down.
Trying to stop the tide with sandcastles was futile; the waves kept crashing in and washing the walls away faster than they could dig.
He kept whispering answers to the locked box, but the code needed numbers and his hints were futile against the secret lock.
entries.spellingNote: Futile has 'ti' pronounced like 'tile' and ends with -ile.

entries.definition: Brave and polite; showing courage and kindness, often when helping or protecting others.
entries.example: The gallant pupil raced into the drizzle to pull the soaked kitten from the drain and carried it gently back to Mrs Khan's porch.
examples: The gallant pupil raced into the drizzle to pull the soaked kitten from the drain and carried it gently back to Mrs Khan's porch.
In the school play the knight looked gallant as he bowed and promised to protect the village from the dragon.
Even though his boots were muddy, the gallant friend offered his dry scarf to warm Sara during the cold walk home.
entries.spellingNote: Gallant has two Ls and ends with -ant, like 'gallant knight'.

entries.definition: Willing to give or share time, things, or praise with others without expecting much in return.
entries.example: The generous pupil gave half his packed lunch to his friend who had forgotten theirs, and they shared sandwiches under the oak tree.
examples: The generous pupil gave half his packed lunch to his friend who had forgotten theirs, and they shared sandwiches under the oak tree.
Mrs Patel was generous with stickers and praise, so every small success in class felt like a celebration.
When the cake sale raised money, the generous donors paid extra so the school trip could include the whole class.
entries.spellingNote: Generous begins with 'gen-' and uses -rous, not -ous or -is.

entries.definition: real, honest, or sincere
entries.example: When Sami said sorry for breaking the model rocket, his apology sounded genuine. He did not blame anyone else; he brought glue, stayed late, and helped rebuild the bent fins.
examples: When Sami said sorry for breaking the model rocket, his apology sounded genuine. He did not blame anyone else; he brought glue, stayed late, and helped rebuild the bent fins.
The jeweller showed Mum how to spot a genuine pearl by its uneven surface and soft shine. The plastic copy looked perfect, but that perfection was the clue that it was fake.
A genuine smile spread across the runner's face when she saw her little brother at the finish line. It was not posed for the camera; it burst out before she could hide it.
entries.spellingNote: Starts gen- and ends -uine.

entries.definition: Extremely large in size, much bigger than normal.
entries.example: A gigantic oak towered in the park, its trunk so wide the whole class could not reach around it even with their arms linked.
examples: A gigantic oak towered in the park, its trunk so wide the whole class could not reach around it even with their arms linked.
They discovered a gigantic footprint on the mud trail and imagined a friendly giant had walked by the night before.
At the museum a gigantic dinosaur skeleton loomed above the visitors, making soft whispers feel tiny under its bones.
entries.spellingNote: Gigantic starts with 'gi' like giant, not 'gih-'; no double g.

entries.definition: A dull or dark feeling or appearance that makes a place or a person seem sad, cheerless or not bright.
entries.example: The sky looked gloomy all morning as the fog crept in, and the class whispered about whether the school trip might be cancelled.
examples: The sky looked gloomy all morning as the fog crept in, and the class whispered about whether the school trip might be cancelled.
Grandpa sat by the window with a gloomy face after the bad news, but he still smiled when the dog jumped into his lap.
The garden seemed gloomy under the heavy clouds, so we put on coats and decided to search for worms by torchlight instead.
entries.spellingNote: gloomy has double o followed by my; remember the two o letters before the ending -my.

entries.definition: Moving in a smooth, elegant, and controlled way that looks pleasant and easy to watch.
entries.example: The dancer moved graceful across the stage, her arms and feet telling the story while the audience held its breath.
examples: The dancer moved graceful across the stage, her arms and feet telling the story while the audience held its breath.
The deer leapt over the stream with a graceful jump, and Tom whispered that it looked like a picture in a nature book.
When the ice skater spun, she looked graceful under the bright lights, and even the judges clapped before the music stopped.
entries.spellingNote: graceful is spelled with -ful at the end, not -fully; think graceful like graceful movement.

entries.definition: Feeling thankful because someone has helped you or given you something good.
entries.example: After the neighbours cleared the snow from our path, I felt grateful and made them a mug of hot chocolate to say thank you.
examples: After the neighbours cleared the snow from our path, I felt grateful and made them a mug of hot chocolate to say thank you.
Lila was grateful for the extra minutes her teacher gave her to finish the test, so she worked carefully on the last question.
When the rescue dog wagged its tail, Ben felt grateful that the shelter staff had looked after it until it found a home.
entries.spellingNote: grateful has only one 'e' after the 'r' — not 'greatful'; think grateful = great + full of thanks.

entries.definition: Serious and unhappy in a way that feels harsh or worrying, often about something difficult or without hope.
entries.example: The teacher's face looked grim when she read the report, and the whole class fell quiet, sensing something was wrong.
examples: The teacher's face looked grim when she read the report, and the whole class fell quiet, sensing something was wrong.
The weather forecast gave a grim warning about floods, so the village packed sandbags and checked the loft for important papers.
After the expedition lost its map, the leader made a grim decision to head back at once so everyone would be safe before dark.
entries.spellingNote: grim is short and has no silent letters; pronounce the 'g' and end with 'im'.

entries.definition: Done quickly without enough thought, which can cause mistakes or poor choices.
entries.example: In a hasty rush to finish his homework, Marcus wrote the wrong answer and missed an easy mark on the test.
examples: In a hasty rush to finish his homework, Marcus wrote the wrong answer and missed an easy mark on the test.
The explorers made a hasty camp when the storm began, forgetting to secure supplies, so wind later scattered the tents.
Because of a hasty decision, the team took the steep path and had to turn back when the rain made it too slippery to continue.
entries.spellingNote: hasty ends with -y and is spelled h-a-s-t-y; remember it comes from 'haste'.

entries.definition: Important traditions, buildings, objects or stories from the past that people keep and value today.
entries.example: The old schoolhouse is part of our town's heritage, so volunteers painted it and turned it into a small museum for visitors.
examples: The old schoolhouse is part of our town's heritage, so volunteers painted it and turned it into a small museum for visitors.
During the festival we learned dances from our family's heritage and tasted recipes passed down from grandparents.
Archaeologists uncovered pottery that became part of the village heritage, helping everyone understand how families lived long ago.
entries.spellingNote: heritage begins with 'her-' like 'herit', not 'heritag'; remember the final -age.

entries.definition: To pause before doing something because you are unsure, nervous, or thinking about it.
entries.example: Tom wanted to answer but began to hesitate, then took a deep breath and gave his opinion to the whole class.
examples: Tom wanted to answer but began to hesitate, then took a deep breath and gave his opinion to the whole class.
When the cat climbed the high wall, Sarah did not hesitate to call for help because it looked too scared to jump down.
At the bakery, Mia would hesitate between the chocolate and the lemon tart, deciding which would taste best for her picnic.
entries.spellingNote: hesitate has an 's' after the 'he'; remember the middle 'si' sound: he-si-tate.

entries.definition: to slow down or make progress more difficult
entries.example: The fallen branches hinder the rescue truck because its wheels cannot reach the flooded street. Volunteers have to clear a path before the medicine can get through.
examples: The fallen branches hinder the rescue truck because its wheels cannot reach the flooded street. Volunteers have to clear a path before the medicine can get through.
A fogged-up visor can hinder a diver's search underwater. Even a strong swimmer struggles when the world turns into green blur.
Too many pop-up messages hinder Noor while she tries to write her story. Each interruption knocks the next sentence out of her head.
entries.spellingNote: hin + der.

entries.definition: The friendly welcome and kind treatment given to guests or visitors in a home or place.
entries.example: The family showed great hospitality to the tired walkers, offering hot soup and blankets by the fire until they warmed up.
examples: The family showed great hospitality to the tired walkers, offering hot soup and blankets by the fire until they warmed up.
At the school fair, the stalls were full of hospitality as neighbours served tea and chatted with newcomers for hours.
The elderly couple's hospitality was famous: every visitor left with a smile, a warm loaf and an invitation to return.
entries.spellingNote: hospitality has 'hospital' then -ity; don't drop the 'i' after the 't'.

entries.definition: Unfriendly or angry in a way that feels like opposition or a threat.
entries.example: The stray dog growled in a hostile way when strangers came too close, so we gave it space and called animal rescue.
examples: The stray dog growled in a hostile way when strangers came too close, so we gave it space and called animal rescue.
During the debate the two teams became hostile, shouting over each other instead of listening to different ideas calmly.
After the argument the mood in the classroom turned hostile, and the teacher asked everyone to take a quiet break to cool down.
entries.spellingNote: hostile is spelled h-o-s-t-i-l-e; remember the 'stile' ending, not 'style'.

entries.definition: not proud or boastful
entries.example: The champion was humble after breaking the school record. She thanked her coach, named the friend who paced her, and said she still had plenty to learn.
examples: The champion was humble after breaking the school record. She thanked her coach, named the friend who paced her, and said she still had plenty to learn.
A humble leader listens before making a decision. In the flood meeting, the mayor let the boat crews speak first because they knew the river best.
The famous chef stayed humble by washing pans with the youngest apprentice after service. He said nobody is too important to clean the kitchen.
entries.spellingNote: The b is sounded softly: hum-ble.

entries.definition: Very peaceful, beautiful and simple, like a perfect scene from a calm countryside or a happy memory.
entries.example: We stayed in an idyllic cottage by the river where mornings smelled of flowers and the only noises were birds and water.
examples: We stayed in an idyllic cottage by the river where mornings smelled of flowers and the only noises were birds and water.
The village looked idyllic in summer, with children playing by the green and everyone sharing strawberries after school.
Her holiday sketchbook was full of idyllic scenes of rolling hills and a small boat on a glassy lake at sunset.
entries.spellingNote: idyllic has two dashes of sound: i-dyl-lic; remember it ends with -ic, not -al.

entries.definition: To start burning or to cause something to start burning, or to begin strong feelings or action.
entries.example: A tiny spark from the camp stove could ignite the dry grass if we weren't careful, so we kept water nearby every time.
examples: A tiny spark from the camp stove could ignite the dry grass if we weren't careful, so we kept water nearby every time.
The coach's speech helped ignite the team's courage, and they played harder than anyone expected in the last ten minutes.
When the chemistry experiment mixed lemon and metal, the teacher warned how heat could ignite gases if lids were left open.
entries.spellingNote: ignite begins with 'ig-' not 'in-'; remember the 'gn' makes the soft 'n' sound.

entries.definition: To light up something so it is easier to see, or to make an idea or fact clearer to understand.
entries.example: The torch will illuminate the cave walls so we can read the markings, and the guide will explain what each sign means.
examples: The torch will illuminate the cave walls so we can read the markings, and the guide will explain what each sign means.
Her clear diagram helped illuminate the tricky maths idea for the whole class, and more pupils understood the puzzle.
In the storm the small lantern will illuminate the kitchen enough to find candles and batteries in the drawer.
entries.spellingNote: illuminate has two l's at the start: i-l-l-u-m-; remember the double l before 'uminate'.

entries.definition: Perfectly clean or tidy, with no stains, marks or mistakes.
entries.example: Mum checked the classroom after the project and said the desk was immaculate, with not a scrap of paper, pencil mark or smudge anywhere.
examples: Mum checked the classroom after the project and said the desk was immaculate, with not a scrap of paper, pencil mark or smudge anywhere.
Grandad polished the old silver until it looked immaculate and the light from the window jumped off the tray as if it were new.
The team's costumes were immaculate at the parade, every badge straight and every shoe spotless as they stood ready to march.
entries.spellingNote: Spell it i-m-m-a-c-u-l-a-t-e; notice the double m after the first i.

entries.definition: Extremely large in size, amount or degree.
entries.example: The cave opened into an immense chamber that swallowed their torchlight, making every tiny sound echo like a drum.
examples: The cave opened into an immense chamber that swallowed their torchlight, making every tiny sound echo like a drum.
When the dam burst, the river sent an immense rush of water down the valley and everyone raced to higher ground.
She felt an immense pride when her painting was chosen to hang at the town hall, the whole room suddenly very important.
entries.spellingNote: Write it i-m-m-e-n-s-e; remember the double m at the start.

entries.definition: Fair and not supporting any one side; treating everyone equally.
entries.example: The teacher stayed impartial when the two friends argued about the game and listened to both sides before deciding what to do.
examples: The teacher stayed impartial when the two friends argued about the game and listened to both sides before deciding what to do.
The referee had to remain impartial during the match, even when the home crowd shouted for a penalty to be given.
Our class judge was chosen because she could be impartial and give the same chance to every idea in the school competition.
entries.spellingNote: Starts with im- and then partial; spell as i-m-p-a-r-t-i-a-l with one r after im-.

entries.definition: Perfectly correct or without any faults or mistakes.
entries.example: Her handwriting was impeccable in the science book, every letter neat and the dates written exactly where the teacher asked.
examples: Her handwriting was impeccable in the science book, every letter neat and the dates written exactly where the teacher asked.
The museum guide gave an impeccable explanation of the old maps, and the visitors nodded, following every careful detail.
The play ran with impeccable timing, each actor arriving at the right moment so the whole audience laughed and clapped together.
entries.spellingNote: Spell it i-m-p-e-c-c-a-b-l-e; notice the double c in the middle.

entries.definition: Rude or cheeky in a way that shows a lack of respect.
entries.example: When Tom answered the grandad's question with an impertinent joke, everyone fell quiet because it sounded disrespectful and cheeky.
examples: When Tom answered the grandad's question with an impertinent joke, everyone fell quiet because it sounded disrespectful and cheeky.
The pupil's impertinent remark to the headteacher led to a serious talk about manners and how to be polite in school.
The reporter's impertinent question upset the guest, who had expected polite and sensible questions about the new project.
entries.spellingNote: Spell i-m-p-e-r-t-i-n-e-n-t; note it's not the same as important despite the similar start.

entries.definition: Large, impressive, or making people feel small because of its size or manner.
entries.example: The old castle sat on the hill, an imposing silhouette against the sky that made the children whisper as they rode past on their bikes.
examples: The old castle sat on the hill, an imposing silhouette against the sky that made the children whisper as they rode past on their bikes.
Her teacher had an imposing presence in the classroom: tall, calm and with a voice that made everyone pay attention.
The statue in the square was so imposing that tourists stopped to take careful photos and listen to the guide's story.
entries.spellingNote: From the verb 'impose'—spell i-m-p-o-s-i-n-g with one s after 'im'.

entries.definition: To make or do something quickly using whatever is available, without planning.
entries.example: When the lights went out during the play, the actors had to improvise a short scene using a torch and a blanket as props to keep the story going.
examples: When the lights went out during the play, the actors had to improvise a short scene using a torch and a blanket as props to keep the story going.
On the camping trip they used a bin bag to improvise raincoats, laughing at how cosy and strange they looked under the tent.
Her science experiment failed, so she had to improvise a new test with spare cups and paperclips to prove her idea to the class.
entries.spellingNote: Spell i-m-p-r-o-v-i-s-e; the ending is -ise, not -ize in British English.

entries.definition: Happening at the beginning of something, or marking its first time.
entries.example: The school's inaugural assembly welcomed new pupils with songs, and everyone smiled as the headteacher cut a ribbon on the stage.
examples: The school's inaugural assembly welcomed new pupils with songs, and everyone smiled as the headteacher cut a ribbon on the stage.
At the inaugural flight of the new air service, passengers cheered when the pilot announced the successful short journey.
The town celebrated the inaugural fair with stalls and games, and even the mayor tried the lucky dip to start the fun.
entries.spellingNote: Spell i-n-a-u-g-u-r-a-l; notice the 'augur' part in the middle.

entries.definition: Having trouble making decisions quickly, often changing your mind.
entries.example: Lucy was indecisive about which jumper to wear and tried three before she finally left, making her friends laugh and the bus nearly leave without her.
examples: Lucy was indecisive about which jumper to wear and tried three before she finally left, making her friends laugh and the bus nearly leave without her.
The team felt indecisive at half-time, arguing about tactics until the coach helped them pick one plan and move on.
Grandad was indecisive in the shop, staring at every flavour of jam so long that the queue grew and he smiled apologetically.
entries.spellingNote: Spell i-n-d-e-c-i-s-i-v-e; watch the sequence deci- and then -sive at the end.

entries.definition: hard-working and busy in a useful way
entries.example: The industrious beekeepers repaired frames, checked the queen, and labelled jars before lunchtime. Their work looked busy, but every movement helped the hive and the honey crop.
examples: The industrious beekeepers repaired frames, checked the queen, and labelled jars before lunchtime. Their work looked busy, but every movement helped the hive and the honey crop.
During the school fair, the industrious team painted signs, folded programmes, and tested the microphone while others argued about balloons. By opening time, their stall was the only one ready.
The industrious ants carried leaves many times larger than their bodies along a narrow forest trail. The path looked chaotic until you noticed that every ant had a job.
entries.spellingNote: industry changes to industrious.

entries.definition: to work out something from clues
entries.example: From the wet umbrella by the door, you can infer that someone came in from the rain. Nobody needs to say it directly; the clue tells the story.
examples: From the wet umbrella by the door, you can infer that someone came in from the rain. Nobody needs to say it directly; the clue tells the story.
The archaeologist could infer from the tiny fish bones that people once ate beside the river. The meal was gone, but the leftovers still spoke.
When the goalkeeper kept glancing at her ankle, the coach could infer that she was hurt. She had not complained, but her movements gave the secret away.
entries.spellingNote: in + fer.

entries.definition: Very clever and original, showing skill and imagination to solve a problem.
entries.example: Her ingenious plan to use a mirror and torch to read the map in the dark saved the expedition and made everyone admire how quickly she thought of it.
examples: Her ingenious plan to use a mirror and torch to read the map in the dark saved the expedition and made everyone admire how quickly she thought of it.
The student built an ingenious machine from old toys that sorted buttons by size, and the whole class wanted instructions to try it too.
His ingenious poem used ordinary words to paint a storm so clearly that the whole class could feel the rain and wind as he read.
entries.spellingNote: Careful: ingenious is spelled i-n-g-e-n-i-o-u-s and is not the same as ingenuous (which means innocent).

entries.definition: The skill of thinking of new and clever ideas, or the ability to solve problems in a smart way.
entries.example: By using string, pencils and a pot lid, the children's ingenuity turned the cardboard box into a working model car that surprised the whole class.
examples: By using string, pencils and a pot lid, the children's ingenuity turned the cardboard box into a working model car that surprised the whole class.
The inventor's ingenuity showed in a small gadget that fixed the bike chain without any tools, making the whole workshop clap.
Her ingenuity in reusing old jars for the science project won a prize because she saved money and made the most interesting display.
entries.spellingNote: Spell i-n-g-e-n-u-i-t-y; remember it ends with -ity, not -ness.

entries.definition: At the beginning or at first, before things changed.
entries.example: Initially the team thought the quiz would be easy, but questions about space made them sit up and work together to find the answers.
examples: Initially the team thought the quiz would be easy, but questions about space made them sit up and work together to find the answers.
He was initially nervous about the stage, yet after the first joke the audience laughed and his confidence grew fast.
Initially the seedlings grew slowly, then a sudden warm week made them shoot up and surprise the whole gardening club.
entries.spellingNote: Spell i-n-i-t-i-a-l-l-y and remember the double l before the -y.

entries.definition: Not guilty of doing something wrong or harmful; someone who has not caused the problem or hurt anyone.
entries.example: Iris looked innocent as she held the broken pencil, though the classroom camera later showed who really dropped it behind the desk.
examples: Iris looked innocent as she held the broken pencil, though the classroom camera later showed who really dropped it behind the desk.
When the puppy chewed Dad's shoe the family wondered if the act was innocent mischief or if someone had left the shoe out on purpose.
