The witness said the child seemed innocent, so the teacher asked questions gently and chose to listen before deciding what to do.
entries.spellingNote: Starts with 'in' then 'nocent' — there are two n letters at the start: i-n-n-o-c-e-n-t.

entries.definition: Rude or disrespectful, especially in the way someone speaks or behaves to a person in authority.
entries.example: Leo's reply sounded insolent when he answered the teacher sharply during the lesson, and he was asked to stay after class.
examples: Leo's reply sounded insolent when he answered the teacher sharply during the lesson, and he was asked to stay after class.
An insolent tone can upset people quickly; the referee warned the players after rude words were shouted across the pitch.
She learned that sounding insolent to her neighbour about the fence problem made the argument worse instead of fixing anything.
entries.spellingNote: Remember the middle 'sol' part: i-n-s-o-l-e-n-t. It is not the same as 'insult' even though they sound similar.

entries.definition: Very strong in feeling, light, heat, taste or action; something that is very powerful or concentrated.
entries.example: The thunderstorm was intense, with sheets of rain and sharp lightning that made us tilt umbrellas, hold hands and hurry home.
examples: The thunderstorm was intense, with sheets of rain and sharp lightning that made us tilt umbrellas, hold hands and hurry home.
His focus during the chess match was intense; he hardly blinked as he worked out a tricky move that could win the whole game.
We felt the heat during the science demo was intense but safe, and it helped us understand how pressure and magma behave.
entries.spellingNote: Spelt i-n-t-e-n-s-e. Watch out for the ending '-ense' — not '-ance' or 'intence'.

entries.definition: Stopped for a short time by something happening suddenly that breaks what was going on.
entries.example: The school assembly was interrupted when the fire alarm began ringing loudly, so pupils filed outside in a straight, calm line.
examples: The school assembly was interrupted when the fire alarm began ringing loudly, so pupils filed outside in a straight, calm line.
Our science lesson was interrupted by a sudden power cut, and we had to finish the experiment by the next day with torchlight.
The film night was interrupted when the storm knocked out the projector, leaving everyone in the dark until an adult could fix it.
entries.spellingNote: From the verb interrupt: remember the two r letters in the middle — i-n-t-e-r-r-u-p-t; past tense adds -ed to make interrupted.

entries.definition: fearless and adventurous
entries.example: The intrepid cave diver clipped a guide rope to her belt before entering the dark underwater tunnel. She was fearless, but not foolish; every bold move had a safety plan.
examples: The intrepid cave diver clipped a guide rope to her belt before entering the dark underwater tunnel. She was fearless, but not foolish; every bold move had a safety plan.
An intrepid botanist climbed the misty mountain to find a flower that bloomed only above the clouds. The path was steep, but curiosity pulled her higher.
The intrepid journalist walked toward the erupting volcano with a helmet, notebook, and shaking camera. Most people ran away from the ash cloud; she went closer to report what was happening.
entries.spellingNote: Starts with in-, not en-.

entries.definition: A system of supplying water to land or crops to help them grow, often using channels, pipes or sprinklers.
entries.example: The farmer explained irrigation, showing how the canal and pipes carry water to thirsty crops across the dry field during summer and autumn.
examples: The farmer explained irrigation, showing how the canal and pipes carry water to thirsty crops across the dry field during summer and autumn.
In history class we learned that ancient civilisations built irrigation channels near rivers like the Nile to grow extra food for towns.
At the allotment we set up irrigation with a timer and hose so the beans kept growing even when no one could water them each day.
entries.spellingNote: Spelt i-r-r-i-g-a-t-i-o-n with two r's after the first i; do not confuse it with 'irritation'.

entries.definition: Alone or far away from other places, people or things; separated so that you are by yourself.
entries.example: The tiny island felt isolated after the storm because the ferry was cancelled and the phone line stayed dead for two days.
examples: The tiny island felt isolated after the storm because the ferry was cancelled and the phone line stayed dead for two days.
Working alone in the observatory can feel isolated, but the quiet night sky also makes discoveries feel very special.
After moving to a new school at the top of the hill, she sometimes felt isolated until a neighbour invited her for tea.
entries.spellingNote: Spelt i-s-o-l-a-t-e-d; remember the 'sol' in the middle, not 'sal' or 'insulated'.

entries.definition: Very cheerful and friendly; enjoying company and making others smile.
entries.example: Grandpa was jovial at the picnic, telling funny stories and making everyone grin as the sun warmed the green meadow.
examples: Grandpa was jovial at the picnic, telling funny stories and making everyone grin as the sun warmed the green meadow.
Her teacher became jovial at the end of term, clapping and singing silly songs to cheer up the whole class.
The captain's jovial laugh on the boat eased the children's nerves during the fog and helped them enjoy the trip.
entries.spellingNote: Spelt j-o-v-i-a-l; starts with 'jov' and ends with '-ial' — not 'joviall'.

entries.definition: Extremely happy and proud, often showing it loudly after a great success or victory.
entries.example: The team were jubilant after winning the cup; they hugged, cheered and waved flags under the noisy stadium lights.
examples: The team were jubilant after winning the cup; they hugged, cheered and waved flags under the noisy stadium lights.
She felt jubilant when she found her lost cat asleep by the garden shed, and she cried with happiness on the step.
The crowd grew jubilant as the parade passed, balloons floating above and faces shining with pride and applause.
entries.spellingNote: Spelt j-u-b-i-l-a-n-t; remember the 'ju' start and the '-ant' ending — not 'jubilent'.

entries.definition: Fair treatment where rules are applied so people get what they deserve; making sure things are right and fair.
entries.example: When the playground bully said sorry and helped repair the shed, the teacher tried to find justice by making a fair decision for everyone.
examples: When the playground bully said sorry and helped repair the shed, the teacher tried to find justice by making a fair decision for everyone.
The court's job is to aim for justice, listening to both sides and deciding what is right under the law to keep people safe.
The school council met to talk about justice after someone was unfairly blamed, and they agreed on a rule that felt fair.
entries.spellingNote: Spelt j-u-s-t-i-c-e; the ending '-ice' is like the word 'nice', not '-is' or '-ess'.

entries.definition: Very eager or enthusiastic about something, or having a sharp edge or strong sense.
entries.example: Zara is keen to join the science club; she reads books about rockets every night and builds models at weekends.
examples: Zara is keen to join the science club; she reads books about rockets every night and builds models at weekends.
He was keen on helping in the garden, digging holes carefully and learning how to plant seeds the correct way.
Our class is keen for the visit to the museum, counting the days and planning questions for the guide.
entries.spellingNote: Short word spelt k-e-e-n; note the two e letters in the middle.

entries.definition: A small, usually edible, part inside a nut or seed; the soft centre or core of something.
entries.example: I found a yellow kernel of corn hiding inside the popcorn bowl and pretended it was a tiny treasure from the cinema.
examples: I found a yellow kernel of corn hiding inside the popcorn bowl and pretended it was a tiny treasure from the cinema.
Inside the chestnut the small kernel is soft and tasty once it is cooked and peeled, perfect for a winter snack by the fire.
The computer's core works like a kernel; it is the small part that helps all the other programmes start and run smoothly.
entries.spellingNote: Spelt k-e-r-n-e-l; do not confuse with the similar-sounding word 'colonel' which is spelled very differently.

entries.definition: Facts, information or skills you get by learning, observing or being taught; what a person knows.
entries.example: Sam's knowledge of local birds helped him win the nature quiz when he named every bird by its song and feather patterns.
examples: Sam's knowledge of local birds helped him win the nature quiz when he named every bird by its song and feather patterns.
The library filled with books is a place to grow knowledge, where quiet reading gives you facts and bright ideas to share.
She used her knowledge of maps to guide the lost hikers back to the campsite before nightfall and everyone was relieved.
entries.spellingNote: Spelt k-n-o-w-l-e-d-g-e with a silent k at the start and 'dg' making the j sound in the middle.

entries.definition: A long wooden pole with a sharp metal tip used long ago by soldiers on horseback, or any tool used to pierce or cut into something.
entries.example: At the school fair a boy carried a wooden lance for the knight game, pretending to joust while friends cheered and a flag snapped in the wind.
examples: At the school fair a boy carried a wooden lance for the knight game, pretending to joust while friends cheered and a flag snapped in the wind.
The museum guide showed a bronze lance found in a river and explained how people once used it for hunting and battle on horseback.
In the science lab the vet used a small, careful lance to let air out of the swollen bubble on the model before the whole thing burst.
entries.spellingNote: Ends with -nce; the 'ce' makes an 's' sound, so spell lance with 'l-a-n-c-e'.

entries.definition: Very generous or produced in large amounts, often rich, expensive or covered with fancy decorations.
entries.example: The school reward day felt lavish: long tables groaned with cakes and decorations glittered, and every winner got a shiny ribbon.
examples: The school reward day felt lavish: long tables groaned with cakes and decorations glittered, and every winner got a shiny ribbon.
At the royal banquet the room looked lavish, with bright tapestries, golden plates and performers dancing under tall candles.
Grandparents threw a lavish picnic for their grandchildren, with colourful balloons, games, lots of food and a magician performing tricks.
entries.spellingNote: Starts with 'lav-' and ends with '-ish'; remember the final letters are i-s-h, not -eous or -ous.

entries.definition: Not very strict; willing to be gentle when giving punishments or making rules.
entries.example: Mrs Patel was lenient about the homework because many children were ill, so she gave an extra week to finish the work.
examples: Mrs Patel was lenient about the homework because many children were ill, so she gave an extra week to finish the work.
The coach was lenient after the team lost, reminding them to try harder next time but not keeping anyone out of the next match.
My dad was surprisingly lenient when I broke the vase; he explained why it mattered and let me tidy up instead of shouting.
entries.spellingNote: Lenient has 'len-' then '-ient'; do not spell it with 'lie-' or with an extra e.

entries.definition: Very slow and lacking energy or interest, as if tired, sleepy or unwilling to move quickly.
entries.example: After the long rainy day Tim felt lethargic, dragging his feet home and doing his homework very slowly while yawning on every page.
examples: After the long rainy day Tim felt lethargic, dragging his feet home and doing his homework very slowly while yawning on every page.
The hedgehog appeared lethargic after the cold night, barely moving and curling into a tighter ball until the sun warmed the garden.
During the heatwave the whole class seemed lethargic, with slow answers, heavy lids and no one volunteering for the extra game.
entries.spellingNote: Contains 'tharg' in the middle; remember it is spelled l-e-t-h-a-r-g-i-c, not 'lethargy' which ends '-y'.

entries.definition: The freedom to make your own choices and act without being controlled, as long as it does not hurt others.
entries.example: The protest called for liberty, with people holding signs and saying they wanted the right to choose their leaders and speak freely.
examples: The protest called for liberty, with people holding signs and saying they wanted the right to choose their leaders and speak freely.
At school we discussed how the pirate ship crew traded small freedoms for strict rules, learning that liberty can come with responsibility.
When the caged bird was opened it flew off into the park and sang loudly, a tiny picture of liberty against the bright sky.
entries.spellingNote: Liberty ends with '-erty', not '-ary'; remember l-i-b-e-r-t-y.

entries.definition: To stand or hang around a place without an obvious purpose, often making people worry or feel uncomfortable.
entries.example: The shop owner asked the teenagers not to loiter by the door because customers were nervous and the workers needed space to move.
examples: The shop owner asked the teenagers not to loiter by the door because customers were nervous and the workers needed space to move.
We saw a fox loiter near the compost bin for ages before it hurried away with a small shiny wrapper in its mouth.
Paul was told not to loiter after school; he should go straight home unless he had a clear reason to be with friends in the park.
entries.spellingNote: Spelled l-o-i-t-e-r; the 'oi' makes the 'oy' sound, like in 'join'.

entries.definition: Always supporting someone or something and staying true to them, especially in hard times.
entries.example: Nora stayed loyal to her friend even when others laughed, sitting beside her and offering a sandwich during lunch break.
examples: Nora stayed loyal to her friend even when others laughed, sitting beside her and offering a sandwich during lunch break.
The old dog was loyal to the farmer, waiting by the gate every morning no matter how windy or wet the weather.
Fans remained loyal to the tiny football club through many seasons, singing the same song and turning up in cheerful raincoats.
entries.spellingNote: Contains the vowel pair 'oy' like in 'boy' and ends with a single 'l'.

entries.definition: Very clear and easy to understand, or being awake and able to think clearly.
entries.example: After a good night's sleep Sam wrote a lucid paragraph about the experiment, with clear steps everyone could follow.
examples: After a good night's sleep Sam wrote a lucid paragraph about the experiment, with clear steps everyone could follow.
During the lesson the teacher gave a lucid explanation of how volcanoes work, and suddenly the whole class pictured the hot rock beneath the ground.
Grandma's story was suddenly lucid after her rest, and she named all the places she had visited when she was younger.
entries.spellingNote: Short word spelled l-u-c-i-d; the 'c' makes an 's' sound here, pronounced 'LOO-sid'.

entries.definition: Very grand, beautiful and impressive in a way that makes you feel respect or wonder.
entries.example: We watched a majestic whale breach near the boat, water cascading like a curtain and everyone holding their breath at the sight.
examples: We watched a majestic whale breach near the boat, water cascading like a curtain and everyone holding their breath at the sight.
The old oak looked majestic against the evening sky, its wide branches shining and squirrels leaping like tiny daredevils.
At the castle the tour guide described a majestic hall where kings once walked, with tall windows and banners that whispered history.
entries.spellingNote: Contains 'majest-' like in 'majesty' and ends '-ic'; watch for the common misspelling 'magestic'.

entries.definition: Fully grown and developed, or acting in a sensible and responsible way for your age.
entries.example: After caring for the injured bird for weeks, Leah felt more mature and proud when it finally flew away from the garden hedge.
examples: After caring for the injured bird for weeks, Leah felt more mature and proud when it finally flew away from the garden hedge.
A mature tree in the playground gave deep shade and acorns every autumn, taller and stronger than the saplings that once stood there.
When Tom chose to apologise and help fix the broken shelf, his teacher said he had been very mature about taking responsibility.
entries.spellingNote: Ends with '-ture'; remember the 'a' before 'ture' and do not add extra letters like 'maturee'.

entries.definition: too small in amount; not enough
entries.example: The explorers had a meagre supper of three crackers and a spoonful of beans each. Nobody complained, but everyone stared at the empty pot afterward.
examples: The explorers had a meagre supper of three crackers and a spoonful of beans each. Nobody complained, but everyone stared at the empty pot afterward.
The charity match raised a meagre amount at first because rain kept the crowd away. Then one local business doubled the total with a surprise donation.
The plant survived on a meagre trickle of water from a cracked pipe. Its leaves were small, but somehow it stayed alive.
entries.spellingNote: British spelling: meagre.

entries.definition: Moving slowly in a winding or indirect way, like a path or a river that curves and twists.
entries.example: The stream was meandering through the meadow, carving gentle curves between patches of wildflowers and old stones.
examples: The stream was meandering through the meadow, carving gentle curves between patches of wildflowers and old stones.
Our walk took a meandering route through the village lanes, stopping at a bakery and then following hedges where rabbits darted.
Her story was softly meandering, full of memories that wandered from one childhood summer to another without hurrying.
entries.spellingNote: From the verb 'meander' with '-ing' added; remember the 'ea' after 'm' and double letters are not used here.

entries.definition: A deep, quiet sadness that lasts for a while and makes things seem a little dull or heavy.
entries.example: A soft, melancholy tune played on the radio as Lucy watched the rain smear the windows, thinking of the friend who had moved away.
examples: A soft, melancholy tune played on the radio as Lucy watched the rain smear the windows, thinking of the friend who had moved away.
The painter mixed blues and greys into one picture to show a melancholy morning when fog covered the harbour and boats drifted slowly.
After saying goodbye the children felt a gentle, shared melancholy; they whispered stories of the sleepover until the lights went out.
entries.spellingNote: Spelled m-e-l-a-n-c-h-o-l-y; the 'ch' makes a 'k' sound and the ending is '-oly', not '-oly' with a silent e.

entries.definition: Looking or sounding as if something bad or dangerous might happen; making someone feel frightened or worried.
entries.example: The sky turned green and the thunder sounded menacing as we raced home across the field, worried the storm would break windows.
examples: The sky turned green and the thunder sounded menacing as we raced home across the field, worried the storm would break windows.
A stray dog growled and held a menacing stare near the bin, so Mum called for help instead of trying to scare it away.
A shadow moved behind the door and the steps became slow and menacing, making the whole house feel uneasy at night.
entries.spellingNote: Menacing has one 's' and ends with -ing; not 'menacsing'.

entries.definition: Enjoying small tricks or playful trouble that is not meant to seriously hurt anyone; a cheeky kind of troublemaking.
entries.example: The mischievous squirrel stole the picnic sandwich and darted up the tree before anyone could catch it, leaving Mum laughing and annoyed.
examples: The mischievous squirrel stole the picnic sandwich and darted up the tree before anyone could catch it, leaving Mum laughing and annoyed.
Tom left a mischievous note in his sister's school book that made her smile and then chase him around the playground.
A mischievous wind flipped our homework into the puddle, so we raced to rescue the soggy drawings.
entries.spellingNote: Spelled mischievous, not mischievious or mischevious; it has three syllables: mis-chie-vous.

entries.definition: Very unhappy, uncomfortable, or feeling bad because things are unpleasant or have gone wrong.
entries.example: After standing in the cold rain with wet shoes, I felt miserable and wanted to go home and make a hot chocolate.
examples: After standing in the cold rain with wet shoes, I felt miserable and wanted to go home and make a hot chocolate.
The rescued kitten looked miserable on its blanket until it was fed and warmed by the kind vet.
Our camping trip was miserable when the tent leaked, the food went soggy and everyone had a cough.
entries.spellingNote: Miserable has 'mis-' at the start and ends with -able, not -ible.

entries.definition: not boastful; not too proud
entries.example: Although Leila won the chess tournament, she stayed modest and thanked the classmates who had practised with her. She smiled at the trophy but did not wave it around.
examples: Although Leila won the chess tournament, she stayed modest and thanked the classmates who had practised with her. She smiled at the trophy but did not wave it around.
The scientist was modest about the discovery, saying the whole team deserved credit. Reporters wanted a hero, but she kept pointing to the lab notebooks full of shared work.
The cottage was modest, with two small rooms and a tin roof, but every window had flowers. It was not grand, yet it felt cared for.
entries.spellingNote: mod + est.

entries.definition: A very small piece or amount of food, often just a bite or scrap.
entries.example: Grandad offered me a tiny morsel of his chocolate, and I savoured the sweet taste like a little treasure.
examples: Grandad offered me a tiny morsel of his chocolate, and I savoured the sweet taste like a little treasure.
The mouse carried a morsel of bread through the gap in the wall to hide it under the floorboards.
The baker broke off a morsel of warm cake for the dog, then realised he should not feed treats to animals in the shop.
entries.spellingNote: Morsel ends with -sel, not -cel or -sal.

entries.definition: Showing deep sadness, often quietly and slowly, like the feeling at a funeral or when someone misses someone they love.
entries.example: A mournful bell tolled at the village funeral, and everyone walked slowly behind the coffin with bowed heads.
examples: A mournful bell tolled at the village funeral, and everyone walked slowly behind the coffin with bowed heads.
He played a mournful tune on the violin that made the classroom go very quiet and some pupils wipe their eyes.
The old dog gave a mournful howl when his owner left, then lay by the door waiting all evening.
entries.spellingNote: Mournful uses 'mourn' + 'ful' (one 'l'); not 'mournfull'.

entries.definition: A building where objects of art, history or science are collected, cared for and shown to the public.
entries.example: We walked through the museum and peered at the dinosaur skeleton, imagining the giant bones moving across the plains long ago.
examples: We walked through the museum and peered at the dinosaur skeleton, imagining the giant bones moving across the plains long ago.
In the night the museum guards imagined paintings whispering, but the only sound was the echo of footsteps in the marble hall.
She built a tiny museum of shells on her shelf, labelling each one with where she found it on holiday.
entries.spellingNote: Museum ends with -eum; pronounced mu-ZEE-um in British English.

entries.definition: To bring people together in one place, or to find and gather up courage or strength to do something.
entries.example: The teacher asked us to muster by the gate, so we formed a line for the school trip while the rain dripped from our coats.
examples: The teacher asked us to muster by the gate, so we formed a line for the school trip while the rain dripped from our coats.
He tried to muster enough courage to slide down the tall tree, hands shaking as he looked at the ground far below.
At the farm we muster the sheep into the yard before counting them and checking for missing lambs.
entries.spellingNote: Muster has one 't' and one 'r' — not 'mustter'.

entries.definition: Related to a country's ships, sailors or sea forces; connected with the navy.
entries.example: The town honoured its naval heroes with a parade of flags and wreaths beside the harbour on Remembrance Day.
examples: The town honoured its naval heroes with a parade of flags and wreaths beside the harbour on Remembrance Day.
Our class project showed a wooden model of a naval ship that sailed in a famous battle long ago.
Weather reports warned of strong winds, so the naval base kept all small boats tied up tightly to the piers.
entries.spellingNote: Naval is an adjective from navy; it ends with -al.

entries.definition: The part of a country's armed forces that uses ships, submarines and sailors to protect the seas.
entries.example: My uncle joined the navy and sent a postcard from a far island where he helped on a big supply ship during the winter.
examples: My uncle joined the navy and sent a postcard from a far island where he helped on a big supply ship during the winter.
The navy ship sailed into the harbour for exercises, and the town crowded the quay to watch the sailors.
She loved the navy uniform in the costume box and pretended to be a captain navigating rough seas in the bath.
entries.spellingNote: Navy ends with -y and is pronounced 'nay-vee'.

entries.definition: To fail to look after or pay attention to someone or something that needs care, often causing harm or trouble.
entries.example: The garden began to look overgrown when the family started to neglect the flowerbeds and forget to water the plants each week.
examples: The garden began to look overgrown when the family started to neglect the flowerbeds and forget to water the plants each week.
If you neglect to charge your tablet before a long journey, it will run out of battery and you may miss your music.
Neighbours reported a house that showed signs of neglect, with broken windows and rubbish piled high in the yard.
entries.spellingNote: Neglect has 'neg-' then 'lect'; do not add an extra 'i' or swap letters.

entries.definition: Feeling worried or anxious, often with a quick heartbeat or shaky hands before something important happens.
entries.example: I felt nervous before the school play and my knees knocked, but the applause after the first line made me smile.
examples: I felt nervous before the school play and my knees knocked, but the applause after the first line made me smile.
The hamster gets nervous if you suddenly open the cage, so we speak softly and move slowly to calm it down.
During the exam, she felt nervous and reread every question twice until the teacher told us the time was nearly up.
entries.spellingNote: Nervous ends with -ous, not -ious.

entries.definition: The closest family member(s) who should be told if something important or an emergency happens to you; often used in official forms.
entries.example: The hospital asked for the name of my next of kin so they could contact someone quickly if my operation had any problems.
examples: The hospital asked for the name of my next of kin so they could contact someone quickly if my operation had any problems.
On the form we wrote our mother's name as next of kin, and the teacher explained why the school needs someone to call.
During the trip we kept a card in each pocket with our next of kin details in case we got lost or separated from the group.
entries.spellingNote: "Next of kin" is a three-word phrase with no apostrophe and is used exactly like that on forms.

entries.definition: Something or someone that is worth noticing because they are special, important or stand out from the rest.
entries.example: The scientist made a notable discovery when she found tiny fossils under the school pond that changed what we thought about the old river.
examples: The scientist made a notable discovery when she found tiny fossils under the school pond that changed what we thought about the old river.
At the end of term the teacher gave a notable award to Sam for his kind actions that everyone in class still talks about.
The castle has a notable tower that can be seen from the top of the hill and people travel for miles to sketch it.
entries.spellingNote: Notable is spelled with one 't' and ends in -able, not -ible.

entries.definition: Food and drink that your body needs to grow, stay healthy and have energy to play and think.
entries.example: The campers packed fruit and sandwiches for nourishment, knowing they would need energy for the long hike up the windy ridge.
examples: The campers packed fruit and sandwiches for nourishment, knowing they would need energy for the long hike up the windy ridge.
After the storm the family shared warm soup as nourishment and a way to feel stronger while they fixed the roof.
Plants also need nourishment from soil and sunlight; without enough they wilted on the windowsill during the dry week.
entries.spellingNote: Nourishment comes from the verb 'nourish' and is spelled n-o-u-r-i-s-h-m-e-n-t.

entries.definition: A short article that tells about a person's life and death, usually printed in a newspaper or online to remember them.
entries.example: The school newspaper printed an obituary for the retired librarian, sharing her love of books and the stories she told generations of children.
examples: The school newspaper printed an obituary for the retired librarian, sharing her love of books and the stories she told generations of children.
Grandma kept a clipping of the wartime doctor's obituary because it described the brave rescue he led during the flood.
When the famous explorer passed away, the museum wrote an obituary that explained his trips and the strange maps he brought home.
entries.spellingNote: Obituary is spelled o-b-i-t-u-a-r-y; remember the 'bi' after the first 'o'.

entries.definition: to watch or notice carefully
entries.example: The scientist had to observe the ants for an hour before writing anything down. At first they looked random, but slowly a clear trail appeared between the nest and the apple core.
examples: The scientist had to observe the ants for an hour before writing anything down. At first they looked random, but slowly a clear trail appeared between the nest and the apple core.
During the eclipse, the class used special glasses to observe the moon crossing the sun. Nobody looked directly, because real discovery still needs safety.
A good artist will observe how light lands on a glass of water before painting it. The sparkle, shadow, and bent straw all matter.
entries.spellingNote: ob + serve.

entries.definition: stubborn and refusing to change your mind
entries.example: The obstinate mule planted its hooves in the mud and refused to move, even when the farmer offered apples. It had decided the bridge was suspicious, and no argument changed its mind.
examples: The obstinate mule planted its hooves in the mud and refused to move, even when the farmer offered apples. It had decided the bridge was suspicious, and no argument changed its mind.
Nina became obstinate during the group project and would not change the poster colour. Her idea was not terrible, but her refusal to listen slowed everyone down.
The old printer was almost obstinate, rejecting every page unless someone tapped the left corner twice. It seemed stubborn enough to have opinions.
entries.spellingNote: ob + stin + ate.

entries.definition: something that blocks the way or prevents progress
entries.example: The fallen oak was an obstruction across the only road to the village. The ambulance could see the houses ahead, but it could not pass until the trunk was cut apart.
examples: The fallen oak was an obstruction across the only road to the village. The ambulance could see the houses ahead, but it could not pass until the trunk was cut apart.
A small toy became a dangerous obstruction in the robot's path. Its sensors saw the block and stopped the machine before it crushed the gears.
The referee removed an obstruction from the running lane before the race began. One loose hurdle could trip a sprinter at full speed.
entries.spellingNote: ob + struct + ion.

entries.definition: A chance to do something that might lead to something good or important.
entries.example: Sabi saw an opportunity to join the science club when the teacher asked for volunteers to test the rocket model over the weekend.
examples: Sabi saw an opportunity to join the science club when the teacher asked for volunteers to test the rocket model over the weekend.
During the school fair there was an opportunity to help run the stall and learn how to count money and cheer customers.
When the puddle froze, Tom took the opportunity to practise his skating and decided he wanted lessons after that day.
entries.spellingNote: Opportunity has two p's and ends in -unity: o-p-p-o-r-t-u-n-i-t-y.

entries.definition: hopeful that good things will happen
entries.example: The coach stayed optimistic after the team lost its first two matches. She pointed to the faster passes and better defending, insisting the score was not the whole story.
examples: The coach stayed optimistic after the team lost its first two matches. She pointed to the faster passes and better defending, insisting the score was not the whole story.
Scientists were optimistic when the damaged reef showed new coral growth. It was only a pale patch at first, but it proved the reef was not finished.
Even with grey clouds above the picnic, Dad was optimistic and packed the kite. He said the wind might turn a gloomy afternoon into the best flying weather.
entries.spellingNote: op + ti + mis + tic.

entries.definition: A home where children who have no parents are cared for by adults and live together.
entries.example: The band collected coats for children at the orphanage so everyone would be warm during the icy winter breaks from school.
examples: The band collected coats for children at the orphanage so everyone would be warm during the icy winter breaks from school.
When the classroom learned about the old orphanage, they made a mural to show all the games the children might have played long ago.
A family visited the orphanage to bring books and read stories to the children, who clapped at the funny parts each time.
entries.spellingNote: Orphanage ends with -age; spell it o-r-p-h-a-n-a-g-e.

entries.definition: Very shocking, unfair or extreme in a way that surprises or upsets people.
entries.example: It felt outrageous when the museum closed the dinosaur section without warning, just days before their class trip that everyone had planned for.
examples: It felt outrageous when the museum closed the dinosaur section without warning, just days before their class trip that everyone had planned for.
The magician made an outrageous claim that he could lift the car, and the crowd held its breath until he showed a clever trick instead.
Lily thought it was outrageous that the playground rules were changed overnight, so she wrote a polite note asking for an explanation.
entries.spellingNote: Outrageous starts with 'out' then 'rage' and ends '-ous'; spell it o-u-t-r-a-g-e-o-u-s.

entries.definition: The roof of the mouth or a person's sense of taste and what flavours they enjoy.
entries.example: After trying three different soups, Asha decided her palate liked the spicy one best and made notes for the cooking club competition.
examples: After trying three different soups, Asha decided her palate liked the spicy one best and made notes for the cooking club competition.
The chef taught us that the palate can tell sweet from bitter, so tasting small amounts helps when you are inventing a new recipe.
During the nature walk Tom learned that a deer’s palate will choose young shoots over dry leaves, which helps explain where they graze.
entries.spellingNote: Palate is spelled p-a-l-a-t-e and is different from palette (used for paint colours).

entries.definition: A very wide and clear view of a place, usually seen from high up so you can see lots at once.
entries.example: From the hilltop we had a panoramic view of the town, the river winding like a silver ribbon and the sea in the distance.
examples: From the hilltop we had a panoramic view of the town, the river winding like a silver ribbon and the sea in the distance.
The photographers climbed the old tower to capture a panoramic view of the festival tents and colourful crowds below.
At sunrise the panoramic view from the lookout showed the mist lifting from the valley and the distant mountains turning gold.
entries.spellingNote: Panoramic view is two words; 'panoramic' means wide and comes before 'view'.

entries.definition: More important than anything else; of the highest concern or priority.
entries.example: Keeping the team safe was paramount during the mountain trip, so the leader checked equipment twice before anyone climbed.
examples: Keeping the team safe was paramount during the mountain trip, so the leader checked equipment twice before anyone climbed.
For the school project, accuracy was paramount, so students rechecked their facts and measurements before handing it in.
When the bees swarmed near the picnic, staying calm and quiet was paramount to avoid frightening them and causing harm.
entries.spellingNote: Paramount starts with 'para-' and not 'perma-'; spell it p-a-r-a-m-o-u-n-t.

entries.definition: very dry, especially because of heat
entries.example: After the long drought, the parched field cracked into hard plates of earth. When rain finally came, the soil drank so fast that puddles vanished in minutes.
examples: After the long drought, the parched field cracked into hard plates of earth. When rain finally came, the soil drank so fast that puddles vanished in minutes.
The marathon runner reached the water station with a parched throat and dusty lips. The cup was small, but it felt like treasure.
The parched houseplant leaned toward the window, its leaves curled like tired hands. One good watering lifted it by the next morning.
entries.spellingNote: parch + ed.

entries.definition: The ability to wait calmly and not get angry or upset when things take time or are difficult.
entries.example: Building the kite took patience because the string kept tangling, and Mia sat quietly untangling it until it was ready to fly.
examples: Building the kite took patience because the string kept tangling, and Mia sat quietly untangling it until it was ready to fly.
When the plant grew slowly, the class practised patience by watering it carefully and recording tiny changes each week.
Sam had patience during the long queue, reading his book so he did not get bored while waiting for his turn to see the play.
entries.spellingNote: Patience ends in -ence, not -ance; spell it p-a-t-i-e-n-c-e.

entries.definition: Showing love or strong support for your country, often by celebrating its people, history or symbols.
entries.example: On the national day the children waved flags and sang songs, feeling patriotic as they learned about heroes from the past.
examples: On the national day the children waved flags and sang songs, feeling patriotic as they learned about heroes from the past.
Granddad wore his medals to the parade, a quiet and patriotic way to remember the friends he served with long ago.
The class art project made a big poster of the flag to show a patriotic respect for their town's history and veterans.
entries.spellingNote: Patriotic is spelled p-a-t-r-i-o-t-i-c; it comes from 'patriot' with an -ic ending.

entries.definition: strange or unusual
entries.example: A peculiar ticking came from the old suitcase, though nobody had packed a clock. The sound stopped whenever Grandpa walked into the room, which made it even stranger.
examples: A peculiar ticking came from the old suitcase, though nobody had packed a clock. The sound stopped whenever Grandpa walked into the room, which made it even stranger.
The octopus made a peculiar escape by squeezing through a hole smaller than a coin. It looked impossible until the aquarium keeper explained how soft its body was.
There was a peculiar rule in the tiny library: every returned book had to be placed on the blue chair first. Nobody remembered why, but everyone obeyed it.
entries.spellingNote: pe + cu + liar.

entries.definition: The one before the last; second to last in a list or sequence.
entries.example: In the relay race Ben ran the penultimate leg, passing the baton carefully so his friend could sprint the final stretch to the finish.
examples: In the relay race Ben ran the penultimate leg, passing the baton carefully so his friend could sprint the final stretch to the finish.
On the bookshelf the penultimate chapter had a surprising clue that helped Leyla solve the mystery before the last page.
During the music concert the penultimate song was slow and moving, making the final lively tune feel like a celebration afterwards.
entries.spellingNote: Penultimate starts with 'pen-' and means 'almost'; spell it p-e-n-u-l-t-i-m-a-t-e.

entries.definition: Very dangerous or likely to cause harm, where people or animals must be careful to avoid injury.
entries.example: The fishermen looked at the dark sea and decided the crossing would be perilous, with huge waves tossing the little boat and wind that could flip it.
examples: The fishermen looked at the dark sea and decided the crossing would be perilous, with huge waves tossing the little boat and wind that could flip it.
We found a steep path up the cliff and agreed it was perilous for a school trip, so the teacher marked a safer route through the woods instead.
A single, broken rope above the ravine made the rescue feel perilous; everyone shivered as they waited for the expert to check it first.
entries.spellingNote: Perilous ends with -ous like many adjectives that describe a state or quality (peril + -ous).

entries.definition: confused because something is difficult to understand
entries.example: The detective was perplexed because the muddy footprints stopped in the middle of the kitchen. There was no open window, no second door, and no mud beyond that point.
examples: The detective was perplexed because the muddy footprints stopped in the middle of the kitchen. There was no open window, no second door, and no mud beyond that point.
The class was perplexed when the magnet picked up one coin but ignored another that looked almost the same. The teacher smiled because the puzzle was exactly the point of the experiment.
Dad looked perplexed at the flat-pack instructions, which showed twelve screws but the bag contained eleven. He turned the page upside down, hoping it would suddenly make sense.
entries.spellingNote: per + plex + ed.

entries.definition: continuing firmly and not giving up
entries.example: The persistent inventor tested forty paper-wing designs before one glided across the hall. Each crash gave her a new clue instead of a reason to quit.
examples: The persistent inventor tested forty paper-wing designs before one glided across the hall. Each crash gave her a new clue instead of a reason to quit.
A persistent knocking echoed from inside the old pipes all night. Even after Dad tightened the tap, the sound returned every ten seconds.
The persistent athlete kept practising free throws after the lights clicked off in the gym. He missed plenty, but he would not leave until ten went in cleanly.
entries.spellingNote: per + sist + ent.

entries.definition: expecting bad things to happen
entries.example: Mert was pessimistic about the school play because the scenery collapsed during rehearsal. He expected opening night to fail, even after everyone else had fixed the stage.
examples: Mert was pessimistic about the school play because the scenery collapsed during rehearsal. He expected opening night to fail, even after everyone else had fixed the stage.
The weather app was pessimistic, showing rain symbols for every hour of the camping trip. Mum packed waterproofs, but she also packed marshmallows just in case.
A pessimistic investor saw one bad sales report and predicted disaster for the whole company. The calmer analysts waited for more evidence before panicking.
entries.spellingNote: Double s in pessimistic.

entries.definition: To keep annoying or bothering someone by asking for things or interrupting them again and again.
entries.example: During homework time Tom tried not to pester his sister, but he kept asking for help with one tricky maths question until she sighed and helped.
examples: During homework time Tom tried not to pester his sister, but he kept asking for help with one tricky maths question until she sighed and helped.
The puppy would pester the gardener by tugging at his coat while he planted seeds, wanting attention and a game every few minutes.
If you pester the teacher about extra playtime every day, she will say no and you might miss the chance to earn it with good work instead.
entries.spellingNote: Pester has a simple -er ending; remember the middle vowel is an 'e' (p-e-s-t-e-r).

entries.definition: Being the first to try new ideas, methods, or discoveries and leading the way for others to follow.
entries.example: Her pioneering study of city trees showed how small parks cool streets, and other towns began copying her planting ideas that winter.
examples: Her pioneering study of city trees showed how small parks cool streets, and other towns began copying her planting ideas that winter.
The young inventor built a pioneering little robot that could tidy a room, and classmates crowded round to see what it would do next.
A pioneering group of explorers used new maps and gadgets to cross a frozen plain, opening a safer route for later travellers.
entries.spellingNote: Pioneering comes from 'pioneer' plus -ing; double-check the middle 'eo' and the -ing ending.

entries.definition: Seeming likely to be true or reasonable, so that people can believe it could happen or be correct.
entries.example: The detective found a plausible reason for the missing loaf of bread: the dog had been seen near the counter with crumbs on its whiskers.
examples: The detective found a plausible reason for the missing loaf of bread: the dog had been seen near the counter with crumbs on its whiskers.
Mia gave a plausible explanation for being late, saying her bike chain broke and she had to walk home pushing it in the rain.
When the science experiment failed, Tom had a plausible idea that the thermometer was broken, so the class checked and replaced it.
entries.spellingNote: Plausible ends with -ible; remember the 'au' in the middle (pl-au-s-ible).

entries.definition: All the feathers of a bird, especially when they are bright, patterned, or used for display.
entries.example: The peacock showed off its colourful plumage across the garden, each feather catching the sun and making everyone stop to stare in surprise.
examples: The peacock showed off its colourful plumage across the garden, each feather catching the sun and making everyone stop to stare in surprise.
During the nature walk we found a fallen feather from a buzzard, and our guide explained how plumage keeps birds warm and helps them fly.
A tiny robin with fluffy plumage hopped onto the windowsill and watched the classroom, its red breast puffed up against the cold morning.
entries.spellingNote: Plumage ends in -age like many nouns; remember the 'plu-' start, not 'ple-'.

entries.definition: The state of not having enough money or basic things needed for a healthy, safe life, like food, clothes, or shelter.
entries.example: The story showed how poverty made it hard for the family to buy warm coats, and the whole community organised a collection to help them through winter.
examples: The story showed how poverty made it hard for the family to buy warm coats, and the whole community organised a collection to help them through winter.
She learned about global poverty at school and was surprised that children in some countries could not go to school because they needed to work to survive.
After the flood many homes were damaged and local groups worked together to offer food and shelter to people facing sudden poverty.
entries.spellingNote: Poverty has the -ty ending; remember the vowel 'o' after the 'p' (po-ver-ty).

entries.definition: Exactly correct and detailed, with no extra or missing parts; very accurate.
entries.example: For the science test she drew the circuit with precise labels so the teacher could see exactly which wires and bulbs were used in the experiment.
examples: For the science test she drew the circuit with precise labels so the teacher could see exactly which wires and bulbs were used in the experiment.
The clockmaker needs precise measurements to fix the tiny gears, or the watch will lose time and stop working properly.
When building the model bridge the team made precise cuts for the wood, because even a small mistake could make the bridge collapse.
entries.spellingNote: Precise has a soft 'c' sounding like 's' and ends with -ise in British English (precise).

entries.definition: respected and admired because of high quality or success
entries.example: Ada won a place at a prestigious music school where students audition from all over the country. The letter felt heavy in her hands because the school's name meant excellence.
examples: Ada won a place at a prestigious music school where students audition from all over the country. The letter felt heavy in her hands because the school's name meant excellence.
The scientist received a prestigious award for discovering a new way to track ocean plastic. Even people outside her field recognised the medal.
A prestigious tournament can make young players nervous before the first whistle. The crowd, cameras, and history of the event all add pressure.
entries.spellingNote: prestige becomes prestigious.

entries.definition: To keep something safe from harm or change so it stays the same, or to keep food so it lasts longer.
entries.example: We helped preserve the old school garden by planting new hedges, and everyone promised to water the seedlings every week until they grew strong.
examples: We helped preserve the old school garden by planting new hedges, and everyone promised to water the seedlings every week until they grew strong.
Grandma taught us how to preserve jam by boiling fruit with sugar so it could be eaten months later on cold winter mornings.
The volunteers worked to preserve the riverbank by removing litter and planting reeds to stop soil washing away during storms.
entries.spellingNote: Preserve has 'pre-' meaning 'before' and the double 's' sound but only one 's' in the middle (pre-serve).

entries.definition: important, well known, or easy to notice
entries.example: The lighthouse stood in a prominent position on the cliff, visible to every ship entering the bay. Even in fog, its shape rose above the smaller buildings.
examples: The lighthouse stood in a prominent position on the cliff, visible to every ship entering the bay. Even in fog, its shape rose above the smaller buildings.
A prominent scar crossed the old captain's eyebrow, so children noticed it before they noticed his medals. He said it came from a storm, not a sword fight.
The article placed the warning in a prominent box at the top of the page. The editor wanted nobody to miss it.
entries.spellingNote: prom + in + ent.

entries.definition: To offer something to someone, especially in a polite or formal way.
entries.example: At the meeting she decided to proffer a folded map to the captain, explaining the route she had planned for the explorers to follow.
examples: At the meeting she decided to proffer a folded map to the captain, explaining the route she had planned for the explorers to follow.
When the stray kitten arrived, Mark went to proffer some milk, hoping the little animal would trust him and come closer to be helped.
During the debate an elderly scientist chose to proffer new evidence, carefully placing her notes on the table so everyone could read them.
entries.spellingNote: Proffer has two f's in the middle: pro-ff-er; remember the double 'f' when you write it.

entries.definition: To grow well, be successful, or do well, especially in money, health, or life in general.
entries.example: With careful care of the soil and plenty of rain, the little farm began to prosper, and the children watched new crops sprout taller every month.
examples: With careful care of the soil and plenty of rain, the little farm began to prosper, and the children watched new crops sprout taller every month.
When the small business treated customers kindly and fixed mistakes quickly, it began to prosper and the owner hired another helper.
A community that shares skills and helps each other tends to prosper, with happier families and stronger schools over time.
entries.spellingNote: Prosper starts with 'pro-' meaning forward; note there is only one 's' in the middle (pro-sper).

entries.definition: successful and wealthy
entries.example: The harbour town became prosperous after the new railway brought fish, visitors, and trade. Empty warehouses turned into busy shops, and the school finally got a library.
examples: The harbour town became prosperous after the new railway brought fish, visitors, and trade. Empty warehouses turned into busy shops, and the school finally got a library.
A prosperous farm does not just have money; it has healthy soil, strong animals, and enough stored grain for a bad year. Success shows in more than one barn.
The market looked prosperous on festival morning, with spice stalls, flower carts, and bakers selling out before noon. Even the musicians earned more coins than usual.
entries.spellingNote: prosper + ous.

entries.definition: Oddly attractive or charming in an old-fashioned way, often because something is small and unusual.
entries.example: We walked past a quaint little tea shop with mismatched chairs and hand-painted signs, and it felt like stepping into a storybook town.
examples: We walked past a quaint little tea shop with mismatched chairs and hand-painted signs, and it felt like stepping into a storybook town.
Her grandmother's cottage smelled of biscuits and had a quaint clock that ticked loudly, reminding everyone of quiet Sunday afternoons long ago.
The museum had a quaint model of the village, complete with tiny thatched roofs and a river painted by a careful old artist.
entries.spellingNote: Quaint begins with 'qu-' like queen; the 'ai' makes the long 'a' sound (qu-aint).

entries.definition: Doubtful or not clearly right, true, or safe; something you might not fully believe or trust.
entries.example: The teacher marked the online source as questionable because its facts did not match books in the library and no author was named for the article.
examples: The teacher marked the online source as questionable because its facts did not match books in the library and no author was named for the article.
They found questionable footprints by the shed that didn't match the cat or dog, so everyone wondered what animal could have been there at night.
When the offer to buy the old bike seemed too good to be true, Jamie called his dad because the deal looked questionable and needed checking.
entries.spellingNote: Questionable keeps the root 'question' and adds -able; check the middle '-tion-' and the -able ending.

entries.definition: Brightly shining or glowing, or showing great happiness and warmth that others can see.
entries.example: At the school concert, Mia stood centre stage and looked radiant as the spotlights warmed her face and the audience clapped loudly.
examples: At the school concert, Mia stood centre stage and looked radiant as the spotlights warmed her face and the audience clapped loudly.
After the rain stopped, the garden looked radiant with sunlight on every wet leaf while the puddles sparkled in the lane.
When Grandad saw his old friends arrive, he was radiant with surprise and joy, smiling so wide that everyone laughed with him.
entries.spellingNote: Remember 'radiant' has 'di' in the middle, not 'ia' — think of 'radiate' to help spell it.

entries.definition: To violently damage or destroy something, leaving it badly harmed or ruined.
entries.example: The storm began to ravage the seaside town overnight, tearing off roofs and flooding shops so people could not open them in the morning.
examples: The storm began to ravage the seaside town overnight, tearing off roofs and flooding shops so people could not open them in the morning.
When the beetles attacked the apple trees, they began to ravage the orchard, stripping leaves and leaving the fruit wilted and small.
Neglect and storms can ravage the old castle, leaving collapsed walls and ivy sweeping through empty halls like a wild blanket.
entries.spellingNote: Note the spelling 'ravage' uses a double 'a' sound but only one 'a' letter; remember the 'v' after the 'ra'.

entries.definition: A person who refuses to obey rules or authority, often trying to change or resist them.
entries.example: Tom felt like a rebel when he quietly painted a mural for the classroom wall after asking permission was refused by the teacher.
examples: Tom felt like a rebel when he quietly painted a mural for the classroom wall after asking permission was refused by the teacher.
In the story, the smallest villager became a rebel and challenged the mayor's unfair rule, rallying families to demand a change.
As a rebel in the club, Ella suggested different games and refused to follow the old list, which started friendly arguments that ended in new ideas.
entries.spellingNote: Rebel has one 'l' at the end; remember the pair 're-bel' like two short parts to the word.

entries.definition: An organised fight or refusal to obey by a group of people against those in power or against the rules.
entries.example: The village's small rebellion began when farmers stopped paying the tolls and marched to the castle to demand fairer rules from the lord.
examples: The village's small rebellion began when farmers stopped paying the tolls and marched to the castle to demand fairer rules from the lord.
At school, a lunchtime rebellion started when half the class refused to eat soggy sandwiches and petitioned for fresher meals instead.
History lessons told how the rebellion grew quickly as towns joined together, making leaders nervous and forcing a meeting to find a solution.
entries.spellingNote: Remember 'rebellion' has double 'l' in the middle and ends with '-ion', like many noun forms of action.

entries.definition: Acting without thinking about danger or the possible bad results; careless about safety.
entries.example: Leo made a reckless choice to climb the tall fence near the river, and his friends shouted because the ground below looked slippery and dangerous.
examples: Leo made a reckless choice to climb the tall fence near the river, and his friends shouted because the ground below looked slippery and dangerous.
Driving the go-kart too fast around the corner was reckless, and the instructor had to step in before someone got hurt.
Jasmine's reckless borrowing of her sister's jacket without asking led to a missing favourite and a angry argument at home.
entries.spellingNote: Reckless has 'ck' in the middle and double 's' at the end; remember the hard 'k' sound uses 'ck'.

entries.definition: To move or pull back from a position or to become less strong or clear, like water moving away from the shore.
entries.example: After the tide started to recede, children ran to collect shells on the newly exposed sand while boats rested on the beach.
examples: After the tide started to recede, children ran to collect shells on the newly exposed sand while boats rested on the beach.
As the fog began to recede in the morning, the outline of the old church appeared and everyone could see the steeple again.
When the crowds recede after the parade, street cleaners arrive and the city looks much calmer and ready for the next day.
entries.spellingNote: Recede has 're' at the start and 'cede' like 'cede ground'; notice the 'c-e-d-e' pattern.

entries.definition: To improve something by removing mistakes or unwanted parts, making it purer, clearer, or more effective.
entries.example: The science class had to refine their experiment plan three times, cutting small errors so their results would be clear and reliable.
examples: The science class had to refine their experiment plan three times, cutting small errors so their results would be clear and reliable.
Bakers refine a recipe by changing tiny amounts of sugar or flour until the cake tastes just right for the competition.
An artist will refine a drawing, erasing stray lines and adjusting shapes, until the picture looks finished and pleasing to the eye.
entries.spellingNote: Refine starts with 're-' meaning 'again' and ends with '-fine'; don't confuse the 'f' with a 'ph'.

entries.definition: To say no to something or decide not to accept or do it.
entries.example: When offered a slice of cake she did not like, Sabi decided to refuse the plate and chose a fruit instead to keep her tummy happy.
examples: When offered a slice of cake she did not like, Sabi decided to refuse the plate and chose a fruit instead to keep her tummy happy.
The goalkeeper had to refuse the reporter's question about the secret plan, because the final match was still two days away.
Tom decided to refuse the extra homework from the club because he needed time to help his little sister with reading after school.
entries.spellingNote: Refuse (say no) is spelled the same as refuse (rubbish); remember meaning from the sentence to tell them apart.

entries.definition: A large group of soldiers in the army organised as a unit, or any large organised group working together in a strict way.
entries.example: During the school history trip, we saw a photograph of a regiment lined up in perfect rows as the sergeant checked their uniforms and boots.
examples: During the school history trip, we saw a photograph of a regiment lined up in perfect rows as the sergeant checked their uniforms and boots.
The gardeners worked like a regiment, each person with a clear task, so the park was tidy and the flowerbeds were neat by lunchtime.
When the festival began, the marching band moved as if part of a regiment, stepping in time and making a powerful, organised sound down the street.
entries.spellingNote: Regiment has 'regi-' at the start, not 'rege-'; pronounce the 'g' softly like 'rej'.

entries.definition: To make something stronger or more certain by adding extra support, materials, or proof.
entries.example: The bridge crew used extra steel bars to reinforce the old beams so the footbridge would be safe for everyone walking to school.
examples: The bridge crew used extra steel bars to reinforce the old beams so the footbridge would be safe for everyone walking to school.
Praise and clear rules can reinforce good behaviour in class, helping pupils understand what is expected and why it matters.
To reinforce his hypothesis, Mia repeated the experiment and recorded matching results, which made the teacher nod and smile at her careful work.
entries.spellingNote: Reinforce uses 'rein-' like adding a 'rein' to control a horse; the middle is 'force', so spelled 'rein-force'.

entries.definition: not willing or not keen to do something
entries.example: At the science museum, Aylin was reluctant to touch the meteorite sample until the guide explained it sat safely behind glass. She wanted to be brave, but the strange black rock looked as if it had just fallen from space.
examples: At the science museum, Aylin was reluctant to touch the meteorite sample until the guide explained it sat safely behind glass. She wanted to be brave, but the strange black rock looked as if it had just fallen from space.

The goalkeeper was reluctant to leave the pitch after saving two penalties, even though the coach waved him over for a rest. He kept looking back at the goal, unwilling to stop while the match still felt alive.
When the rescue boat rocked beside the pier, the dog was reluctant to jump aboard. The trainer waited quietly, letting the dog decide when the boat felt safe.
entries.spellingNote: Ends with -ant, not -ent.

entries.definition: Far away in place or time, or something that operates from a distance, like a remote control.
entries.example: The farmhouse was remote, set at the end of a long lane with no neighbours for miles, so the children loved the quiet nights full of stars.
examples: The farmhouse was remote, set at the end of a long lane with no neighbours for miles, so the children loved the quiet nights full of stars.
Grandma used a small remote to turn on the radio from her armchair because the buttons were easier to press from where she sat.
We studied a remote island on the map that had strange birds no one had seen before, which made the whole class whisper with curiosity.
entries.spellingNote: Remote has 're-' at the start and ends with 'mote'; remember the 'e' after 'r' and before 'm'.

entries.definition: To fill something up again or replace what has been used so there is a fresh supply.
entries.example: After the long hike, we had to replenish our water bottles at a spring so everyone could drink and feel ready to continue the walk.
examples: After the long hike, we had to replenish our water bottles at a spring so everyone could drink and feel ready to continue the walk.
The kitchen staff replenish the snack boxes each morning so pupils always find fruit and crackers at breaktime.
When the library shelf ran low, the librarian ordered new books to replenish the collection and keep readers excited to borrow more.
entries.spellingNote: Replenish has 'plen' in the middle from 'plenty' ideas; remember the 'pl' after 're-'.

entries.definition: able to recover after difficulty
entries.example: The resilient tree bent during the storm, lost three branches, and still pushed out new leaves in spring. It did not escape damage, but it recovered.
examples: The resilient tree bent during the storm, lost three branches, and still pushed out new leaves in spring. It did not escape damage, but it recovered.
After losing the first set badly, the resilient tennis player changed her plan and fought back point by point. The crowd could see her confidence returning.
The coastal town was resilient after the flood. Families cleared mud from the bakery, reopened the school hall, and painted new water lines on the wall as a warning.
entries.spellingNote: re + sil + ient.

entries.definition: A short, welcome break from something tiring, difficult or unpleasant, giving time to rest or recover.
entries.example: After two hours of heavy gardening, Mum brought out juice and we had a small respite on the doorstep before finishing the hedges.
examples: After two hours of heavy gardening, Mum brought out juice and we had a small respite on the doorstep before finishing the hedges.
The long walk up the hill became easier when the teacher gave everyone a five-minute respite to breathe and look at the view.
During the noisy drill, the emergency team moved the children to a quiet room so they could have a brief respite from the alarm sounds.
entries.spellingNote: Respite has the letters 'res' then 'pite' — pronounce the first syllable 'RES' and the second softly.

entries.definition: A duty or job that someone must do, often showing that you can be trusted to take care of something or someone.
entries.example: Every evening, Mia takes the responsibility for feeding the hamster and checking its water before doing her homework.
examples: Every evening, Mia takes the responsibility for feeding the hamster and checking its water before doing her homework.
As class monitor, Jamal felt the responsibility to hand out books and keep the classroom tidy for everyone.
Looking after the baby plant was Dad's test of responsibility; if it survived, she would get to plant a seed of her own.
entries.spellingNote: Responsibility is long — remember the middle has 'sibil' (s-i-b-i-l) then 'ity' at the end.

entries.definition: To go and get something and bring it back, or to get information from somewhere and use it again.
entries.example: I asked Scout to fetch the ball and he ran to retrieve it from under the fence, wagging his tail proudly.
examples: I asked Scout to fetch the ball and he ran to retrieve it from under the fence, wagging his tail proudly.
The scientist used a small robot to retrieve the soil sample from the moon-like test area in the field.
When the story disappeared from the screen, the teacher showed us how to retrieve our work from the saved files.
entries.spellingNote: Remember 'retrieve' begins with 're-' meaning 'again' and has 'trie' in the middle, not 'try'.

entries.definition: Past tense of retrieve: something that was fetched or brought back, or information that was got back.
entries.example: Grandad smiled as he retrieved the old map from the attic trunk and spread it on the table to show us the islands.
examples: Grandad smiled as he retrieved the old map from the attic trunk and spread it on the table to show us the islands.
The diver retrieved the lost camera from the seabed and everyone cheered when the photos were safe and dry.
After the thunderstorm, the dog retrieved the soaking letter from the puddle and nudged it towards the letterbox.
entries.spellingNote: Add '-ed' to retrieve to make 'retrieved'; keep the same spelling before the ending.

entries.definition: Very stiff or fixed so it does not bend, change or adapt easily; strict and not flexible.
entries.example: The teacher used a rigid ruler that would not bend, so we measured the board line exactly and drew a straight border.
examples: The teacher used a rigid ruler that would not bend, so we measured the board line exactly and drew a straight border.
When the branch became rigid from cold, the birds could not bend it and had to find a warmer place to rest.
His rigid plan for the trip left no time for detours, which upset Anna because she loved small surprises on walks.
entries.spellingNote: Rigid has a short 'i' sound and only one 'g' — r-i-g-i-d.

entries.definition: A noisy, often violent crowd scene where people break rules, destroy property, or fight because of strong anger or disorder.
entries.example: When the match was cancelled, a small crowd grew angry and a few started shouting; police rushed in as the situation nearly became a riot.
examples: When the match was cancelled, a small crowd grew angry and a few started shouting; police rushed in as the situation nearly became a riot.
In the story, a misunderstanding in the market turned into a riot, and the town bell had to warn everyone to stay inside.
The teacher explained how a peaceful protest can sadly turn into a riot if people begin to break windows and shout threats.
entries.spellingNote: Riot is short — remember the two vowels 'i' and 'o' in order: r-i-o-t.

entries.definition: A list or schedule that shows who must do a particular job and when, often used at school or work.
entries.example: The classroom rota told us who would be responsible for watering the plants each day, and I was excited to be on it for Friday.
examples: The classroom rota told us who would be responsible for watering the plants each day, and I was excited to be on it for Friday.
Each week the kitchen rota showed that Dad would cook on Saturdays and everyone else had smaller duties during the week.
At the animal centre the volunteer rota made sure that every dog had someone to walk it and check its food on time.
entries.spellingNote: Rota is a short British word — r-o-t-a — and is pronounced like 'ROW-tuh'.

entries.definition: Something you do regularly in the same way, like a set of steps or habits you follow every day.
entries.example: Every morning my routine was the same: brush teeth, make the bed and pack my school bag before breakfast.
examples: Every morning my routine was the same: brush teeth, make the bed and pack my school bag before breakfast.
The dance teacher taught us a new routine step by step until everyone could perform it without looking at their notes.
When the storm arrived, Mum changed our bedtime routine so we could check the radio and candles before lights-out.
entries.spellingNote: Routine comes from French; remember the 'u' after the 'r' and the ending '-ine'.

entries.definition: Relating to the countryside or small villages, not the busy town or city; often open, quiet and with farms.
entries.example: Grandma lives in a rural village where tractors pass the cottage and there's a small stream behind her garden for frogs.
examples: Grandma lives in a rural village where tractors pass the cottage and there's a small stream behind her garden for frogs.
The school trip to the rural farm taught us about hens and fields, very different from our usual city park lessons.
On a rural lane we saw stars like a blanket above us because there were no streetlights to hide the night sky.
entries.spellingNote: Rural has two 'r' sounds close together — r-u-r-a-l — say it slowly: 'roo-ral'.

entries.definition: Very fierce, violent or cruel; something wild and intense that causes strong fear or damage.
entries.example: The sudden savage storm ripped leaves from trees and battered the windows, leaving the garden looking almost unrecognisable.
examples: The sudden savage storm ripped leaves from trees and battered the windows, leaving the garden looking almost unrecognisable.
In the tale the knight faced a savage beast, fierce and growling, that protected the cave where the treasure lay.
The coach warned us the winter could be savage on the mountainside, so we needed warm clothes and careful planning.
entries.spellingNote: Savage is spelled s-a-v-a-g-e; the final 'e' is silent but important for correct spelling.

entries.definition: not enough; hard to find
entries.example: During the heatwave, clean water became scarce in the village, so every family filled only one bucket at the pump. People used each cup carefully because nobody knew when the next delivery would arrive.
examples: During the heatwave, clean water became scarce in the village, so every family filled only one bucket at the pump. People used each cup carefully because nobody knew when the next delivery would arrive.
On the island, fresh fruit was scarce after the storm delayed the supply boat. The shopkeeper saved the last oranges for the youngest children.
Tickets for the final were scarce because the small stadium held only a few thousand fans. By breakfast, every seat had already been sold.
entries.spellingNote: The c comes before e.

entries.definition: To throw or drop things in different directions so they spread over an area, or to cause people or animals to go quickly away.
entries.example: The children decided to scatter seeds across the patch of soil, then stepped back to watch the birds arrive and peck them up.
examples: The children decided to scatter seeds across the patch of soil, then stepped back to watch the birds arrive and peck them up.
When Mum opened the biscuit tin, the dog knocked it over and made the biscuits scatter across the kitchen floor as we all laughed.
A gust of wind caused the picnic napkins to scatter along the path, and we chased them while the hens looked on in confusion.
entries.spellingNote: Scatter has a double 't' — s-c-a-t-t-e-r — remember to write both 't's.

entries.definition: Safe from danger or theft, or fastened so it will not move; also to get or make something certain or protected.
entries.example: I secure my bike with a heavy lock to the rail so it won't get taken, and I always check the lock before leaving school.
examples: I secure my bike with a heavy lock to the rail so it won't get taken, and I always check the lock before leaving school.
The archaeologists secure the ancient box with careful straps before lifting it so nothing inside can fall out and break.
She worked hard to secure a place in the choir, practising every evening until the teacher offered her the solo.
entries.spellingNote: Secure starts with 'se-' and ends '-cure' like 'cure' — s-e-c-u-r-e; do not drop the 'e'.

entries.definition: Not happening often; almost never.
entries.example: Grandad came to our school once and now seldom visits during term time, so everyone savoured the day's special stories and cakes.
examples: Grandad came to our school once and now seldom visits during term time, so everyone savoured the day's special stories and cakes.
The little blue comet is seldom seen from our town, so the amateur astronomers set up telescopes and compared frantic notes all night.
Our class seldom gets a whole afternoon free, so when we did we raced outside, built a fort and pretended to be explorers for hours.
entries.spellingNote: Seldom is short and simple: s-e-l-d-o-m; do not add extra letters at the end.

entries.definition: calm and peaceful
entries.example: The lake was serene before sunrise, with no boats, no wind, and only one duck drawing a line across the water. Even the noisy campsite seemed to hold its breath.
examples: The lake was serene before sunrise, with no boats, no wind, and only one duck drawing a line across the water. Even the noisy campsite seemed to hold its breath.
Inside the old library, the reading room felt serene despite the busy street outside. Tall shelves softened every sound, and dust floated calmly in the golden light.
The astronaut described Earth as serene from orbit. From that height, storms looked like slow white swirls instead of danger.
entries.spellingNote: se + rene.

entries.definition: Very bad, serious, or harsh in a way that causes worry or strong effects.
entries.example: After a severe storm ripped off roofs, the school closed and everyone helped make lists of what needed fixing first.
examples: After a severe storm ripped off roofs, the school closed and everyone helped make lists of what needed fixing first.
The doctor warned that the cut was severe and needed careful cleaning and stitches so it would heal without infection.
When the teacher saw the severe cheating on the test, she held a long meeting to explain why honesty matters in school projects.
entries.spellingNote: Spells s-e-v-e-r-e; remember the two 'e's with 'se' at the start and 're' at the end.

entries.definition: Clever at understanding situations and making good decisions, especially about people or money.
entries.example: A shrewd pupil noticed the pattern of clues in the treasure map and guessed the teacher's hiding place before anyone else.
examples: A shrewd pupil noticed the pattern of clues in the treasure map and guessed the teacher's hiding place before anyone else.
The market stall owner gave a shrewd discount to the family who bought many jars, knowing they would tell other shoppers about his stall.
In the history lesson the shrewd general formed an unusual alliance that surprised his enemies and changed the course of the campaign.
entries.spellingNote: Shrewd ends with 'wd' and has 'shrew' at the start: s-h-r-e-w-d.

entries.definition: honest and truly meant
entries.example: Her sincere thank-you note mentioned the exact moment her friend had helped, not just a quick polite phrase. That detail made the kindness feel truly remembered.
