examples: Her sincere thank-you note mentioned the exact moment her friend had helped, not just a quick polite phrase. That detail made the kindness feel truly remembered.
The captain gave a sincere speech after losing the final. He praised the other team first, then admitted where his own team needed to improve.
A sincere promise feels different from a showy one. When Jonah said he would feed the neighbour's cat, he set an alarm and actually did it every morning.
entries.spellingNote: sin + cere.

entries.definition: Enjoying being with other people and making friends; friendly and outgoing.
entries.example: At the new club Nora was so sociable that she introduced everyone and soon a quiet corner turned into a laughing circle of friends.
examples: At the new club Nora was so sociable that she introduced everyone and soon a quiet corner turned into a laughing circle of friends.
Our puppy is very sociable and wags its tail for strangers and neighbours, which makes walks full of happy meetings.
When the class had a team task the most sociable children helped others join in, so shy pupils felt safe to try new ideas.
entries.spellingNote: Sociable has the root 'soci-' (people) and ends '-able'; spell it s-o-c-i-a-b-l-e.

entries.definition: Very serious, quiet, and respectful, often for an important event.
entries.example: During the school assembly we stood in a solemn circle to remember the old headteacher and listened to gentle stories about their kindness.
examples: During the school assembly we stood in a solemn circle to remember the old headteacher and listened to gentle stories about their kindness.
The captain gave a solemn promise before the match that everyone would play fair, and the team nodded as if the words were a pact.
As the church bell tolled the family wore solemn faces and carried the framed photograph slowly towards the grave with steady steps.
entries.spellingNote: Write solemn as s-o-l-e-m-n; the final 'n' is kept in spelling though you might not hear it strongly when speaking.

entries.definition: Spread out thinly with only a few things in an area; not dense.
entries.example: The plants on the dry hill were sparse, with only a few tough grasses and flowers brave enough to grow between the rocks.
examples: The plants on the dry hill were sparse, with only a few tough grasses and flowers brave enough to grow between the rocks.
In the tiny village the shops were sparse, so residents travelled to the nearest town for even simple groceries and medicines.
Our campsite felt sparse at dawn; tents were far apart, the fire was small and the sky above was huge and starry.
entries.spellingNote: Remember sparse has one 'r' and ends with 'se': s-p-a-r-s-e, not 'sparse' with extra letters.

entries.definition: Wanting to hurt, annoy or upset someone on purpose because of anger or jealousy.
entries.example: After losing the game, Leo left a spiteful note on the scoreboard and the teacher had to remind everyone that words can hurt as much as a shove.
examples: After losing the game, Leo left a spiteful note on the scoreboard and the teacher had to remind everyone that words can hurt as much as a shove.
She was so spiteful that she hid her sister's favourite book; later she felt guilty when she saw how upset her sister became until it was found.
A spiteful comment spread at lunchtime and it took several kind apologies to mend the playground friendships that had been broken.
entries.spellingNote: Ends with '-ful' like helpful: s-p-i-t-e-f-u-l, not '-full'.

entries.definition: Very good, beautiful, or impressive; excellent.
entries.example: The school play was splendid: the costumes gleamed, the acting surprised us all and the audience gave a long cheering applause.
examples: The school play was splendid: the costumes gleamed, the acting surprised us all and the audience gave a long cheering applause.
We had a splendid view from the hilltop where the sunrise painted the clouds pink and everyone took quiet, happy photographs.
Mum made a splendid cake with bright icing and tiny flags, and it tasted like the kind of treat that makes a rainy day feel sunny.
entries.spellingNote: Splendid has 'splend' then 'id': s-p-l-e-n-d-i-d; remember the 'd' before the final 'id'.

entries.definition: Not likely to change or fall; steady and firm. It also means a building where horses live.
entries.example: The ladder felt stable against the wall, so Sam climbed up carefully to rescue the stuck kite without wobbling or slipping.
examples: The ladder felt stable against the wall, so Sam climbed up carefully to rescue the stuck kite without wobbling or slipping.
After the vet checked the mare, she followed the stable routine so the horse stayed calm and fed, even during noisy storms.
Our friendship stayed stable through disagreements because we talked things over and forgave each other instead of shouting.
entries.spellingNote: Stable ends with '-able' like many adjectives: s-t-a-b-l-e.

entries.definition: To walk slowly and calmly for pleasure.
entries.example: We took a slow evening stroll along the seafront, counting boats and collecting smooth pebbles while the sky turned gold and pink.
examples: We took a slow evening stroll along the seafront, counting boats and collecting smooth pebbles while the sky turned gold and pink.
After lunch the pair decided to stroll through the park and found a hidden pond where frogs leapt and dragonflies flickered.
Grandma likes to stroll to the corner shop, chatting to neighbours, and she always returns with a small treat tucked in her pocket.
entries.spellingNote: Stroll uses a double 'l' at the end: s-t-r-o-l-l.

entries.definition: A careful plan or method for reaching a goal or solving a problem.
entries.example: Before the chess match the team formed a strategy, practising moves and predicting opponents so each player knew their job.
examples: Before the chess match the team formed a strategy, practising moves and predicting opponents so each player knew their job.
For the science fair our strategy was to test one thing at a time, write careful notes and make a bright poster that explained every step.
The rescue crew used a clear strategy to get everyone out of the cave: ropes, lights and a check-list so no one was forgotten.
entries.spellingNote: Strategy is spelled s-t-r-a-t-e-g-y; don't swap the 'e' for an 'a' in the last syllable.

entries.definition: Very strict and exact, with strong rules or controls that are not easy to change.
entries.example: The laboratory had stringent safety rules: goggles on at all times, equipment checked twice and no running near the chemicals.
examples: The laboratory had stringent safety rules: goggles on at all times, equipment checked twice and no running near the chemicals.
When the hike crossed fragile ground the park put in stringent limits on where we could walk so the flowers would not be trampled.
The school introduced stringent timing for exams, so teachers practised clear instructions and students learned to check their work fast and calm.
entries.spellingNote: Stringent starts with 'string' and ends '-ent': s-t-r-i-n-g-e-n-t; do not write 'stringant'.

entries.definition: Strongly built and able to stand hard use or bad weather without easily breaking or falling apart.
entries.example: The sturdy wooden table stayed level when the class piled books, pencils and a small globe on it during the busy art lesson.
examples: The sturdy wooden table stayed level when the class piled books, pencils and a small globe on it during the busy art lesson.
Leyla wore sturdy boots on the muddy field trip, so her feet stayed dry and she could climb the slippery bank with confidence.
After the storm, everyone admired the sturdy stone wall that had kept the playground safe while the trees around it fell.
entries.spellingNote: sturdy is spelled s-t-u-r-d-y; note the 'u' after 'st'.

entries.definition: Not obvious; small or delicate in a way that needs careful notice or thought to understand.
entries.example: The subtle change in the sky's colour warned Leo of a coming storm before the first wind gust shook the leaves.
examples: The subtle change in the sky's colour warned Leo of a coming storm before the first wind gust shook the leaves.
Becky used a subtle smile to show she forgave her friend, but only the teacher noticed how relieved she was.
The detective spotted a subtle footprint by the shed that helped solve the village mystery when compared to others.
entries.spellingNote: subtle is spelled s-u-b-t-l-e; the 'b' is silent when you say the word.

entries.definition: Achieved what was wanted or reached a goal that you tried to do.
entries.example: Our football team succeeded in scoring the winning goal in the final minute after two months of training and a very noisy crowd.
examples: Our football team succeeded in scoring the winning goal in the final minute after two months of training and a very noisy crowd.
Asha succeeded in making the science model float when she changed the weight, and the whole class cheered her idea.
The small seedling succeeded in growing through the cracked pavement and surprised everyone walking down the street.
entries.spellingNote: succeeded is spelled s-u-c-c-e-e-d-e-d with two c's and two e's in the middle.

entries.definition: Very hot and a bit uncomfortable because the air feels heavy and sticky; can also describe a warm, rich atmosphere.
entries.example: The sultry summer evening made the river smell of warm grass and the cricket chorus sounded slower than usual.
examples: The sultry summer evening made the river smell of warm grass and the cricket chorus sounded slower than usual.
We left the sultry tent after the scout sleepover because the heat and damp air made everyone feel faint and tired.
The soft, sultry music filled the room and gave the history lesson a very different, warmer mood than usual.
entries.spellingNote: sultry is spelled s-u-l-t-r-y; remember the l comes before the t.

entries.definition: Higher in rank, quality, skill, or status; better than others in some way. Can also mean acting as if better than others.
entries.example: The new running shoes felt superior on the playground because they gripped the track and helped Jamie win his race.
examples: The new running shoes felt superior on the playground because they gripped the track and helped Jamie win his race.
At chess club, Lina used a superior strategy, so she won every round and then helped her teammates learn.
The teacher warned about a superior attitude after Tom bragged he was smarter than everyone, which upset his friend.
entries.spellingNote: superior begins with 'super' and ends with '-ior'.

entries.definition: uncomfortably hot
entries.example: The classroom was sweltering by afternoon, and even the glue sticks felt soft. The teacher moved the lesson under the trees where a little breeze survived.
examples: The classroom was sweltering by afternoon, and even the glue sticks felt soft. The teacher moved the lesson under the trees where a little breeze survived.
In the sweltering underground station, commuters fanned themselves with tickets while the announcement board delayed every train. The air felt trapped and heavy.
The footballers trained in sweltering heat, so the coach ordered water breaks every ten minutes. Running hard was dangerous when the pitch shimmered like a pan.
entries.spellingNote: swelter + ing.

entries.definition: A close living relationship between different kinds of plants or animals in which they often help each other and both benefit.
entries.example: The symbiotic relationship between the clownfish and its sea anemone helps both stay safe and share food in the bright reef.
examples: The symbiotic relationship between the clownfish and its sea anemone helps both stay safe and share food in the bright reef.
In the school garden the worms and plants had a symbiotic partnership: worms loosened soil while plants fed tiny creatures.
Scientists studied a symbiotic pair of bacteria and fungi that helped trees recover and grow faster after the wildfire.
entries.spellingNote: symbiotic starts with 'sym-' like 'symmetry' and ends with 'biotic' meaning life.

entries.definition: Boring because something goes on for a long time with little change or interest.
entries.example: Folding one hundred paper cranes felt tedious to Mei until she imagined them flying, and she kept folding quietly for an hour.
examples: Folding one hundred paper cranes felt tedious to Mei until she imagined them flying, and she kept folding quietly for an hour.
The long, tedious maths worksheet made the whole class yawn, so the teacher added a quick game to lift their spirits.
Their walk home became tedious when the rain slowed them down and there was nothing but similar houses to look at for miles.
entries.spellingNote: tedious is spelled t-e-d-i-o-u-s; note the 'ious' ending.

entries.definition: Lasting only for a short time; not permanent or meant to stay forever.
entries.example: The temporary bridge across the stream was built from planks and ropes so villagers could cross while the old bridge was repaired.
examples: The temporary bridge across the stream was built from planks and ropes so villagers could cross while the old bridge was repaired.
Sofia wore a temporary cast painted with stars until the doctor decided her arm had healed enough to be checked again.
The classroom had a temporary seating plan for the exams, with name cards stuck to desks for one week only.
entries.spellingNote: temporary is spelled t-e-m-p-o-r-a-r-y; beware the common misspelling 'temperary'.

entries.definition: Very frightened; feeling a strong, sudden fear or panic.
entries.example: Evan was terrified when he heard a noise in the dark shed late at night, but his dog barked and they found the lost kitten inside.
examples: Evan was terrified when he heard a noise in the dark shed late at night, but his dog barked and they found the lost kitten inside.
The class was terrified before the assembly about a mysterious noise, then laughed when it turned out to be a creaking door hinge.
On the cliff path, Mia felt terrified as the wind pushed her hair and she gripped the fence until the guide led her to safety.
entries.spellingNote: terrified is spelled t-e-r-r-i-f-i-e-d with two r's after the t.

entries.definition: A small metal or plastic cap worn on the finger to push a needle safely when sewing.
entries.example: Grandma showed Jake how to use a thimble to push the needle through thick denim without pricking his fingertip during sewing time.
examples: Grandma showed Jake how to use a thimble to push the needle through thick denim without pricking his fingertip during sewing time.
The lost thimble rolled under the sewing box for months until the cat batted it out first thing one morning.
At craft club, Amira decorated a tiny thimble to make a hat for a doll and everyone thought the idea was clever.
entries.spellingNote: thimble is spelled t-h-i-m-b-l-e; the 'b' is written and pronounced softly in some accents.

entries.definition: To grow well, be healthy, or do very well and be successful.
entries.example: The seedlings began to thrive after steady rain and warm sun, turning the small patch behind the shed into a green carpet in a week.
examples: The seedlings began to thrive after steady rain and warm sun, turning the small patch behind the shed into a green carpet in a week.
Lola will thrive at the new school because she makes friends easily and loves the science club's experiments.
When the community garden got tidy compost and regular watering, the tomato plants began to thrive on every raised bed.
entries.spellingNote: thrive is spelled t-h-r-i-v-e; when adding -ing drop the 'e' (thriving).

entries.definition: shy, nervous, or lacking courage
entries.example: The timid kitten crept out from under the sofa only when the room became quiet. It sniffed the toy mouse, then dashed back as soon as someone laughed.
examples: The timid kitten crept out from under the sofa only when the room became quiet. It sniffed the toy mouse, then dashed back as soon as someone laughed.
At her first debate club, Priya felt timid and held her notes with both hands. Her idea was clever, but she needed a deep breath before saying it aloud.
The timid deer paused at the edge of the clearing, ears twitching at every snapped twig. It wanted the fresh grass, but the open space felt dangerous.
entries.spellingNote: Short word: ti + mid.

entries.definition: Willing to accept other people's opinions, habits or differences; able to deal with difficult conditions calmly.
entries.example: Mrs Khan is tolerant of noisy students during creative work as long as they are learning, so her classroom stays lively and fair.
examples: Mrs Khan is tolerant of noisy students during creative work as long as they are learning, so her classroom stays lively and fair.
The plants were tolerant of some shade, so they grew well under the apple tree while the sun shone on the lawn.
Being tolerant with his little sister helped Sam stay calm when she spilled paint and they cleaned it up together as a team.
entries.spellingNote: tolerant is spelled t-o-l-e-r-a-n-t; related to the verb tolerate.

entries.definition: Very calm and peaceful, with little or no noise or disturbance.
entries.example: We sat by the tranquil pond as dragonflies skimmed the surface and Mrs Patel read a story while the sun warmed our coats and no one spoke.
examples: We sat by the tranquil pond as dragonflies skimmed the surface and Mrs Patel read a story while the sun warmed our coats and no one spoke.
After the storm the garden looked tranquil, the puddles reflecting grey clouds and the robin hopped about without any hurry or fear.
Grandad found a tranquil corner in the museum where he could sketch the old maps for an hour without the bustle of the crowd nearby.
entries.spellingNote: Ends with -quil, not -cal; remember the 'qu' and the final 'l'.

entries.definition: The crime of betraying your country, for example by helping its enemies or giving them secret information.
entries.example: In the history lesson the class learned how a spy was accused of treason for sending secret letters to the enemy during the war and facing a trial.
examples: In the history lesson the class learned how a spy was accused of treason for sending secret letters to the enemy during the war and facing a trial.
Tom's made-up tale about selling maps to a rival kingdom sounded like treason to the teacher, who asked him very carefully where he had found the maps.
The old castle held files about treason trials where people had to prove they were loyal or else face severe consequences from the court.
entries.spellingNote: Contains 'ea' which sounds like the long 'ee' in reason; do not confuse with 'trison' or 'treason'.

entries.definition: Very large, great, or impressive in amount, size, strength, or feeling.
entries.example: We felt a tremendous gust of wind that lifted our hats as the ferry crossed the river mouth during a wild spring storm and everyone held on tight.
examples: We felt a tremendous gust of wind that lifted our hats as the ferry crossed the river mouth during a wild spring storm and everyone held on tight.
A tremendous cheer rang out when Sara scored the winning goal, and even the teacher's clipboard jumped with the noise from the playground.
The ancient oak cast a tremendous shadow across the playground, big enough for the whole class to sit inside and pretend it was a secret camp.
entries.spellingNote: Has just one 'm' (tremendous) and ends with -dous; watch the middle 'men' part.

entries.definition: A group of people who live together or share the same ancestors, customs, or rules.
entries.example: During the museum visit we saw a picture of a coastal tribe that hunted fish, made nets and passed songs down through many generations.
examples: During the museum visit we saw a picture of a coastal tribe that hunted fish, made nets and passed songs down through many generations.
In the story the explorers made friends with a small tribe who taught them how to find fresh water in the dry desert and which plants were safe.
The classroom split into a pretend tribe for our history game, each team choosing a name, a leader and tasks to survive a week in the wild.
entries.spellingNote: The final 'e' is silent and makes the vowel 'i' a long sound, so pronounce it like 'tribe' not 'trib'.

entries.definition: Feeling or showing great joy and pride because of a victory or success.
entries.example: After finishing the tricky puzzle, Sofia held the final piece aloft and looked triumphant as her friends clapped and laughed around her table.
examples: After finishing the tricky puzzle, Sofia held the final piece aloft and looked triumphant as her friends clapped and laughed around her table.
The football team returned triumphant from the cup match, singing down the High Street with the shiny trophy balanced between them.
Professor Chen gave a triumphant smile when his experiment finally worked and bright bubbles rose from the mixture as the bell rang.
entries.spellingNote: Comes from 'triumph' and has 'ph' representing an 'f' sound; remember the -ant ending.

entries.definition: Not fair or reasonable; treating people in a way that is wrong or unfair.
entries.example: The class thought it was unjust when only one child was blamed for the missing book before anyone asked simple questions or checked the shelf.
examples: The class thought it was unjust when only one child was blamed for the missing book before anyone asked simple questions or checked the shelf.
When the judge ignored clear evidence, the villagers said the decision felt unjust and asked for a new hearing to look at the facts.
Lena cried because being punished for a game she did not play seemed unjust, so the teachers promised to investigate what had happened.
entries.spellingNote: Built from 'un-' + 'just'; do not add an extra 'e' or change the order of letters.

entries.definition: Being the only one of its kind; special in a way that no other thing or person is.
entries.example: Grandma showed us a unique shell with colours no one else in class had ever seen and we passed it around very quietly so we could study every stripe.
examples: Grandma showed us a unique shell with colours no one else in class had ever seen and we passed it around very quietly so we could study every stripe.
The team's banner was unique because each child had painted a tiny picture on it, making the whole thing unlike any other school's flag.
Sam's handwriting was unique: his letters slanted like little hills, and everyone could spot a note from him on the table straight away.
entries.spellingNote: Ends with a silent 'e' that makes the 'que' sound; do not add extra letters before the 'ue'.

entries.definition: Relating to a town or city, usually with many buildings, roads and lots of people.
entries.example: On the urban walk we counted buses, tall shops and a pigeon nest tucked above a bakery's sign on busy Market Street, then compared notes at lunch.
examples: On the urban walk we counted buses, tall shops and a pigeon nest tucked above a bakery's sign on busy Market Street, then compared notes at lunch.
The science project looked at an urban park and the countryside to see which had more insects on a sunny summer afternoon near our school.
Their story set in an urban neighbourhood showed how children used alleyways and rooftops for secret games and quick shortcuts to school.
entries.spellingNote: Starts with 'ur' and contains no 'o'; remember the short 'u' sound at the start.

entries.definition: Needing quick attention or action; very important to deal with straight away.
entries.example: The vet said it was urgent to get the injured sparrow to a wildlife centre before nightfall, so we hurried to make a small cardboard box for it.
examples: The vet said it was urgent to get the injured sparrow to a wildlife centre before nightfall, so we hurried to make a small cardboard box for it.
When the kitchen began to smell of smoke, an urgent phone call from Dad sent everyone outside while the fire engine raced down the street.
Elif found an urgent note on her desk asking her to bring the gold certificate to the headteacher before the whole school gathered for assembly.
entries.spellingNote: Has 'urg' with a soft 'g' sound and ends -ent; remember the 'g' before the 'e' gives the sound.

entries.definition: Not clear or exact; hard to understand or describe because important details are missing.
entries.example: The teacher's vague instructions left us unsure whether we should draw a map or write a story for homework, so half the class did one and half did the other.
examples: The teacher's vague instructions left us unsure whether we should draw a map or write a story for homework, so half the class did one and half did the other.
In the traveller's diary the directions were vague like 'follow the river', which made finding the camp a slow and puzzling task at dusk.
Nora's answer about the missing pen was vague and the teacher asked her to give more details, like where she was sitting and what time she last saw it.
entries.spellingNote: Ends with -gue and a silent 'e'; the 'g' is hard, not a soft 'j' sound.

entries.definition: very brave, especially in difficulty
entries.example: The valiant firefighter crawled through smoke to find the family dog, even after everyone thought the house was empty. She came out coughing, with the trembling dog tucked under her coat.
examples: The valiant firefighter crawled through smoke to find the family dog, even after everyone thought the house was empty. She came out coughing, with the trembling dog tucked under her coat.
In the final minutes, the valiant goalkeeper played on with a bruised shoulder and still blocked the winning shot. The crowd cheered because bravery mattered as much as the score.
The valiant lifeboat crew launched into freezing waves when a fishing boat lost power at night. Their orange boat looked tiny beside the storm, but they kept going.
entries.spellingNote: va + liant.

entries.definition: green with healthy plants
entries.example: After spring rain, the valley turned verdant, with grass, moss, and young leaves covering every slope. From the hilltop, it looked as if someone had painted the world green overnight.
examples: After spring rain, the valley turned verdant, with grass, moss, and young leaves covering every slope. From the hilltop, it looked as if someone had painted the world green overnight.
The abandoned railway became a verdant path after years without trains. Ferns grew between the sleepers, and butterflies drifted where engines once smoked.
The satellite photo showed a verdant strip along the river cutting through the dry land. Wherever the water reached, green life followed.
entries.spellingNote: ver + dant.

entries.definition: To go somewhere or try something that could be risky or new; it can also mean a risky journey or project.
entries.example: The two friends decided to venture into the abandoned boathouse at dusk, whispering as their torches painted strange shapes across the wooden walls.
examples: The two friends decided to venture into the abandoned boathouse at dusk, whispering as their torches painted strange shapes across the wooden walls.
Our science fair venture to build a tiny weather station felt risky and difficult, but every mistake taught the team something useful for the next day.
Grandad warned them not to venture past the old fence alone because the meadow had hidden holes after the heavy rain and the ground was soft.
entries.spellingNote: Ends with -ture pronounced like 'chuh'; keep the 'e' at the end but it is not sounded.

entries.definition: To check that something is true, correct or accurate by looking for evidence or asking someone.
entries.example: Before handing in the poster, we had to verify each measurement and label so the teacher would not find any mistakes during the fair.
examples: Before handing in the poster, we had to verify each measurement and label so the teacher would not find any mistakes during the fair.
The librarian asked us to verify our names and class before she could let us borrow the rare history book from the locked shelf.
At the coach gate the leader needed to verify Mum's permission letter and check the emergency contact before we could climb aboard for the trip.
entries.spellingNote: Ends with -fy pronounced /-faɪ/ and has three syllables: ver-i-fy.

entries.definition: Able to be used for many different jobs or to do many different activities well.
entries.example: The versatile backpack had pockets for books, a fold-out lunch mat and straps for the water bottle, so Tom used it for school and short hikes.
examples: The versatile backpack had pockets for books, a fold-out lunch mat and straps for the water bottle, so Tom used it for school and short hikes.
Our classroom tablet is so versatile that it plays videos, helps with maths problems and records our science experiments on the same day.
Grandma's kitchen knife is versatile: she uses the same blade to slice bread, chop apples and prepare herbs for the family supper.
entries.spellingNote: Remember it ends with -ile: ver-sa-tile; the middle has 'sat' reversed as 'satile'.

entries.definition: Full of bright colour or life; exciting and energetic to look at or feel.
entries.example: The market looked vibrant with red apples, bright scarves fluttering and music making everyone smile as they tried new food stalls.
examples: The market looked vibrant with red apples, bright scarves fluttering and music making everyone smile as they tried new food stalls.
Her painting used vibrant colours so the sunflowers seemed to dance and even made the classroom feel warmer on a dull day.
The town's parade was vibrant: flags waved, drummers marched and children in colourful costumes laughed in the spring rain.
entries.spellingNote: Remember the -brant ending, not -brent; vibrant has a short 'i' sound like 'vib'.

entries.definition: Very clear, bright or full of detail, so it feels easy to imagine or remember.
entries.example: I had a vivid picture in my head of the dragon with green scales and orange eyes after reading the story at bedtime.
examples: I had a vivid picture in my head of the dragon with green scales and orange eyes after reading the story at bedtime.
The witness gave a vivid description of the lost kitten, saying it had a white paw and a small scar above its nose.
Her memory of the seaside was vivid: the salty wind, the bright kite and the warm sand between her toes on the last day of holiday.
entries.spellingNote: Vivid has two short 'vi' parts: vi-vid; double the idea of brightness.

entries.definition: Needing care or protection because something or someone can be easily harmed or upset.
entries.example: The little hedgehog looked vulnerable on the road, so Lily put it in a box and asked the wildlife rescue for help.
examples: The little hedgehog looked vulnerable on the road, so Lily put it in a box and asked the wildlife rescue for help.
When the bridge was broken, the village was vulnerable to flooding until engineers fixed the supports and cleared the river.
After the storm, the old cottage was vulnerable to cold draughts because several roof tiles and window panes were missing.
entries.spellingNote: Notice the -able ending like 'capable' and the middle 'ner' sound: vul-ner-able.

entries.definition: Walked through shallow water or soft ground, usually with effort and wet shoes or clothes.
entries.example: We waded through the muddy stream to collect pond snails, careful not to slip on the stones under the water.
examples: We waded through the muddy stream to collect pond snails, careful not to slip on the stones under the water.
After the rain, Tom waded across the flooded playground to reach his bike, his socks squelching as he stepped carefully.
The rescue team waded into the field where the sheep were stuck, guiding each animal back to firmer ground one at a time.
entries.spellingNote: Past tense of 'wade' is 'waded'—add -ed like most regular verbs.

entries.definition: To walk around without a fixed route or to let your thoughts move from one thing to another.
entries.example: Esra would often wander near the stream after school, finding unusual leaves and listening to birds until dinner time.
examples: Esra would often wander near the stream after school, finding unusual leaves and listening to birds until dinner time.
During the museum visit, Jack let his eyes wander across the big painting, spotting tiny hidden animals and secret details.
The puppy started to wander away from the campsite, so Sam called it back gently before it reached the tall grass.
entries.spellingNote: Two n's sound the same: wan-der; remember the double-syllable rhythm when you say it.

entries.definition: careful because you think there may be danger
entries.example: The cat was wary of the delivery robot humming along the pavement. It watched from under a parked car, ready to run if the machine came too close.
examples: The cat was wary of the delivery robot humming along the pavement. It watched from under a parked car, ready to run if the machine came too close.
A good historian is wary of a dramatic diary entry until checking who wrote it and why. Exciting stories can still be misleading.
The mountain guide was wary when fresh snow covered the old trail. It looked smooth and pretty, but she knew hidden ice could turn one step into a fall.
entries.spellingNote: Wary has no e after w.

entries.definition: very tired, especially after effort
entries.example: By sunset, the weary hikers had stopped joking and were counting the bends in the path. When the hut finally appeared, even the muddy steps looked beautiful.
examples: By sunset, the weary hikers had stopped joking and were counting the bends in the path. When the hut finally appeared, even the muddy steps looked beautiful.
The weary doctor rubbed her eyes after a night shift in the emergency ward. She still smiled at the next patient, but her voice had the softness of someone who needed sleep.
After rehearsing the dance twelve times, the weary children flopped onto the stage floor. Their costumes sparkled, but their legs felt like wet rope.
entries.spellingNote: Weary means tired; wary means careful.

entries.definition: Becoming dry, weak or damaged, often used for plants or for a very strongly critical look or remark.
entries.example: The scientist watched the plant's leaves going brown and withering under the heat lamp when the water bottle cracked.
examples: The scientist watched the plant's leaves going brown and withering under the heat lamp when the water bottle cracked.
Her withering look stopped the noisy class; everyone sat down quickly and felt a little embarrassed and silent.
After the frost, the once-green garden showed withering stems and curled petals that had been caught by the sudden cold night.
entries.spellingNote: Wither + -ing gives withering; keep the single 'h' after the initial 'wit'.

entries.definition: To become dry and weak, like a plant that loses water, or to slowly lose strength or confidence.
entries.example: Without sunlight and rain, the classroom plant began to wither, its green leaves curling into brown spears over a week.
examples: Without sunlight and rain, the classroom plant began to wither, its green leaves curling into brown spears over a week.
His confidence started to wither after several failed attempts, but his friends helped him try again until he succeeded.
The old poem spoke of how hope can wither if people stop talking kindly to each other during hard times.
entries.spellingNote: W-i-t-h-e-r, think of 'with' + 'er'—a short, single-syllable verb plus -er.

entries.definition: Deserving respect, attention or effort because of good qualities or importance.
entries.example: The book was worthy of a prize because it helped the whole class learn about kindness and courage in a funny way.
examples: The book was worthy of a prize because it helped the whole class learn about kindness and courage in a funny way.
She felt worthy of the medal after months of practice and fair play, proving she had worked hard and been kind to others.
The old oak was worthy of protection by the town; children climbed its low branches and families picnicked in its shade.
entries.spellingNote: Ends with -thy like 'healthy' (no e before the y): wor-thy.

entries.definition: Very unhappy, uncomfortable, or in a bad condition; something that causes pity or disgust.
entries.example: After the long storm, the wretched kitten shivered under the bench until Ellie wrapped it in her jumper and called for help.
examples: After the long storm, the wretched kitten shivered under the bench until Ellie wrapped it in her jumper and called for help.
He felt wretched when he realised he had lost the project notes, but his classmates helped him start again the next day.
The explorers found the old ship in a wretched state, torn sails and rusty metal showing how long it had been forgotten at sea.
entries.spellingNote: Starts with wre- like 'wreck'; remember the ch sound is soft: wretched.

entries.definition: A sudden twist or jerk, or a tool used to turn nuts and bolts; can also mean a strong feeling of sadness when something is lost.
entries.example: Dad used a wrench to loosen the rusty bolt, and then there was a small wrench in his heart as he said goodbye to the old shed.
examples: Dad used a wrench to loosen the rusty bolt, and then there was a small wrench in his heart as he said goodbye to the old shed.
Sam felt a wrench of sadness when the last page of the comic tore out—he had loved that story for years.
The mechanic reached for the correct-sized wrench and turned the wheel nut carefully so the bike would be safe for the race.
entries.spellingNote: One word, one breath: w-r-e-n-c-h. Not to be confused with 'rench' or 'branch'.

entries.definition: To have a strong, often sad wish for something that is missing or seems far away.
entries.example: Maria would yearn for the sea when she was stuck in the city, imagining the sound of waves and salty air every lunchtime.
examples: Maria would yearn for the sea when she was stuck in the city, imagining the sound of waves and salty air every lunchtime.
After months apart, the old friends would yearn to meet again, counting down the days until the school reunion.
On cold nights he would yearn for summer sunlight to warm the garden, watching the calendar pages flip slowly by.
entries.spellingNote: Spelled y-e-a-r-n; the 'ear' part sounds like the body part 'ear'.

entries.definition: Extremely enthusiastic and eager about something, showing strong energy and determination to support, do, or promote it.
entries.example: Our science club leader was zealous about the volcano model, staying after school to mix safe baking soda and vinegar so our eruption was louder than ever.
examples: Our science club leader was zealous about the volcano model, staying after school to mix safe baking soda and vinegar so our eruption was louder than ever.
At the museum the guide was zealous about the ancient coins, pointing out tiny marks and telling every story until the whole class understood why they mattered.
During the beach clean-up a zealous neighbour collected rubbish faster than anyone, encouraging others with a bright whistle and a joking dare to keep going.
entries.spellingNote: Spelled z-e-a-l-o-u-s. The 'ea' makes a short 'e' sound like in 'head', so it is pronounced 'ZEL-us'.

entries.definition: to make something louder, stronger, or greater
entries.example: The microphone helped amplify the headteacher's voice so even the children at the back of the hall could hear. Without it, the announcement disappeared under the rain hammering the roof.
examples: The microphone helped amplify the headteacher's voice so even the children at the back of the hall could hear. Without it, the announcement disappeared under the rain hammering the roof.
The canyon walls seemed to amplify every shout. One small hello bounced back as if a crowd of invisible hikers were answering.
A rumour can amplify fear when people repeat it without checking. By lunchtime, one missing science beaker had become a story about a dangerous explosion.
entries.spellingNote: am + pli + fy.

entries.definition: famous and respected in a particular area
entries.example: An eminent astronomer visited the school and explained black holes with a rubber sheet and marbles. The hall was packed because she was respected around the world.
examples: An eminent astronomer visited the school and explained black holes with a rubber sheet and marbles. The hall was packed because she was respected around the world.
The hospital asked an eminent surgeon to advise on the difficult operation. Younger doctors listened carefully because she had solved cases others would not touch.
An eminent historian can change how people understand a famous battle. When Professor Shah found new letters, museums rewrote their display labels.
entries.spellingNote: em + in + ent.
